units.la: Viro admodum Reverendo ac clarissimo Domino JOHANNI MELLETO. Serenissimæ ac Celsissimæ Dominæ Principis Colignio-wirtembergicæ Concionatori fidelissimo, simulque Ecclesiæ Reformatæ Sanct Marianæ in Alsatia, pastori primario vigilantissimo, Domino fratri ac Symmystæ, in Christo plurimùm colendo,
units.tr: To the most reverend and most distinguished man, Mr. JOHN MELLET, most faithful preacher to the most serene and most exalted Princess of Coligny-Württemberg, and at the same time the most watchful chief minister of the Reformed Church of St. Mary in Alsace, my brother and fellow initiate, whom I greatly cherish in Christ,

units.la: Salutem à fonte Salutis!
units.tr: Greetings from the fountain of salvation!

units.la: Redit ad te, Vir admodum Reveren-de & Clarissime, quam jam ab aliquot annis a tua humanitate lætissi-mus impetravi THEOSOPHIA NATURALIS, cuius semina ante quinquennium præterpropter Basi-leæ publici iuris fieri voluere qui nos amant: Sed redit ad te, alio habitu induinduta, non literis expressa sed typis impressa : Cur autem hoc egerim, non est quòd multis rationibus id exponam, omnium instar mihi una erit, operis huiusce sublimitas dignitas & utilitas maxima, ita ut publico subtrahi bona fide vix potuerit: Adhæc singulari tuo ac veré fraterno erga me affectu fretus, non potui quin multorum votis hoc à me efflagitantibus satisfactum irem. Accipe igitur quod tuum est, & curam meam æqui boniq; consulas,oro de cætero, negotium vestrum Irenicum per Scriptorum congruè institutam Communicationem plurimis maximè probari lubens accipio,orandum & laborandum ; Quamvis vero benignissimus Deus laboribus pacificorum hacte-nusita non benedixerit, ut aurea pax Ecclesiæ fuerit restituta, existimandum tamen non est Deum omnem
units.tr: Most reverend and most distinguished sir, the THEOSOPHIA NATURALIS, which I have had the great pleasure of receiving from your kindness for some years now, comes back to you. The seeds of it, as those who love us wished, were made public at Basel about five years ago. But it returns to you dressed in another guise, not expressed in writing but printed in type. As to why I have done this, I need not explain at length with many reasons; one will serve in place of all: the lofty worth, dignity and very great usefulness of this work, so that in good faith it could hardly be withheld from the public. Moreover, relying on your singular and truly brotherly affection towards me, I could not help granting what many people were insistently asking of me. Accept, then, what is yours, and kindly consider my labour fair and good. I beg you, for the future, to think highly of your peacemaking enterprise, which I gladly welcome as being approved by most people through a properly established exchange of writings; it must be prayed for and worked at. Although the most gracious God has not yet blessed the labours of peacemakers so that the golden peace of the Church should be restored, we ought not to think that God will withhold his help from us for ever. There are twelve hours in the day, but at what hour the Lord will choose to act we do not know. Go on, then, honoured sir, in the way you have begun, since your most serene lady, the Princess of Württemberg, has allowed me to read again and again, with the greatest pleasure, your marvellous art of conjugation. We also hope that you will shortly grant it to the public. Meanwhile, farewell, honoured sir, with the reverend Mr. Mimard and Mr. de Blair, together with your most distinguished deacons and elders, my dearest brethren. I commend you all, each one, to God in my prayers, and myself to him and to you, continually. Given at Prati Puri, 1 May, in the year of Christ 1662.

units.la: JOHANNIS MELLET. Theosophiae Naturalis praecognita.
units.tr: JOHANNES MELLET. Preliminaries of Natural Theosophy.

units.la: Theosophia naturalis est disciplina de Deo, ex Lumine naturae, cognoscendo & colendo.
units.tr: Natural theosophy is the discipline concerning God, to be known and worshipped from the light of nature.

units.la: I. Disciplina cum sit, erit methodi-cum homogeneorum praeceptorum Systema.
units.tr: I. Since it is a discipline, it will be a systematic whole of homogeneous precepts arranged by method.

units.la: II. Theosophiae naturalis videnda est Praecognitio & Recognitio ; Illa explicat Theosophiae principium ; Haec ipsum corpus & Systema.
units.tr: II. Two parts of natural theosophy must be considered: the preliminary knowledge and the review. The former explains the principle of theosophy; the latter is the body and system itself.

units.la: III. Principium Theosophiae naturalis est duplex, Experientia & Recta-Ratio.
units.tr: III. The principle of natural theosophy is twofold: experience and right reason.

units.la: IV. Experientia est congruum & universale sensuum testimonium, seu est constans omnium rerum in mundo existen-tium consensus, hanc qui negat, se animal esse negat.
units.tr: IV. Experience is the agreeing and universal testimony of the senses, or the constant consensus of all things existing in the world. Whoever denies this denies that he is an animal.

units.la: V. Recta-Ratio est congruum & universale humanarum facultatum testimonium, seu est naturalis humanarum facultatum in verum, honestum & utile inclinatio : Cujus regula est, omne intelligibile, volibile & possibile, seu omne id quod est intellectui, voluntati & facultati executivæ congruè applicatæ congruum, est concedendum ; Hanc qui negat, se esse hominem negat.
units.tr: V. Right reason is the agreeing and universal testimony of the human faculties, or the natural inclination of the human faculties toward the true, the honourable and the useful. Its rule is this: whatever is intelligible, desirable and possible, that is, whatever is suitably applied to the intellect, the will and the executive faculty, is to be granted. Whoever denies this denies that he is a human being.

units.la: VI. Principia experientiā & recta Ratione nixa sunt efficacissima & utilissima in Summis etiam mysteriis cognoscendis, & vere insaniunt qui eorum usum in Theologia rident.
units.tr: VI. The principles founded on experience and right reason are most effective and most useful even for knowing the highest mysteries, and those who mock their use in theology are truly insane.

units.la: VII. Theosophiæ partes duæ sunt, prior de Deo cognoscendo, posterior de eodem colendo.
units.tr: VII. Theosophy has two parts: the first concerns knowing God, the second concerns worshipping the same God.

units.la: CAPUT PRIMUM. De Dei definitione & consideratione varia.
units.tr: CAPUT PRIMUM. Of the definition of God and his various aspects.

units.la: DEus[?] est Ens primum infinitæ perfectionis, seu est Ens omni modo gradu (adeoq; essentia, subsistentia & efficacia) perfectissimum, unde eo perfectius nec esse nec concipi potest.
units.tr: God is the First Being of infinite perfection, or is the Being most perfect in every respect (and so in essence, subsistence and efficacy), so that nothing more perfect can be or be conceived.

units.la: I. Cùm sit infinitum ens, infinitæ potè-runt eius descriptiones dari, satius tamen est eam primo adhibere quam omnes sanę mentis præditi sine dubitatione admittunt.
units.tr: I. Since he is an infinite being, infinite descriptions of him could be given; yet it is better to employ first that one which all people of sound mind admit without doubt.

units.la: II. Deus seu ens primum considerandum est absolute vel relate: Ibi in se, hîc quoad cætera entia spectari debet.
units.tr: II. God, or the First Being, must be considered either absolutely or relatively: the former looks at him in himself, the latter as regards other beings.

units.la: III. Consideratio Dei absoluta expendit primo quod sit, deinde quid sit; illa perpendit Existentiam, hæc Essentiam; licet hæc duo in Deo reipsa non distinguantur, tamen ratione utiliter & necessario.
units.tr: III. The absolute consideration of God examines first that he is, then what he is; the former weighs his existence, the latter his essence. Although these two are not really distinguished in God, they are usefully and necessarily distinguished by reason.

units.la: CAP. II. De Existentia Dei ex argu-mentis generalibus.
units.tr: CAP. II. On the Existence of God from General Arguments.

units.la: Existentia Dei demonstratur argumentis ge-neralibus vel specialibus.
units.tr: The existence of God is demonstrated by general or special arguments.

units.la: Argumenta generalia sunt quæ ex primorum terminorum combinatione fluunt; adeoque à cuiuslibet entis perfectione desumi possunt. Hæc demonstratio respectu intellectus nostri potest dici à priori. Hic observa aliud esse simpliciter demonstrare Deum, aliud, hoc vel illud ens esse Deum, non vero Angelum, cœlum aut simile aliud: Prior demonstratio utpote generalior debet præcedere.
units.tr: General arguments are those that flow from the combination of the first terms; they can therefore be drawn from the perfection of any being whatever. This demonstration can be called a priori with respect to our understanding. Here observe that it is one thing simply to demonstrate God, and another to show that this or that being is God and not an angel, heaven, or something similar. The former demonstration, being more general, must come first.

units.la: Argumenta generalia possunt peti à tribus primis terminis generalissimis, Est, Modus & Gradus.
units.tr: General arguments can be drawn from the three most general first terms, Est, Modus, and Gradus.

units.la: I. Ex termino Est, sic demonstratur esse Deum.
units.tr: I. From the term Est, God's existence is demonstrated thus.

units.la: Aut aliquid est in rerum natura, aut plane nihil est.
units.tr: Either something is in the nature of things, or plainly nothing is.

units.la: 1. Si plane nihil est in rerum natura, neq; nos qui hæc cogitamus, sumus, aut plane insanimus um quoad sensus, tum quoad rationem; At si in-fanimus, sumus. Ergo aliquid est in rerum natura.
units.tr: 1. If plainly nothing is in the nature of things, then neither we who think these things exist, or we are plainly insane, both as regards the senses and as regards reason. But if we are insane, we exist. Therefore something is in the nature of things.

units.la: 2. Si est aliquid in rerum natura, aut tantum unum est in rerum natura, aut plura sunt.
units.tr: 2. If something is in the nature of things, either only one thing is in the nature of things, or there are several.

units.la: a. Si tantum est ens unum, illud aut est factum aut non est factum. Si est ens non factum ubique Deus est, nam ens non factum vocamus Deum. Si vero illud ens unum est factum, fecit seipsum, nam aliud non est. At stultum imo stultissimum & absurdissimum est quod aliquid faciat seipsum, nam quod facit aliquid, illud est, quod fit, illud antequam fiat non est, Ergo quod facit seipsum, illud simul est & non est.
units.tr: a. If only one being exists, it either has been made or has not been made. If it is an unmade being, then God is everywhere, for we call an unmade being God. But if that single being has been made, it made itself, for there is no other. Yet it is foolish, indeed most foolish and most absurd, that something should make itself, for what makes something is, while what is made, before it is made, is not. Therefore what makes itself both is and is not at the same time.

units.la: b. Si vero sunt plura entia in rerum natura, aut omnia sunt non facta, aut omnia facta, aut quædam sunt facta ac quædam non facta: Si omnia sunt non facta, omnia sunt Deus, est ergo Deus: Si quædam sunt non facta, iterum est. Si vero omnia sunt facta quia seipsa fecerunt, fuerunt antequam fuerunt, quod absurdum & ἀπροσδύνατον[?].
units.tr: b. But if there are several beings in the nature of things, either all are unmade, or all are made, or some are made and some unmade. If all are unmade, all are God, so God exists. If some are unmade, again God exists. But if all are made, because they made themselves, they existed before they existed, which is absurd and impossible [ἀδύνατον].

units.la: c. Breviter itaque, id quod est, aut est factum, aut non factum; At non omnia possunt esse facta, nam quodquid fit, fit ab alio; Ergo id a quo factum est, aut est factum, aut non est factum.
units.tr: c. In short, then, what exists is either made or unmade. But not all things can be made, for whatever is made is made by another. Therefore that by which it was made is either made or unmade.

units.la: Si non est factum, Deus est.
units.tr: If it is not made, God exists.

units.la: Si vero id a quo est factum , factum est , factum est ab alio ; Ergo tandem aut perveniendum erit ad aliquod non factum , aut procedendum in infinitum , aut circulus committendus ; At utrumque est absurdum . Nam processus in infinitum non est in causis subordinatis , Ergo est aliqua causa prima non facta ; Ergo est Deus ; Aut si non est aliqua causa prima , nulla est causalitas , Ergo nihil est factum .
units.tr: But if that by which it was made was itself made, then it was made by another. Therefore we must in the end arrive at something unmade, or proceed to infinity, or fall into a circle; but each of these is absurd. For a process to infinity does not occur among subordinate causes. Therefore there is some first cause that is unmade; therefore God exists. Or if there is no first cause, there is no causality, and therefore nothing has been made.

units.la: Circulus autem & processus in infinitum in causis subordinatis & coordinatis non datur ; haec producit illam, illa aliam, alia primam vel mediate vel immediate ; Ergo vel tota illa collectio subordinatorum aut coordinatorum est facta vel non facta, Si est non facta, est ergo Deus ; Si tota est facta, ergo aut non est tota omnium entium collectio, aut taliquid[?] fecit seipsum , utrumque est absurdum .
units.tr: A circle, however, and a process to infinity, do not occur among subordinate and coordinate causes; one thing produces another, that another, and another the first, either mediately or immediately. Therefore either that whole collection of subordinate or coordinate causes was made or was not made. If it was not made, God exists. If the whole was made, then either there is no whole collection of all beings, or something made itself; both are absurd.

units.la: II. Ex Modis Entis intimis sic demonstratur esse Deum.
units.tr: II. From the inner Modes of Being, God's existence is demonstrated thus.

units.la: Omne ens est unum , verum , bonum , & sic deinceps per omnes entis modos ; Ergo aut est perfectissime unum ens , verum , bonum , aut non est tale ens .
units.tr: Every being is one, true, good, and so on through all the modes of being. Therefore it is either most perfectly one, true, and good, or it is not such a being.

units.la: Si est tale ens , utique Deus est , nam tale ens vocamus Deum . Si non est tale ens, non perfectè bonum est melius ente perfectè bono, ens non perfectè perfectum est perfectius ente perfectè perfecto, & sic deinceps, nam id quod est, perfectius est eo quod non est ; At prius est absurdum.
units.tr: If it is such a being, then certainly God exists, for we call such a being God. If it is not such a being, then what is not perfectly good is less good than what is perfectly good, and what is not perfectly perfect is less perfect than what is perfectly perfect, and so on; for that which is, is more perfect than that which is not. But the former is absurd.

units.la: III. Ex Gradibus Entium sic demonstratur esse Deum.
units.tr: III. From the Degrees of Beings, God's existence is demonstrated thus.

units.la: Omne ens est unum, verum, bonum, Ergo aut est ens summè unum, verum, bonum, aut non est tantum.
units.tr: Every being is one, true, and good. Therefore either it is a being that is supremely one, true, and good, or it is not merely a being.

units.la: Si est tantum ens, utique Deus est, nam tantum ens vocamus Deum.
units.tr: If it is merely a being, then certainly God exists, for we call a mere being God.

units.la: Si non est tantum ens, ens minùs bonum est me-lius optimo, adeoque pars melior toto, nam id quod est, melius est eo, quod non est : Ergo est ens summè unum, verum, bonum, id est, Deus.
units.tr: If it is not merely a being, then a being that is less good is inferior to the best, and so a part is better than the whole, for that which is, is better than that which is not. Therefore there is a being that is supremely one, true, and good, that is, God.

units.la: CAP. III. De Existentia Dei ex argu-mentis specialibus.
units.tr: CAP. III. On the Existence of God from Special Arguments.

units.la: Argumenta specialia quibus Existentia Dei demonstratur sunt illa quæ à rerum creatarum constitutione petuntur, adeoque aspe-ciali terminorū combinatione oriuntur: Hæc rectè dicūtur à posteriori, quia semper ab esse-ctis [?]ctis ad causas ascendunt. Duo autem in his argumentis maxime sunt observanda; primo ut sint clarissima, ipsaq; quæstione demonstrandâ notiora; deinde ut sint firmissima, nullâque instantiâ eludi queant. Ob primum requisitum, alia aliis personis congruunt, sic homines plebei sunt convincendi ex rebus testatissimis non dubiis aut obscuris.
units.tr: The special arguments by which the existence of God is demonstrated are those drawn from the constitution of created things, and so arising from a particular combination of terms. They are rightly called a posteriori, because they always ascend from effects to causes. In these arguments two things above all must be observed. First, they should be very clear and better known than the question itself that is to be demonstrated. Second, they should be very firm and not be evaded by any counter-instance. Because of the first requirement, different arguments suit different people; thus common folk are to be convinced from the most attested facts, not from doubtful or obscure ones.

units.la: I. Argumenta specialia sumuntur vel à tota rerum universitate, vel ab ejus partibus infignioribus: illa sunt à Macrocosmo hæc à Microcosmo desumenda: possunt quidem à singulis rebus creatis sumi argumenta, nam quot sunt creaturæ, tot sunt argumenta Existentiæ Divinæ, verum ob evidentiam, hæc sunt præferenda.
units.tr: I. Special arguments are taken either from the whole universe of things or from its more prominent parts. The former are to be drawn from the Macrocosm, the latter from the Microcosm. Arguments may indeed be taken from single created things, for as many as there are creatures, so many are the arguments for the existence of the Divine; but on account of their evidence, the former are to be preferred.

units.la: II. Ex Macrocosmo sic demonstratur esse Deum.
units.tr: II. From the Macrocosm God is demonstrated to exist in this way.

units.la: In Macrocosmo aut nullus est ordo & harmonia, aut aliquis est ordo & harmonia.
units.tr: In the Macrocosm there is either no order and harmony, or there is some order and harmony.

units.la: Si nullus est ordo & harmonia, omnia erunt frustra & sunt casu & incongrue, at hoc repugnat experientiæ & rationi, quæ omnium rerum subordinationem vel coordinationem manifeste docet.
units.tr: If there is no order and harmony, all things will be in vain, and will be by chance and without fitness; but this contradicts experience and reason, which plainly teach the subordination and coordination of all things.

units.la: Si vero est harmonia & ordo in universo, necessaria quoque erit ordinans universale; Si est ordinans universale, utiq; illud habet scientiam, voluntatem ac potentiam omnia ordinandi. Erit ergo ens perfectissimum, id est, Deus.
units.tr: But if there is harmony and order in the universe, there must also be a universal orderer; and if there is a universal orderer, he surely has the knowledge, will and power to order all things. He will therefore be the most perfect being, that is, God.

units.la: Explicatur & amplificatur hæc demonstratio, si proponatur Logicè, ostendaturque neque Exemplarem, neque Efficientem, neque Finalem rerum causam esse in rerum natura, si nō sit Deus.
units.tr: This demonstration is explained and amplified if it is set out logically, and it is shown that, if there is no God, there is in the nature of things neither an exemplary, nor an efficient, nor a final cause of things.

units.la: III. Ex Macrocosmi partibus demonstratur esse Deum, sive singula absoluta, in se, sive cum aliis collata spectentur. Hinc oritur scala naturæ, per quam ascendit ad Deum & perpendit ejus Modum & Gradum.
units.tr: III. From the parts of the Macrocosm God is demonstrated to exist, whether single things are considered in themselves or compared with one another. Hence arises the ladder of nature, by which one ascends to God and weighs his manner and degree.

units.la: IV. Ex Macrocosmi partibus clarissima & efficacissima argumenta suppeditat homo: Sic enim ex natura hominis demonstratur esse Deum.
units.tr: IV. From the parts of the Macrocosm, man supplies the clearest and most effective arguments. For thus from the nature of man God is demonstrated to exist.

units.la: Si non est Deus, homo est animal, imò corpus imperfectissimum, absurdum est consequens, ut patet ex definitione hominis, quod sit animal rationale: connexum probatur per partes:
units.tr: If there is no God, man is an animal, indeed the most imperfect of bodies; the consequence is absurd, as is plain from the definition of man, that he is a rational animal. The connection is proved part by part:

units.la: 1. Primum argumentum sumitur ab ipsius Intellectu. Si nullus est Deus, homo est animal stultissimum, ratio quia stultus est, qui eum[?] qui non est, timet: At homo timet; conscientiæ enim enim natur etiam 2. minis Sitio, q scient tam, q impo 3 nisfa Simum libus, teft, alia, moen & ea De H enim ac divinitatis sensus omnibus hominibus natura est insitus : Et si homo est stultissimum est etiam imperfectissimum animal.
units.tr: 1. The first argument is taken from man's understanding. If there is no God, man is the most foolish animal, for he is foolish who fears what does not exist; but man fears, for conscience trembles at the thought of a judge, and the sense of God and of divinity is implanted by nature in all men. And if man is the most foolish, he is also the most imperfect animal.

units.la: 2. Secundum Argumentum sumitur ab hominis appetitu seu voluntate.
units.tr: 2. The second argument is taken from man's appetite or will.

units.la: Si non est Deus homo, est animal pessimum, ratio, quia appetit incongruentissima, appetit enim scientiam, honestatem ac potestatem talem ac tantam, quae sine Deo esse nequit. Et quae plane sunt impossibilia, ea quoque sunt incongrua.
units.tr: If there is no God, man is the most wretched animal, the reason being that he desires the most incongruous things; for he desires knowledge, goodness and power of such a kind and size that they cannot exist without God. And things that are plainly impossible are also incongruous.

units.la: 3. Tertium argumentum sumitur ab homi-nis facultate executiva, adeoque ejus statu.
units.tr: 3. The third argument is taken from man's executive faculty, and so from his condition.

units.la: Si non est Deus, homo est animal infœlicissi-mum, ratio, quia appetit inutilia, neglectis uti-libus, imo appetit ea quae asse qui nusquam po-test, dein probatur, quia magis appetit spiritu-alia, æterna, uno verbo, ea quae Deo, id est, sum-mo entisunt vicinora, quam corporalia, caduca, & ea quae huius sunt generis.
units.tr: If there is no God, man is the most unhappy animal, the reason being that he desires useless things and neglects useful ones; indeed he desires what he can never attain. It is then proved that he desires spiritual and eternal things more, in a word, those things which are nearer to God, that is, the highest being, than corporeal and perishable things and those of that kind.

units.la: CAP. IV. De Fundamentis Atheismi evertendi.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV. On Overturning the Foundations of Atheism.

units.la: Hactenus de argumentis Existentiæ Dei, se-quitur ut præcipua etiam Atheorum argumenta solvamus, idque duabus de causis, tum ut iis, os obthuretur, tum ut tentatæ conscientiæ sese extricare possint.
units.tr: Having so far treated the arguments for the existence of God, it follows that we should also resolve the chief arguments of the atheists, for two reasons: first, so that their mouths may be stopped, and second, so that tempted consciences may be able to extricate themselves.

units.la: Fundamenta Atheorum sunt generalia vel specialia, illa oriuntur ex terminorum generalium combinatione, hæc ex speciali rerum constitutione. Quamvis primæ primorum terminorum combinationes sint evidentissimæ, attamen ob ipsarum altitudinem, & latitudinem, suamque incapacitatem, sæpius in iis hæret mens humana; quam perplexitatem arripiunt hi insani homines.
units.tr: The foundations of the atheists are either general or special. The former arise from the combination of general terms, the latter from the particular constitution of things. Although the first combinations of the first terms are most evident, nevertheless, on account of their height and breadth and the mind's own incapacity, the human mind often sticks fast in them; and these mad men seize upon this perplexity.

units.la: Observentur itaque Theoremata sequen-tia;
units.tr: Let the following theorems therefore be observed:

units.la: I. Etsi finitæ menti sit incomprehensibile, quomodo aliquodens negative sit à se ipso, id est, prorsus non sit ab alio, attamen omnia principia eam cogunt, ut firmissime statuat quod sit aliquodens tale; nam ipsa mens humana clarissime videt quod debeat afferere aliqua sibi incomprehensibilia. Hoc principium usum habet summum in summis mysteriis.
units.tr: I. Although it is incomprehensible to a finite mind how something should exist negatively from itself, that is, not at all from another, yet all principles compel it to hold most firmly that there is something of this kind; for the human mind itself sees most clearly that it must affirm some things that are incomprehensible to it. This principle has its greatest use in the greatest mysteries.

units.la: II Etsi non repugnet processus in infinitum ex parte principiatorum, repugnat tamen ex parte principiorum, ille enim nunquam absolvitur, at hic absolutus præsupponitur, si ex eo oriri aliquid debeat: Nec in causis per accidens potest habere locum, quia omnis causa per accidens necessario reducitur ad causam per se.
units.tr: II. Although an infinite process is not repugnant on the side of the things caused, it is repugnant on the side of the causes: the former never reaches an end, whereas the latter is presupposed as complete if anything is to arise from it. Nor can it take place among accidental causes, because every accidental cause is necessarily reduced to a cause per se.

units.la: III. Cùm omnis effectus praesupponat causam suam, id est, sibi proportionalem, etsi non repugnet circulus causarum finitus, quo aliqua se mutuò producunt vel conservant, ita tamen ut aliqua causa superior illam coordinationem instituerit, repugnat tamen circulus causarum infinitus, quo nulla causa agnoscitur praeter coordinatam.
units.tr: III. Since every effect presupposes its cause, that is, one proportionate to it, a finite circle of causes, by which some things mutually produce or preserve one another, is not repugnant, provided that some higher cause has established that coordination; but an infinite circle of causes, in which no cause is recognized except those coordinated, is repugnant.

units.la: IV. Etsi de illo principio, esse est melius quam non esse, non sequitur quod necessario in rerum natura existant omnes possibiles entitatis modi & gradus, necessario tamen ex illo sequitur quòd perfectissimus entitatis modus & gradus necessario sit in rerum natura; Nam ob perfectissimi modi & gradûs existentiam non est necessaria existentia modorum ac graduum non perfectissimorum.
units.tr: IV. Although from the principle that it is better to be than not to be it does not follow that all possible modes and degrees of being necessarily exist in the nature of things, it does necessarily follow from it that the most perfect mode and degree of being necessarily exists in the nature of things; for, given the existence of the most perfect mode and degree, the existence of the less perfect modes and degrees is not necessary.

units.la: V. Licet in rerum creatarum constitutione, primâ fronte videantur aliqua occurrere quae perfectioni divinae repugnent, tamen re accuratius perpensâ, & divinis attributis inter se collatis, omnis difficultas evanescit: Nam attributa divina se mutuò explicant probant ac amplificant, exempli gratiâ, peccata in mundo non tollunt divinam bonitatem ob divinam sapientiam ac potentiam. Sunt autem diuina attributa universa naturæ radices, omnium & scientiæ, adeoq; totius Encyclopædiæ claves.
units.tr: V. Although in the constitution of created things some things may at first sight seem to conflict with the divine perfection, nevertheless, when the matter is weighed more accurately and the divine attributes are compared with one another, every difficulty vanishes. For the divine attributes explain, prove and amplify one another; for example, sins in the world do not remove the divine goodness, on account of the divine wisdom and power. Moreover, the divine attributes are the roots of all nature, the keys of all knowledge and thus of the whole encyclopaedia.

units.la: VI Ordo & harmonia universi consideratur vel imperfectè, immediatè respectu partium tantum & causarum secundarum; vel perfectè, mediatè & respectu totius, adeoq; ratione causarum superiorum; Priori modo aliqua apparet confusio & discordantia in rerum natura, posteriori nulla, quia defectus causarum inferiorum compensatur effectu ac perfectione superiorum: Sic licet inanimata non cognoscant finem, cognoscit tamen author naturæ, sicut sagittæ scopum cognoscit sagittarius.
units.tr: VI. The order and harmony of the universe may be considered either imperfectly, immediately, with respect to the parts only and the secondary causes; or perfectly, mediately, and with respect to the whole, and thus in view of the higher causes. In the former way some confusion and discord appears in the nature of things; in the latter, none, because the defect of the lower causes is compensated by the effect and perfection of the higher. So, although inanimate things do not know their end, the author of nature knows it, just as the archer knows the mark of his arrow.

units.la: VII. Licet consuetudo diuturna possit plurimum in humano genere, attamen nisi Deus esset, nulla tenus humanæ facultates in ea objecta, eo modo & gradu inclinarentur vel inclinari possent, prout experientia eas inclinari demonstrat; Esset enim illa consuetudo ipsorum plane contraria.
units.tr: VII. Although long-standing custom can have great force in the human race, nevertheless, were there no God, the human faculties could in no way be inclined, or be capable of being inclined, toward those objects in the manner and degree in which experience shows that they are inclined; for that custom would be wholly contrary to their nature.

units.la: VIII. Licet quidam de Deo dubitarint, quidam etiam ipsum negarint, id tamen potius ex voluntatis malitia, quàm intellectus ignorantia profectum est, nisi forsan subtilis quaedam insania fuerit, Quamvis multorum conscientia errret circa conclusiones practicas, nunquam tamen errat circa principia prima practica: Ac licet sceleratissimorum hominum conscientia aliquandiu stertat, nunquam tamen extinguitur, quamcunq; vim sibi faciant.
units.tr: VIII. Although some have doubted concerning God, and some have even denied him, this has arisen from the malice of the will rather than from the ignorance of the intellect, unless perhaps it is some subtle kind of madness. Although the conscience of many may err concerning practical conclusions, it never errs concerning the first practical principles; and although the conscience of the most wicked men may slumber for a while, it is never extinguished, however much they do violence to it.

units.la: CAP. V. De modo inve[?]niendi naturam Dei.
units.tr: CHAPTER V. On the method of discovering the nature of God.

units.la: Hactenus de Existentia Dei, sequitur ut agamus de ipsius Essentia.
units.tr: So far, concerning the existence of God. It follows that we should treat of his essence.

units.la: I. Essentia Dei quia est infinita, erit incomprehensibilis creaturae finitae: attamen quia est perfectissima erit maxime sua natura intelligibilis, cum esse sit primum ac proprium intellectus obiectum.
units.tr: I. Because the essence of God is infinite, it will be incomprehensible to a finite creature. Yet because it is most perfect, it will be most intelligible in its own nature, since being is the first and proper object of the intellect.

units.la: II. Essentia Dei cognoscitur Lumine naturae, gratiae & gloriae, de his tractant Theologi de illo Philosophi. Nos itaque lumine naturae divinam essentiam, existentiam investigatu-ri, ri, quædam præmittemus præcognita de fun-damento & modo, quâ nimirum ratione Philosophus eam cognoscere possit.
units.tr: II. The essence of God is known by the light of nature, grace and glory. Theologians treat of the last two, philosophers of the first. We, therefore, are about to investigate the divine essence and existence by the light of nature, and first we will set out some preliminary points concerning the foundation and the mode, namely by what method the philosopher can come to know it.

units.la: III. Fundamentum naturaliter cognoscendi Deum est triplex, nimirum Panharmonia re-rum, Divina Sufficientia & Efficientia.
units.tr: III. The foundation for knowing God naturally is threefold, namely the panharmony of things, divine sufficiency and efficiency.

units.la: IV. Panharmonia rerū est, qua omnia entia realia veram & intrinsecam convenientiam inter se habent, ita ut mens creata ab uno possit ordinatè discurrere ad aliud. Hæc conveni-entia nec est æquivoca[?], seu Deus vel res creatæ non vera entia[?], nec univoca, sed [?] eadem æqualia[?], sed analoga, id est, realis quidem, sed non æqualis consistit, consistit autem in primis ac communissimis termi-nis.
units.tr: IV. The panharmony of things is that by which all real beings have a true and intrinsic agreement with one another, so that a created mind can pass in an orderly way from one to another. This agreement is neither equivocal (as if God or created things were not true beings), nor univocal (as if they were the same and equal), but analogous: it is real, yet not equal, and it consists in the first and most common terms.

units.la: V. Divina Sufficientia est quâ ipse omni modo & gradu est perfectissimus : Hinc sequitur omnem omnino imperfectionem ab ipso removendam, & omnem omnino perfectionem ipsi tribuendam esse.
units.tr: V. Divine sufficiency is that by which he is most perfect in every way and in every degree. Hence it follows that every imperfection must be wholly removed from him, and every perfection wholly ascribed to him.

units.la: VI. Divina Efficientia est quâ Deus omnes perfectiones omnibus & singulis creaturis communicat, at nihil potest alii dare quod non habeat, vel æquipollenti vel eminenti modo.
units.tr: VI. Divine efficiency is that by which God communicates all perfections to all and each of the creatures. But he can give to another nothing that he does not have, either equivalently or in an eminent way.

units.la: VII. Sic fuit fundamentum cognitionis Dei naturalis, sequitur modus qui consideratur in genere & in specie.
units.tr: VII. Thus was the foundation of natural knowledge of God. There follows the mode, which is considered in general and in particular.

units.la: VIII. Modus cognoscendi naturam Dei in genere fundatur in panharmonia omnium entium, quâ entia omnia, essentias modos ac gradus sibi similes, adeoq; à mente huma-na inter se conferri possunt. Hæc collatio est clavis omnium notificationum, nam mens non solum a pari ad par, sed etiam a simili ad simile, a minori ad majus, item a dissimili uno ad dissimile alterum discurrere potest, vi illius principii catholici, quatenus[?] in tertio conveniunt, ac prout in illo tertio conveniunt, vel non conveni-unt, ita quoq; inter se.
units.tr: VIII. The mode of knowing the nature of God in general is grounded in the panharmony of all beings, by which all beings, with their essences, modes and degrees, are similar to one another and so can be compared with one another by the human mind. This comparison is the key to all knowledge. For the mind can reason not only from equal to equal, but also from like to like, from lesser to greater, and likewise from one unlike thing to another unlike thing, by virtue of that catholic principle: insofar as things agree in a third thing, and as they agree or do not agree in that third thing, so also they agree or do not agree with one another.

units.la: IX. Modus cognoscendi Deum in specie est via negationis, eminentia & causalitatis.
units.tr: IX. The mode of knowing God in particular is the way of negation, of eminence and of causality.

units.la: X. Via Negationis est qua omnes creaturarum imperfectiones a Deo removentur: Hæc via est omnium facillima ac tutissima, quia facilius ac edoctius scitur[?] quid non sit res, quam quid sit, nam ex combinatione negationum tandem differentia rei cognoscitur; Hinc pleraq; Dei attributa unt negativa; Ejusq; regula est, percurre omnes creaturarum imperfectiones, easq; de Deo remove. Hæc progreditur a minori ad majus, ideoque vel ascenascendit à specialibus ad generalia, vel descendit à generalibus ad specialia. Prior modus sic se habet, Deus non est homo, nec animal, nec corpus vivum, nec mixtum, ergo nec ipsorum imperfectiones habet: Posteriorita[?], Deus non est corpus, Ergo nec mixtum, nec vivum, &c. Solent autem attributa Dei negativè prius desumi a remotione imperfectionum generalium.
units.tr: X. The way of negation is that by which all imperfections of creatures are removed from God. This way is the easiest and safest of all, because it is more easily and more readily known what a thing is not than what it is; for from the combination of negations the difference of a thing is at last known. Hence most of the attributes of God are negative. Its rule is: run through all the imperfections of creatures and remove them from God. This proceeds from lesser to greater, and so either ascends from particulars to generals, or descends from generals to particulars. The former runs thus: God is not man, nor animal, nor living body, nor compound; therefore he has none of their imperfections. The latter: God is not a body; therefore neither compound, nor living, etc. Moreover, the attributes of God are usually taken first, negatively, from the removal of the general imperfections.

units.la: XI. Via Eminentia est qua omnes Creaturarum perfectiones, Deo in summo gradu attribuuntur: perfectiones Creaturarum sunt duplices, aliæ dicunt perfectionem sine imperfectione, & hæ primo competunt Deo, secundario creaturis, ut Intellectus, Voluntas & Potentia Executiva, earumq; dotes; aliæ vero dicunt perfectionem cum imperfectione mixtam, quæ Creaturis competunt proprie, Deo tantum tropice, ut Lux, Firmitas, Sensus, & hæ per viam negationis sunt purgandæ[?]: Hæc autem Theologis nostris commendamus, nam in Jobo, Psalmis & Prophetis, sed maxime in Jobo est frequentissima hæc scala.
units.tr: XI. The way of eminence is that by which all perfections of creatures are attributed to God in the highest degree. The perfections of creatures are twofold. Some are perfection without imperfection, and these belong to God primarily and to creatures secondarily, such as intellect, will and executive power and their endowments. Others are perfection mixed with imperfection, which belong properly to creatures and to God only tropically, such as light, firmness, sense; and these must be purged by the way of negation. We commend this to our theologians, for in Job, the Psalms and the Prophets, but most of all in Job, this ladder is very frequent.

units.la: XII. Via Cau[illegible, ~2 letters]latis est qua omnes Creaturarum tanquam Effectorum perfectiones tribuuntur Deo, ceu primæ & perfectissimæ causæ: Hæc vocatur demonstratio a posteriori quæ ab effectis ascendit ad causas. At-
units.tr: XII. The way of causality is that by which all perfections of creatures, as of effects, are attributed to God as the first and most perfect cause. This is called demonstration a posteriori, which ascends from effects to causes. At-

units.la: XIII. Atque haec est triplex scala perquam Philosophus a quolibet ente creato, ejusve modo & gradu potest ac debet, ad Deum adscendere; Cui utilissime additur demonstratio ab aequalibus, qua ab una adeoq; qualibet perfectione divina mens nostra deducitur ad quamlibet aliam, & haec est firmissima demonstratio. Nos autem imposterum vel omnes vel pleraque vias conjungemus, imprimis dabimus operam, ut ex eo quod sit Ens non factum adeo-q; ex primo termino Ens omnes demonstren-tur.
units.tr: XIII. And this is the threefold ladder by which a philosopher can and must ascend to God from any created being, or from its mode and degree. To this is most usefully added demonstration from equals, by which our mind is led from one divine perfection, or any one, to any other; and this is the firmest demonstration. We, however, will henceforth join all or most of the ways together; especially we will take pains to demonstrate all of them from the fact that God is an uncreated being, and so from the first term, Ens (being).

units.la: CAP. VI. De Demonstratione propri-etatum seu attributorum Dei quate-nus est Ens primum.
units.tr: CAP. VI. On the demonstration of the properties or attributes of God insofar as he is the First Being.

units.la: Sic se habent præcognita demonstrationis, se-quitur ipsa demonstratio, ubi observandum est duplicem posse adhiberi methodum, alia enim est via inventionis, alia Explicationis, illa est præmittenda huic, illa ostendit, quod sint attributa Dei, hæc quid sint: Proprietatis & attri-butinomen hic indifferenter usurpabitur,
units.tr: Such are the preliminaries of the demonstration. There follows the demonstration itself, and here it must be noted that two methods may be used. One is the way of discovery, the other of explication. The former is to be placed before the latter: the former shows that they are attributes of God, the latter what they are. The terms property and attribute will be used here interchangeably.

units.la: [illegible, ~4 letters] idq; ἀνθρωποπαθῶς, quod intelligendum Θεο-πρεπῶς
units.tr: [illegible] and this anthropopathically [ἀνθρωποπαθῶς], which is to be understood theoprepically [Θεοπρεπῶς].

units.la: I. Proprietates Dei sunt Attributa Dei es-sentialia, per qua Veritas ac Maiestas Essentia Divina a nobis concipitur, & ab aliis distinguitur, vel sunt, ipsa Dei Essentia per plures inadaquatos conceptus nobis repraesentata.
units.tr: I. The properties of God are essential attributes of God, through which the truth and majesty of the divine essence is conceived by us and distinguished from others, or they are the very essence of God represented to us through several inadequate concepts.

units.la: 1. Ab Essentia Dei realiter non distinguntur; Sunt enim ipsa essentia, & ipse Deus, quia, primo Essentia Dei per se & ex se est simplicissima, summe & infinite perfecta; Et dein, illae de essentia divina non in concreto solum, sed etiam in abstracto, idq; non tantum in casibus obliquis sed & rectis vere & proprie praedicantur: Deniq; si essent distinctae, singulae essent finitae vel infinitae; Si illud, ipsa etiam infinitas [?] foret finita quod ἀσύγγαλον [?]; Si hoc, tunc aliquid a Deo realiter distinctum foret infinitum, & sic, vel Deus per se non erit infinitus, vel plura erunt infinita, quae omnia sunt ἀπροσδιόνυσα [?].
units.tr: 1. They are not really distinct from the essence of God. For they are the essence itself and God himself, because first, the essence of God is in itself and from itself most simple, supremely and infinitely perfect; and then, those things are predicated of the divine essence truly and properly not only in the concrete but also in the abstract, and not only in the oblique cases but also in the nominative. Finally, if they were distinct, each would be either finite or infinite. If the former, the infinity itself would be finite, which [?]; if the latter, then something really distinct from God would be infinite, and so either God per se would not be infinite, or there would be several infinites, all of which are [?].

units.la: 2. Proprietates Dei a se invicem realiter non distinguuntur. In Deo enim non est ἄλλο ἢ ἄλλο, ob simplicissimam unitatem a qua omnis differentia realis abest; Deinde quaelibet est infinita non solum in perfectione alicuius generis, sed Simpliciter, in tota Latitudine entis;
units.tr: 2. The properties of God are not really distinct from one another. For in God there is not one thing and another thing, on account of the most simple unity from which all real difference is absent. Then each is infinite not only in the perfection of some kind, but simply, in the whole breadth of being.

units.la: 3. Proprietates Dei distinguuntur sola ratione; Tum propter infinitam & eminentissimam Dei perfectionem, simulq; finitudinem & angustiam nostri intellectus, qui tantum finita capit, unde unicam illam perfectionem, non unico, sed pluribus inadæquatis conceptibus apprehendit; Tum propter fundamentum quod reperitur, non quidem ἔσωθεν, & a parte rei, infe & realiter, sed [illegible, ~9 letters], Virtualiter, effectivè & obiectivè, ob scilicet diversas in diversis obiectis ἐνεργείας[?], licèt enim unica & simplicissima sit essentia & perfectio Divina, non tamen operatur secundùm adæquatam suam rationem.
units.tr: 3. The properties of God are distinguished by reason alone. This is partly because of the infinite and most eminent perfection of God, together with the finitude and narrowness of our intellect, which grasps only finite things; so it apprehends that single perfection not by one but by several inadequate concepts. It is partly because of the ground that is found, not indeed intrinsically and on the part of the thing, really, but [illegible], virtually, effectively and objectively, namely on account of the diverse energies [?] in diverse objects. For although the divine essence and perfection is one and most simple, it does not operate according to its adequate nature.

units.la: 4. Nullæ proprietates Dei possunt esse vel concipi creaturis formaliter communicabiles, quin implicetur aperta contradictio, & statuatur oppositum in apposito.
units.tr: 4. No properties of God can be, or be conceived to be, formally communicable to creatures without implying an open contradiction and positing the opposite in the same thing.

units.la: II. Proprietates seu Attributa Dei considerantur Sigillatim, vel Coniunctim.
units.tr: II. The properties or attributes of God are considered severally or jointly.

units.la: Illo modo competunt ei vel quatenus est Ens primum, vel quatenus est Spiritus.
units.tr: In the first way they belong to him either insofar as he is the First Being, or insofar as he is Spirit.

units.la: Qua Ens primum, ei competit Independentia, Simplicitas, Omnimoda perfectio, Infinitas, Immensitas, Æternitas, Incomprehensibili-tas, & Immutabilitas.
units.tr: As the First Being, there belong to him independence, simplicity, all-round perfection, infinity, immensity, eternity, incomprehensibility, and immutability.

units.la: III. Independentia est Dei Proprietas five Attributum per quod Essentia Divina à nobis concipitur, ut à nullo plane principio & causa dependens.
units.tr: III. Independence is a property or attribute of God through which the divine essence is conceived by us as depending on no principle and cause whatever.

units.la: Est enim prima causa efficiens & finalis in quam omnia resolvuntur : Demonstrat hoc ipsum ratio ; Si Deus est ens non factum, est prorsus independens, id est, nullatenus est ab alio cum imperfectione ; Nam quidquid ab alio dependet, id sit ab alio à quo dependet, quatenus nimirum ab illo dependet. Cum autem modus operandi sequatur modum essendi, etiam Deus in agendo & operando erit ἁπλῶς independens, licet, ex mera sua indulgentia, causis secundis utatur quandoq;
units.tr: For he is the first efficient and final cause into which all things are resolved. Reason itself demonstrates this: If God is a being not made, he is wholly independent, that is, in no way from another with imperfection; for whatever depends on another is from that on which it depends, insofar as it depends on it. Since the mode of operating follows the mode of being, God too in acting and working will be simply independent, although from his mere indulgence he sometimes uses secondary causes.

units.la: IV. Simplicitas est Dei proprietas sive attributum per quod Essentia Divina à nobis concipitur ut, omni modo & gradu, compositionis & componibilitatis carens.
units.tr: IV. Simplicity is a property or attribute of God through which the divine essence is conceived by us as lacking every mode and degree of composition and composability.

units.la: Hæc absoluta Dei simplicitas inde probatur quòd sit absolutè independens & perfectissimè unus ac idem, nihilq; sit in ipso quod non sit ipse : Et dein, Si Deus est ens non factum, est simpli-cissimus, nam si esset compositus, esset à compositione, & a componentibus foret ac dependeret, nec esset perfectissimus, quia penderet ab imperfectis, scilicet suis partibus: Negata autem compositione in genere, negantur quoque singulæ compositiones in specie, & quidem gradatim, negata compositione subtiliori, multo magis negantur crassiores. Quare Deus nec ex essentia & existentia, nec ex natura & suppositio, nec ex potentia & actu, nec ex substantia & accidente, nec ex partibus integrantibus, ne-de-nique [?] ex essentialibus materia & forma compositus est, sed prorsus indivisibilis, incorporeus. &c.
units.tr: This absolute simplicity of God is proved from the fact that he is absolutely independent and most perfectly one and the same, and there is nothing in him that is not himself. Further, if God is a being not made, he is most simple, for if he were composite, he would be from composition, and would be and depend on his components, nor would he be most perfect, because he would depend on imperfect things, namely his parts. Composition being denied in general, the single compositions in particular are denied too, and indeed by degrees: once a subtler composition is denied, the cruder ones are denied much more. Hence God is composed neither of essence and existence, nor of nature and supposit, nor of potency and act, nor of substance and accident, nor of integrating parts, nor finally of essential matter and form, but is wholly indivisible and incorporeal, etc.

units.la: V. Omnimoda perfectio est Dei attributum per quod essentia Divina a nobis concipitur ut omnimodo graduq, in se & a se perfectissima, ita ut nullatenus possit esse vel concipi ens perfectius.
units.tr: V. All-round perfection is the attribute of God through which the divine essence is conceived by us as in every way and degree most perfect in itself and from itself, so that no more perfect being can possibly be or be conceived.

units.la: Hanc Dei αὐτοτελεότητα [?], hoc pacto, demonstrat ratio, Si Deus est ens non factum sed negative a seipso, est ens perfectissimum, id est, ab omni imperfectione liberrimum, & omnis perfectionis plenissimum; nam si Deus non est perfectissimus, utiq; ab alio est ad certam perfectionem determinatus, Ergo & factus & dependens, & necessario melius esset ens minus perfectum quam perfectum, quia Deus est ens summe necessarium.
units.tr: Reason demonstrates this self-sufficiency [αὐτοτελεότης] of God in this way: If God is a being not made but, in the negative sense, from himself, he is the most perfect being, that is, most free from all imperfection and most full of all perfection; for if God is not most perfect, he is assuredly determined by another to a certain perfection, and therefore both made and dependent; and necessarily a less perfect being would be better than a perfect one, because God is a being supremely necessary.

units.la: Hinc denique patet quod omnes quæ in regno naturæ, gratiæ & gloriæ occurrunt perfectiones, suo modo in se contineat, vide cap. præcedens.
units.tr: Hence finally it is clear that he contains in his own way all the perfections that occur in the realm of nature, grace and glory; see the preceding chapter.

units.la: VI. Infinitas est Dei attributum sive proprietas per quam essentia Divina a nobis concipitur, ut omni termino atq; mensurâ carens. Ex omnimoda essentiæ Divinæ perfectione necessario fluit Dei infinitas, quæ nō est proprietas quâ ipse careat terminis debitis, vel non habeat certum suorum attributorum essentialem modum & gradum, sed est omnimoda perfectio, quâ ita omnes entitatis modos & gradus habet in se, ut nullo modo possit vel esse vel cogitari ens perfectius, sed ipse omnes possibiles entitatis gradus eminentissime in se continet. Unde infinita Dei essentia non tantum actu talis, in casu obliquo, sed & actus infinitus, in recto, dicenda est. Infinitas autem hæc respectu loci vocatur Immensitas, & respectu durationis, Æternitas, & denique respectu Intellectus cognoscentis, Incomprehensibilitas.
units.tr: VI. Infinity is an attribute or property of God through which the divine essence is conceived by us as lacking every boundary and measure. From the all-round perfection of the divine essence, the infinity of God necessarily flows. It is not a property by which he lacks due limits, or does not have a certain essential mode and degree of his attributes; rather it is all-round perfection, by which he has in himself all modes and degrees of being, so that no more perfect being can in any way be or be thought, but he himself eminently contains all possible degrees of being. Whence the infinite essence of God is to be called not only infinite in the oblique case, but infinite act in the nominative. This infinity is called immensity with respect to place, eternity with respect to duration, and finally incomprehensibility with respect to the knowing intellect.

units.la: VII. Immensitas est Dei attributum per quod Essentia Divina a nobis concipitur ut carens omni fine ac termino præsentia.
units.tr: VII. Immensity is an attribute of God through which the divine essence is conceived by us as lacking every end and limit of presence.

units.la: Si Deus est ens non factum est Immensus: imsus: Immensitas autem Dei nihil aliud est quā naturalis eius præsetia sine ullo fine aut termino, ita ut Divina Essentia sit sufficiens ad omnia spatia replenda, etiamsi in infinitum augerentur; est autem semper actu præsens sive hæc præ-sentia per ordinem ad loca realia, sive ad spatia imaginaria a nobis concipiatur ac declaretur: Nam si ita non esset Immensus, certum haberet suæ præsentiæ terminum, adeoque nec independens, nec infinitus, nec perfectissimus foret, sed ab aliquo determinate penderet. Unde necessario sequitur quòd Dei Essentia indivisibiliter & inextense sit tota in toto mundo, & tota in singulis eius partibus.
units.tr: If God is a being not made, he is immense. The immensity of God is nothing other than his natural presence without any end or limit, so that the divine essence is sufficient to fill all spaces, even if they were increased to infinity. It is always actually present, whether this presence is conceived and declared by us in relation to real places or to imaginary spaces. For if he were not thus immense, he would have a certain limit to his presence, and so would be neither independent, nor infinite, nor most perfect, but would depend on something determinately. Whence it necessarily follows that the divine essence is indivisibly and unextended whole in the whole world, and whole in each of its parts.

units.la: VIII. Æternitas est Dei proprietas sive attributum per quod essentia Divina a nobis concipitur ut omni termino durationis carens.
units.tr: VIII. Eternity is a property or attribute of God through which the divine essence is conceived by us as lacking every limit of duration.

units.la: Si Deus est ens non factum, æternus est, nec principium nec finem, nec successionem duratio-nis habet, nam si esse cœpit, est factus ac princi-piatus; Si esse desinit est factus ab alio, neq; enim destruet seipsum, cum omne ens appetat sui con-servationem; Si successionis durationem habet utiq; fit: Hinc sequitur Summa Dei necessitas, qua Deus est ens summè necessarium, ita ut sum, me fit impossibile Deum non esse.
units.tr: If God is a being not made, he is eternal: he has neither beginning nor end, nor succession of duration. For if he began to be, he is made and has a beginning; if he ceases to be, he is made by another, for he will not destroy himself, since every being seeks its own preservation; if he has a duration of succession, he is assuredly made. Hence follows the supreme necessity of God, by which God is a being supremely necessary, so that it is impossible for God not to be.

units.la: IX. Incomprehensibilitas est Dei attribu-tum per quod essentia divina a nobis concipitur ut omnium rerum creatarum capacitatem infini-te transcendens.
units.tr: IX. Incomprehensibility is an attribute of God by which the divine essence is conceived by us as infinitely transcending the capacity of all created things.

units.la: Si Deus est ens infinitum est incomprehensibilis, adeoque invisibilis & ineffabilis: Comprehendere enim est rem adæquate videre, id est, in tantum videre in quantum est visibilis, videre autem est rem clare ac evidenter cognoscere prout in se est; Effari denique est adæ-quatum rei conceptum adæquate exprimere.
units.tr: If God is an infinite being, he is incomprehensible, and therefore invisible and ineffable. For to comprehend is to see a thing adequately, that is, to see it as far as it is visible; and to see is to know a thing clearly and evidently as it is in itself. Finally, to express (effari) is to express adequately an adequate concept of a thing.

units.la: Cum autem res finita non sit adæquatè capax infiniti, Deus autem sit infinitus, necessario sequitur Deum esse incomprehensibilem, invisibilem, ac ineffabilem, scilicet respectu creaturarum intelligentium, non vero ratio-ne sui, nam seipsum perfectissimè videt ac ex-primere potest.
units.tr: But since a finite thing is not adequately capable of the infinite, and God is infinite, it necessarily follows that God is incomprehensible, invisible, and ineffable, namely with respect to intelligent creatures, but not by reason of himself, for he sees himself most perfectly and can express himself.

units.la: X. Immutabilitas est Dei proprietas per quam essentia Divina a nobis concipitur, ut carens omni possibilitate mutationis.
units.tr: X. Immutability is an attribute of God through which the divine essence is conceived by us as lacking every possibility of change.

units.la: Si Deus est ens nonfactum est etiam Immuta-bilis, tum ratione essentiæ, tum ratione proprietatum essentialium, nam si mutaretur, fieret ab aliquo, quatenus scilicet mutaretur, itemque dependeret à mutatione; praeterea nec perseElissimus[?] foret nec simplicissimus quia illa muta-tio aut fieret in melius, sic negaretur absoluta eius perfectio antecedenter, aut in deterius, sic iterum negaretur consequenter, aut in pror-sus æquale, sic mutatio foret incongrua ac fru-stranea.
units.tr: If God is an unmade being, he is also immutable, both by reason of his essence and by reason of his essential properties. For if he were changed, he would be made by something, insofar as he were changed, and likewise would depend on change. Moreover, he would be neither most perfect nor most simple, because that change would either be into something better, so that his absolute perfection would be denied antecedently; or into something worse, so that again it would be denied consequently; or into something entirely equal, in which case the change would be incongruous and pointless.

units.la: CAP. VII. De Demonstratione Pro-prietatum Dei quæ ipsi compe-tunt quatenus est Spiritus.
units.tr: CAP. VII. On the Demonstration of the Properties of God which belong to Him insofar as He is Spirit.

units.la: Hactenus de proprietatibus Dei quæ ipsi competunt quatenus est ens primum sequuntur ea quæ ipsi competunt quatenus est Spiritus.
units.tr: Having dealt with the properties of God which belong to Him insofar as He is the first being, what follows concerns those which belong to Him insofar as He is Spirit.

units.la: Si Deus est ens non factum est Substantia, nam si esset accidens esset ens factum & dependens, quia omne accidens dependet a Substantia cuius est accidens;
units.tr: If God is an uncreated being, He is a substance, for if He were an accident He would be a created and dependent being, because every accident depends on the substance of which it is an accident;

units.la: I. Est autem ut ex superioribus patet Substantia perfectissima, nimirum Substantia prima vivens, uno verbo Spiritus.
units.tr: I. Now, as is clear from what has gone before, He is the most perfect substance, namely the first living substance, in a word, Spirit.

units.la: II. Proprietates quæ Deo competunt qua-tenus est Spiritus a nobis concipiuntur vel per modum Subjecti, ut Vita Dei, vel per modum Facultatum,
units.tr: II. The properties which belong to God insofar as He is Spirit are conceived by us either by way of subject, as the life of God, or by way of faculties.

units.la: III. Vita Dei est Dei proprietas per quam essentia divina a nobis concipitur actuosa, intelligendo, volendo, & quae vult potenter efficiendo.
units.tr: III. The life of God is the property of God by which the divine essence is conceived by us as active: understanding, willing, and powerfully effecting what it wills.

units.la: Si Deus est ens non factum & perfectissi-mum est ens vivens ; Ens enim vivens est Sub-statia quæ intrinsecè in suo connaturali ac perfectostatu[?] operatur, seu quæ est perfectum immanentis operationis principium. Vita autem sumitur vel pro actu vel pro potentia activa ; priori modo est operatio perfectiva a principio activo, & intrinseco eius inquo est, elicita, seu est operatio perfectiva intrinsecè a natura eius cuius est emanans ; posteriori modo est ipsum principium activum intrinsecum vitalis operationis, ideoque ipsa rei viventis substantia. Jam si Deus non viveret, nec esset ens independens, utpote cuius actio pendet a principio extrinseco, nec perfectissimum, cum vives in suo genere sit perfectius non viventes ; & actio est proportionalis agenti, actus autem vitæ[?] est nobilissimꝰ, cum & maximè sit intrinsecus, & ad ipsiusmet agentis perfectionē immediatè faciat. In Deo interim actus vitæ primus non distinguitur ab actu vitæ secundo, sed vita Dei est purissimus, perfectissimus ac simplicissimus actus ; Secus nec Deus esset Simplicissimus, nec perfectissimus nec immutabilis. Vita hæc Dei cùm ita sit perfectissima & infinita dicitur immortalitas.
units.tr: If God is an uncreated and most perfect living being, then (for a living being is a substance which operates within itself in its natural and perfect state, that is, which is the perfect principle of immanent operation) life is taken either for act or for active power. In the first sense it is an operation, perfected by the active principle that is intrinsic to the being in which it is, and elicited from it; that is, it is an operation perfected intrinsically by the nature of that of which it is the emanation. In the second sense it is the intrinsic active principle of the vital operation itself, and therefore the very substance of the living thing. Now if God did not live, He would be neither an independent being, since His action would depend on an extrinsic principle, nor most perfect, since a living thing is more perfect in its kind than a non-living one. Moreover, action is proportionate to the agent, and the act of life is the most noble, since it is both most intrinsic and immediately perfects the agent himself. In God, however, the first act of life is not distinguished from the second act of life, but the life of God is a most pure, most perfect and most simple act. Otherwise God would be neither most simple, nor most perfect, nor immutable. This life of God, since it is so perfect and infinite, is called immortality.

units.la: IV. Facultates sunt Dei proprietates per quas essentia divina a nobis concipitur per perse-ctissimas vitalium operationum vires.
units.tr: IV. Faculties are the properties of God by which the divine essence is conceived by us through the most perfect powers of vital operations.

units.la: Hæ nihil sunt aliud quàm purissimi actus, à nobis tamen per modum Facultatum concipiuntur, in quantum facultates permanentem quandam perfectionem exprimunt: Vires autem hæ nullo modo sunt passiva, sed perfectis-simè activa, ideoque superiores Dei proprietates, quæ ipsi competunt quatenus est Ens primum, omnibus ac singulis sunt applicandæ.
units.tr: These are nothing other than most pure acts, yet they are conceived by us by way of faculties, insofar as faculties express a certain permanent perfection. These powers are in no way passive but most perfectly active; therefore the higher properties of God, which belong to Him insofar as He is the First Being, are to be applied to each and all of them.

units.la: V. Facultates divinæ Essentiæ sunt intelle-ctus, Voluntas & Potentia executiva divina.
units.tr: V. The faculties of the divine essence are intellect, will and executive power.

units.la: Cùm Deus sit ens non factum ac simplicissimum, necessa[illegible, ~2 letters]riò est Spiritus, & quidem perse-ctissimus & plane immaterialis : Si Spiritus, utique hæ tres facultates ipsi necessariò competunt, quia, ad intrinsecam Spiritus perfectionem requiruntur.
units.tr: Since God is an uncreated and most simple being, He is necessarily Spirit, and indeed most perfect and wholly immaterial. If He is Spirit, then these three faculties necessarily belong to Him, because they are required for the intrinsic perfection of Spirit.

units.la: VI. In hisce autem spectandus cujusq; facultatis, tum actus, tum virtutes; Actus consi-deratur ratione Dei agentis, Objectorum Agibilium & modi Agendi.
units.tr: VI. In these, however, the consideration of each faculty is to be made, both acts and virtues. The act is considered with respect to God as agent, the objects that can be acted upon, and the mode of acting.

units.la: CAP. VIII. De Intellectu divino.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII. Of the Divine Intellect.

units.la: Intellectus divinus est perfectio seu proprie-tas per quam essentia divina a nobis concipi-tur ut perfectissimé omnia cognoscendi facultas.
units.tr: The divine intellect is that perfection or property by which the divine essence is conceived by us as the faculty of knowing all things in the most perfect way.

units.la: Si Deus non esset natura intellectualis & in-telligens, neq; ens independens, neq; perfectissi-mum foret; Ens enim intelligens præstat non intel-ligenti, ut cuilibet non bruto patet, neq; ens simpliciter primum a quo pendent omnia entia secunda, cum ens intelligens non possit pro-duci ab ente non intelligente.
units.tr: If God were not an intellectual and understanding nature, he would be neither an independent being nor most perfect; for an understanding being is superior to a non-understanding one, as is plain to anyone who is not a brute, nor would he be the being simply first, from whom all secondary beings depend, since an understanding being cannot be produced by a non-understanding being.

units.la: I. Hîc spectandus ipsius facultatis tum actus, nempe intellectio, tum virtutes.
units.tr: I. Here we must consider the acts of this faculty, namely understanding, and its virtues.

units.la: II. Intellectio 'Dei consideratur ratione ipsiusmet Dei Intelligentis, ratione rerum intelle-ctarum, & ratione modi intelligendi ; Ubi no-tandum quòd nulla in Deo sit intellectio acci-dentalis, sed tantum Substantialis.
units.tr: II. The understanding of God is considered in respect of God himself as the one understanding, in respect of the things understood, and in respect of the manner of understanding; where it must be noted that there is in God no accidental understanding, but only a substantial one.

units.la: III. Ratione sui, seu Intelligentis, Deus omnia illa quæcunq; intelligit, intelligit pro-pter se, à se, per se, ac in se, propter se, quatenus il-la intellectio est intima ipsius perfectio & quidem Substantialis ; à se, quatenus ejus intelle-ctio est independens à principio quocunq; et-iam ab ipso objecto extra se, ita ut objecti mu-tabilis variatio nullam inferat in intellectu di-vino mutationem ; Per se, quatenus ipse non utitur specie intelligibili, sed omnia accuratissi-mè videt per suam essentiam ; Denique in se, & quasi ex se, quatenus ille non abstractive, vel se vel alia a se, sed summe intuitive cognoscit, distincta quidem à se, in se, ceu prima causâ, videt eminentissimè, & juxta ipsorum proprias essentias distinctissimè : Uno verbo, divina es-sentia est ipse intellectus, intellectio, finis & principium & quasi species intelligibilis, & de-nique adæquatum suum objectum, quorum si vel unicum negetur, negatur Dei Independen-tia, Simplicitas, omnimoda perfectio, infinitas , æternitas, immutabilitas.
units.tr: III. In respect of himself, or as the one understanding, God understands all those things which he understands on account of himself, from himself, through himself, and in himself. On account of himself, inasmuch as that understanding is his intimate perfection and indeed a substantial one; from himself, inasmuch as his understanding is independent of any principle whatever, even of the object outside himself, so that the variation of a changeable object brings no change into the divine intellect; through himself, inasmuch as he does not use an intelligible species, but sees all things most accurately through his own essence; and lastly in himself, and as it were from himself, inasmuch as he knows not abstractively, either himself or things other than himself, but most intuitively, seeing things distinct from himself in himself, as first cause, in the most eminent way, and most distinctly according to their own proper essences. In a word, the divine essence is itself the intellect, the understanding, the end and principle, and as it were the intelligible species, and finally its adequate object; if even one of these is denied, the independence, simplicity, all-round perfection, infinity, eternity and immutability of God are denied.

units.la: IV. Ratione rerum intellectarum, Deus intelligit omnia cognoscibilia, adeoq; & se & omnia reliqua entia distincta a se, ita ut ipsius intellectio ratione objecti omni modo & gradu sit[?] universalis.
units.tr: IV. In respect of the things understood, God understands all knowable things, and therefore both himself and all other beings distinct from himself, so that his understanding, in respect of its object, is universal in every mode and degree.

units.la: 1. Cognoscit se, secus nec ipse, nec intellectio ipsius esset perfectissima aut independens, quo enim nobilius est intelligibile, eo, æteris talibus, nobilior est intellectio; Nec Deus sibi sufficeret, nisi seipsum comprehen-sive, id est, adæquatè cognosceret.
units.tr: 1. He knows himself; otherwise neither he nor his understanding would be most perfect or independent, for the nobler the object of understanding, the nobler, other things being equal, the understanding is; nor would God be sufficient to himself unless he comprehended himself, that is, knew himself adequately.

units.la: 2. Cognoscit omnia à se distincta, quæcunq; illa sint & esse possint.
units.tr: 2. He knows all things distinct from himself, whatever they are and whatever they can be.

units.la: 3. Vniversalia & Singularia, nisi enim hæc cognosceret, cognitio ipsius esset imperfecta, confusa & inutilis, cùm sola singularia in rerum natura existant,
units.tr: 3. Universals and singulars; for unless he knew these, his knowledge would be imperfect, confused and useless, since only singular things exist in the nature of things.

units.la: 3.[?] Vera & falsa, bona & mala, secus non esset infinita.
units.tr: 3. True and false, good and evil; otherwise his knowledge would not be infinite.

units.la: 4. Non solùm existentia, sed & possibilia;
units.tr: 4. Not only existing things but also possible ones;

units.la: 5. Necessaria & Contingentia, adeoque liberrimos & sui & cujusvis creaturæ intelligentis actus;
units.tr: 5. Necessary and contingent things, and therefore the most free acts both of himself and of every intelligent creature;

units.la: 6. Maxima, media, & minima;
units.tr: 6. The greatest, middling and least things;

units.la: 7. Omnes Substantias & Accidentia, Omnes ipsorum modos & gradus.
units.tr: 7. All substances and accidents, and all their modes and degrees.

units.la: Nisi enim Deus omnia & singula entia, id est, tam positiva quam negativa & privativa perfectissimè cognosceret, nec ipsius cognitio esset infinitæ ac immutabilis perfectionis, nec seipsum comprehenderet, cùm in comprehensione attributorum sive proprietatum suarum[?] horum omnium cognitio includatur.
units.tr: For unless God knew all and each being, that is, positive as well as negative and privative beings, most perfectly, his knowledge would be neither of infinite and unchangeable perfection, nor would he comprehend himself, since the knowledge of all these is included in the comprehension of his attributes or properties.

units.la: V. Ratione modi intelligendi, Deus intel-ligit omnia actu unico, independenti, Simplicissimo, infinito, immobili ac immutabili : Non in tempore, sed ab aeterno ; Non per compositionem & divisionem, aut discursum, sed actu indivisibili ; Non confuse ac universaliter, sed distinctissime ac singularissime ; Non per species intelligibiles, sed per suam essentiam, quia ipsius essentia eminenter in se continet omnia etia etiam possibilia, adeoque tanquam infinitis modis imitabilis ea clarissime repraesentans ; Non apprehensive, sed comprehensive[?] ; Non abstractive, sed intuitive ; Non successive, sed simul, tum ex parte sui, tum ex parte rerum scibilium ; Non ita ut ipsius cognitio dependeat a rebus cognoscibilibus, sed ut res creatae cognoscendae dependeant ab ipsius cognitione ; Non progrediendo a notiori ad ignotius, quasi cognoscat unum sua natura esse notius altero, sed intime, omnia & singula penetrando: Cognoscit autem res bonas quasi immediate, malas vero cognitis bonis, quatenus sunt negationes bonarum.
units.tr: V. In respect of the manner of understanding, God understands all things by one act, independent, most simple, infinite, unmoved and unchangeable; not in time but from eternity; not by composition and division, or discursion, but by an indivisible act; not confusedly and universally, but most distinctly and most singularly; not by intelligible species, but through his own essence, because his essence eminently contains within itself all things, even possible ones, and so, as imitable in infinitely many ways, represents them most clearly; not apprehensively but comprehensively; not abstractively but intuitively; not successively but simultaneously, both on the part of himself and on the part of the knowable things; not in such a way that his knowledge depends on knowable things, but so that created things depend for their being known on his knowledge; not by proceeding from what is better known to what is less known, as though he knew one thing to be by nature better known than another, but intimately, penetrating all things and each thing. He knows good things, indeed, as it were immediately, but evil things through the good things known, inasmuch as they are negations of good things.

units.la: VI. Quamvis autem Scientia Dei sit unica, attamen doctrinae causa dividitur in Scientiam Simplicis intelligentiae & visionis.
units.tr: VI. Although the knowledge of God is one, nevertheless for the sake of teaching it is divided into the knowledge of simple understanding and the knowledge of vision.

units.la: I. Scientia Simplicis intelligentiae est qua Deus videt omnia possibilia, sive sint futura, sive non, & fundatur proxime in ipsa essentia ac omnipotentia Dei;
units.tr: I. The knowledge of simple understanding is that by which God sees all possible things, whether they are going to be or not, and it is founded proximately in the very essence and omnipotence of God.

units.la: 2. Scientia visionis est qua Deus videt certo futura, quae fundatur proxime in voluntate Dei.
units.tr: 2. The knowledge of vision is that by which God sees with certainty future things, and it is founded proximately in the will of God.

units.la: 3. Tertia vero, quae a recentioribus quibusdam fingitur Scientia media qua Deus praescit quid in hoc vel in illo rerum statu, citra summam praedestinationem, futurum esset, est absurda, cum independentiae, immutabilitati & omnipotentiae divinae repugnet.
units.tr: 3. As for the third, which certain more recent writers devise, the so-called middle knowledge, by which God foreknows what would be future in this or that state of things, apart from the sovereign predestination, it is absurd, since it is repugnant to the independence, immutability and omnipotence of God.

units.la: VII. Virtutes quae divino intellectui attribuuntur non significant aliquam distinctionem inter potentiam & actum, nec aliquam facultatis imperfectionem, sed summam eius eminentiam; Eae sumuntur vel a rebus intellectis, vel ab intelligendi modo.
units.tr: VII. The virtues which are attributed to the divine intellect do not signify any distinction between power and act, nor any imperfection of the faculty, but its supreme eminence; they are taken either from the things understood or from the manner of understanding.

units.la: VIII. Ratione rerum intellectarum, est omniscientia qua cognoscit omnia cognoscibilia; Intelligentia qua cognoscit prima rerum principia, adeoque ipsius scientia est altissima & simpliciter a priori; Et Praescientia, qua cognoscit res a se diversas, antequam in seipsis sint.
units.tr: VIII. In respect of the things understood there is omniscience, by which he knows all knowable things; intelligence, by which he knows the first principles of things, and so his knowledge is of the highest kind and simply a priori; and foreknowledge, by which he knows things other than himself before they exist in themselves.

units.la: IX. Modus intelligendi respicit vel intel-lectus {ē}tus applicationem, vel operationem.
units.tr: IX. The manner of understanding regards either the application of the intellect or its operation.

units.la: X. Ratione applicationis est perfectissima & non interrupta considerantia, qua Deus non procedit a non cogitando ad cogitandum, vel ab eo ces-sat, sed ab aeterno in aeternum manet immutabili ac attentissimo cogitationis actu; Quae perfectio aliquando vocatur Vigilantia.
units.tr: X. In respect of application there is a most perfect and uninterrupted consideration, by which God does not proceed from not thinking to thinking, nor does he cease from it, but from eternity into eternity remains in an unchangeable and most attentive act of thought; this perfection is sometimes called vigilance.

units.la: XI. Ratione operationis varia formantur nomina, nam
units.tr: XI. In respect of operation various names are formed, for

units.la: 1. Ratione accurationis dicitur vulgò Scientia;
units.tr: 1. In respect of accuracy it is commonly called knowledge;
