units.la: 2. Ratione penetrationis & infallibilitatis dicitur perspicacia, qua omnia etiam intima oculis ejus patent;
units.tr: 2. In respect of penetration and infallibility it is called perspicacity, by which all things, even the most inward, lie open to his eyes;

units.la: 3. Ratione omnimoda congruentia dicitur Sapientia, qua singula individua, ipsorumque statum perfectissime dignoscit;
units.tr: 3. In respect of complete fitness it is called wisdom, by which he discerns each individual and its state most perfectly;

units.la: 4. Ratione deliberationis dicitur Prudentia.
units.tr: 4. In respect of deliberation it is called prudence.

units.la: s.[?] Et denique ratione executionis dicitur Ars.
units.tr: s. And finally, in respect of execution it is called art.

units.la: XII. Hic omnes habitus & actus intellectuales aliquam imperfectionem includentes sunt removendi a Deo, quales sunt cogitantia, cognitio a posteriori, adeoque experientia docens, discere, dubitatio[?], opinio, conjectura, suspicio, fides fides alterius relatione nitens, & generaliter qua-liscunq; error, nam vel minima ejusmodi im-perfectio, divinas perfectiones supra demon-stratas evertit.
units.tr: XII. Here all habits and intellectual acts that include some imperfection are to be removed from God, such as thinking, knowledge a posteriori, and therefore experience that teaches, learning, doubt, opinion, conjecture, suspicion, faith resting on another's report, and generally every kind of error; for even the slightest such imperfection overturns the divine perfections demonstrated above.

units.la: CAP. IX. De voluntate divina.
units.tr: CAP. IX. Of the divine will.

units.la: VOluntas divina est Dei proprietas per quam essentia divina a nobis concipitur, ut perfectissima Spiritualis appetendi facultas.
units.tr: The divine will is a property of God by which the divine essence is conceived by us as the most perfect faculty of appetite (desire) in spirit.

units.la: Si Deus non haberet voluntatem, nec pri-mum, nec perfectissimum, nec intelligens fo-ret. Competit autem Deo voluntas proprie & accuratè loquendo, neque enim est extrin-seca denominatio, sed est intrinseca divinae naturae perfectio, qua res perfectissime co-gnitas, & suae & ipsarum naturae convenientis-simè appetit.
units.tr: If God had no will, he would be neither first, nor most perfect, nor intelligent. Yet will belongs to God properly and strictly speaking. It is not an extrinsic label; it is an intrinsic perfection of the divine nature, by which he most perfectly desires things that are known to him, and that which is both his own and most fitting to their nature.

units.la: I. Hic etiam videbimus voluntatis divinae tum actum seu volitionem, tum virtutes.
units.tr: I. Here we shall consider the divine will both as act or volition and as attributes.

units.la: II. Volitio Dei consideratur, ratione ipsius-met Dei volentis, ratione rerum volitarum, & ratione modi volendi.
units.tr: II. The volition of God is considered in respect of God himself as willing, in respect of the things willed, and in respect of the mode of willing.

units.la: III. Ratione ipsiusmet Dei volentis, volun-tas divina non est facultas ab essentia diversa, nec ipsamet volitio, seu volendi actus est perse-ctio divinae naturae addita, sed utrumque, sci-licet voluntas & volitio est ipsissima Dei essen-tia, adeoque est simpliciter independens, simpli-cissima, infinita ac immutabilis, tam moraliter ratione constantia, quam metaphysice, ratione entitatis, unde nec incipit nec definit velle, sed omnia quae vult ab aeterno, unico, simplicissimo, prorsusq; immutabili ac irrevocabili actu vult: Hoc mysterium breviter sic demonstratur.
units.tr: III. In respect of God himself as willing, the divine will is not a faculty distinct from the essence, nor is volition itself, that is, the act of willing, a perfection added to the divine nature. Rather, both the will and the volition are the very essence of God. Hence it is simply independent, most simple, infinite and unchangeable, morally in respect of constancy, and metaphysically in respect of being. Therefore God neither begins nor ceases to will, but wills all that he wills from eternity, by one, most simple act, and wills it with an act that is wholly unchangeable and irrevocable. This mystery is briefly demonstrated thus:

units.la: Volitio Dei aut dicit perfectionem intrinsecam aut non dicit.
units.tr: The volition of God either expresses an intrinsic perfection or does not.

units.la: Si non dicit, non est actus vitalis, omnis enim actus vitalis vel est operatio immanens, vel fluit ab operatione immanente;
units.tr: If it does not, it is not a vital act; for every vital act is either an immanent operation or flows from an immanent operation;

units.la: Si dicit intrinsecam perfectionem Dei, (ut re-vera dicit) Ergo, si incipit, ante Deus non fuit perfectus, si definit vel mutatur, postmodum non est Deus perfectus, at utrumque est absurdissi-mum.
units.tr: If it does express an intrinsic perfection of God (as in truth it does), then, if it began, God was not perfect before; if it ceased or changed, God would not be perfect afterwards; but both are most absurd.

units.la: IV. Volitio Dei, ratione rerum volitarum est congruentissima, & cujuslibet naturae accom-modatissima ;
units.tr: IV. The volition of God, in respect of the things willed, is most congruous and most suited to every nature.

units.la: Unde duplex respectu nostri oritur divi-nae voluntatis actus, quorum prior stricte dicitur Volitio, alter Nolitio ; Nam objectum divinæ voluntatis, vel tanquam conveniens ap-probatur, vel tanquam inconveniens improba-tur, sive illa convenientia vel inconvenientia sit talis simpliciter vel secundum quid, in cer-to modo & gradu;
units.tr: Hence, with respect to us, there arise two acts of the divine will, of which the first is strictly called Volition, and the second Nolition. For the object of the divine will is either approved as fitting, or rejected as unfitting, whether that fitness or unfitness is of this kind simply, or in a certain respect, in a certain mode and degree.

units.la: 1. Volitio est actus divinæ voluntatis posi-tivus quo vult res esse simpliciter, vel certo modo & gradu;
units.tr: 1. Volition is a positive act of the divine will by which it wills that things exist simply, or in a certain mode and degree.

units.la: 2. Nolitio est actus divinæ voluntatis po-sitivus, quo vult aliquas res non esse, vel simpliciter, vel certo modo & gradu.
units.tr: 2. Nolition is a positive act of the divine will by which it wills that some things not exist, either simply or in a certain mode and degree.

units.la: Dico autem positivus, quia suspensio vel cessatio a volitione, dicit imperfectionem; Nec nolitio divina est nuda non-applicatio voluntatis, sed est efficax ejusdem determina-tio.
units.tr: I say positive, because suspension or cessation from volition implies imperfection. Nor is divine nolition a mere non-application of the will, but an effective determination of it.

units.la: V. Res circa quas versatur divina voluntas sunt bona vel mala; Bonæ sunt vel summe bona, vel non summe bona.
units.tr: V. The things with which the divine will is concerned are good or evil. The good are either supremely good or not supremely good.

units.la: VI. Rem quæ est summe bona, Deus vult simpliciter & necessario, necessitate scilicet na-tura, ita ut eam non possit non velle, nec alio modo graduq;, quàm ipsius summi boni capa-citas seu volibilitas requirit; Tale summum bonum est unicum, nimirum Solus Deus qui proin Ter Optimus maximus vocatur, ideoq;
units.tr: VI. The thing that is supremely good God wills simply and necessarily, namely by necessity of nature, so that he cannot not will it, nor will it in any other way or degree than the capacity, or willability, of the supreme good itself requires. Such a supreme good is one and unique, namely God alone, who is therefore called Best and Greatest, and so

units.la: [Right edge, clipped fragments of the facing page, lines running off the scan: fe sol[?] / omnia / & adj[?] / im vc[?] / nihil[?] / vl[?] / duplic[?] / tion[?] / libet[?] / prova[?] / proba[?] / Ra[?] / necef[?] / rebus / ficon[?] / decre[?] / melvc[?] / semel[?] / bilitat[?] / Præ / bonæ / media[?] / nonta[?] / quia ip[?]] se solum necessario ac summè amat ; Hinc omnia quæ Deus vult, vult propter se, à se, per se, & adse, unde Deus recte dicitur sumus omnium volitionum finis ; Deus igitur præter se, nihil necessario amat.
units.tr: [Clipped fragments of the facing page, running off the scan and illegible.] he loves himself alone, necessarily and supremely. Hence all that God wills, he wills for himself, from himself, through himself, and toward himself; whence God is rightly called the end of all volitions. Therefore God, apart from himself, necessarily loves nothing.

units.la: VII. Res non summè bonæ considerantur dupliciter, ratione divinæ approbationis & exe-cutionis.
units.tr: VII. Things that are not supremely good are considered in two ways, in respect of divine approval and execution.

units.la: Ratione Divinæ approbationis Deus quamlibet rem amat, prout in se est amabilis, ideoq; pro vario modo & gradu, rerum varie ens approbat.
units.tr: In respect of divine approval, God loves any thing according as it is in itself lovable, and therefore he approves things variously, according to their varying mode and degree of being.

units.la: Ratione executionis, Deus nihil ita amat, ut necessario velit illū[?] existere, secus depederet a rebus creatis : potest itaque eas velle vel nolle si considerentur simpliciter in se, & quasi ante decretum Divinæ voluntatis ; Sed quod semel voluit, id non potest non velle, eo quod semel voluit, idque ob divinam suam immutabilitatem.
units.tr: In respect of execution, God does not so love anything that he necessarily wills it to exist; otherwise it would depend on created things. He can therefore will or not will them, if they are considered simply in themselves, and as it were before the decree of the divine will. But what he has once willed, he cannot not will, because he has willed it once, and this on account of his own immutability.

units.la: Præterea etsi res illæ quæ non sunt summè bonæ, inter se habeant ordinem, finem & media, & Deus velit ut res una sit propter aliam, non tamen Deus vult rem unam propter aliam, quia ipsemet non solum res ipsas, verum etiam verum subordinationem & coordinationem vult independenter ab ipsis, non enim suæ voli-tionis Deus causam impulsivam, exemplarem vel finalem externam habet, sed Deus ipse, eiusque voluntas est prima ac unica suæ volitionis causa impulsiva, exemplaris & finalis; cum enim divina voluntas sit ipsamet Dei essentia, causam nullatenus habere potest.
units.tr: Moreover, although those things which are not supremely good have among themselves an order, an end and means, and God wills that one thing be for the sake of another, God does not will one thing for the sake of another. For he himself wills not only the things themselves, but also their true subordination and coordination, independently of them. God does not have an impulsive, exemplary or external final cause of his volition; God himself, and his will, is the first and only impulsive, exemplary and final cause of his volition. For since the divine will is the very essence of God, it can in no way have a cause.

units.la: VIII. Res malæ circa quas divina voluntas versatur sunt etiam summe malæ vel non summe malæ.[?]
units.tr: VIII. Evil things, with which the divine will is concerned, are also either supremely evil or not supremely evil.

units.la: IX. Rem summe malam seu summum malum Deus nullatenus velle potest, ideoque summum malum simpliciter est impossibile, intel-lige summum malum non in certo genere, sed simpliciter, omni modo gradu[?] tale; Nam Deus T. O. M. ut necessario amat summum bonum, sic necessario summum malum odit.
units.tr: IX. God can in no way will a thing supremely evil, or the supreme evil; therefore the supreme evil simply is impossible. Understand the supreme evil not in a certain kind, but simply, such in every mode and degree. For God, the Best and Greatest, as he necessarily loves the supreme good, so he necessarily hates the supreme evil.

units.la: X. Res malæ quæ non sunt summe tales vel sunt mala culpæ vel pœnæ. Malum culpæ est illegalitas seu peccatum, id est, incongruentia cum norma agendi, adeoque cum voluntate & lege summa, scilicet, Dei: Etsi autem Deus peccata non potest velle voluntate approbationis, secus non essent peccata, attamen potest ea velle voluntate executionis, non ut ea faciat, nam Deus nihil potest facere quod non sit bonum, sed ut ea fieri ab Angelis & hominibus quibusdam permittat. Quod quamvis prima fronte paradoxon videatur, attamen ex lumine rectae rationis est clarissimum; a linea etenim peccata quae fiunt aut fiunt praesciente Deo, aut non praesciente. Si hoc, ergo non est omniscius ab aeterno: Si fiunt praesciente Deo [ut revera fiunt] aut fiunt volente Deo, aut volente ac invito, ita ut ille nollet ea fieri, attamen fiant. Si hoc, Deus non est omnipotens, nam qui non potest obtinere id quod vult, is non potest omnipotens esse; Ergo peccata, etiam atrocissima, quaecunque illa sint, fiunt voluntate Dei, seu vult Deus ea fieri.
units.tr: X. Evil things that are not supremely such are either evils of fault or evils of punishment. The evil of fault is illegality, or sin, that is, incongruity with the rule of action, and so with the will and the supreme law, namely of God. Although God cannot will sins by a will of approval (otherwise they would not be sins), he can nevertheless will them by a will of execution: not that he should do them, for God can do nothing that is not good, but that he should permit them to be done by certain angels and men. Although this may at first sight seem a paradox, it is most clear from the light of right reason. For sins either are done with God foreknowing them, or without his foreknowing. If the latter, then he is not omniscient from eternity. If they are done with God foreknowing them [as in truth they are done], then they are done either with God willing them, or with God willing and yet unwilling, so that he would not want them to be done, and yet they are done. If the latter, God is not omnipotent, for one who cannot obtain what he wills cannot be omnipotent. Therefore sins, even the most atrocious, whatever they may be, are done by the will of God; or God wills them to be done.

units.la: Ratio autem quod Deus possit velle peccata est, quia peccata non sunt summe mala, quamvis enim formaliter & in se mala sint, tamen bona sunt ratione eventus, in quantum sunt media ordinata ad bonum, nam divina omniscientia, justitia ac potentia ea omnia infallibiliter ad bonum valde excellens destinat ac ordinat, quo posito, melius est ut ea sint, quam quod non sint, sic melius fuit quod peccavit Adam ad divinae gloriae illustrationem. Interim major est virtus mala ordinare ad bonum, quam quàm bona, cùm alias bona sint, nam facilius est sanum in sanitate conservare, quàm morbidum ex morbo sanum facere.
units.tr: The reason why God can will sins is that sins are not supremely evil. For although they are formally and in themselves evil, nevertheless they are good in respect of their outcome, insofar as they are means ordained to a good end. For God's omniscience, justice and power infallibly direct and ordain all of them to a most excellent good. Given this, it is better that they should be than that they should not be; thus it was better that Adam sinned, for the illustration of the divine glory. Meanwhile, it is a greater power to order evil to good than to order good things, since good things are good anyway; for it is easier to preserve the healthy in health than to make the sick healthy from sickness.

units.la: XI. Mala pœna sunt ipsa pœna, quæ si sint justa non sunt per se mala, sed bona, bonum enim est malis esse male.
units.tr: XI. Evil punishments are themselves punishments. If they are just, they are not evil in themselves but good, for it is good for evildoers to fare badly.

units.la: Pœna est malum Status seu Passionis propter malum actionis, personæ inflictum, unde pœna tantum Physice, respectu ejus qui punitur, mala est & incongrua, non vero Ethice ac Symbiotice, respectu Legis & Societatis. Et quia pœnæ rationem suæ bonitatis habent, Deus non tantum vult ut eæ sint in rerum naturâ, verum etiam eas approbat atq; efficit.
units.tr: Punishment is an evil of state or suffering inflicted on a person on account of an evil action. Hence punishment is evil and unfitting only physically, with respect to the one who is punished, but not ethically or symbiotically, with respect to the law and society. And because punishments have the character of their goodness, God not only wills that they exist in the nature of things, but also approves and brings them about.

units.la: XII. Hic præterea accuratè notandum est quòd detur mixtum quoddam genus malorum quæ sint & mala culpæ & mala pœnæ ;
units.tr: XII. Here it must also be carefully noted that there is a certain mixed kind of evil, which is both an evil of guilt and an evil of punishment.

units.la: Duplex hic respectus culpæ & pœnæ in uno eodemque actu potest concurrere ; Sic (ut exemplum ex sacris proferamus) Stupratio concubinarum Davidis fuit & malum culpæ respectu Absolonis, & malum pœnæ respectu Davidis : Pro diverso autem respectu diversimodè sunt ad Dei voluntatem hi actus referendi, nam quâ peccata sunt, Deus non est ipsorum causa ; Sed quâ actus pœnales sunt, Deus est ipsorum causa ; Peccatum enim pec-catopunire est virtus.
units.tr: The double respect of guilt and punishment can meet in one and the same act. Thus (to bring an example from Sacred Scripture) the defiling of David's concubines was an evil of guilt with respect to Absalom, and an evil of punishment with respect to David. According to the different respect, however, these acts are to be referred to the will of God in different ways. Insofar as they are sins, God is not their cause; but insofar as they are penal acts, God is their cause, for to punish sin by sin is a virtue.

units.la: XIII. Modus volendi in Deo, ipsius infi-nitæ perfectioni & rerum volitarum conditi-oni est congruentissimus.
units.tr: XIII. The mode of willing in God is most congruous with his infinite perfection and with the condition of the things willed.

units.la: Hunc autem volendi modum & Virtutes & Affectus qui divinæ voluntati tribuuntur, ex-primunt.
units.tr: Both the virtues and the affections attributed to the divine will express this mode of willing.

units.la: XIV. Virtutes divinæ voluntatis sunt gene-raliores, vel specialiores : Generaliores sunt Libertas, Immutabilitas, Sinceritas, Efficacitas, Sanctitas & Prudentia.
units.tr: XIV. The virtues of the divine will are either more general or more special. The more general are liberty, immutability, sincerity, efficacy, holiness and prudence.

units.la: XV. Libertas est divinæ voluntatis perse-ctio quâ seipsam ad actiones circa creaturas, actio-nisq; modos & gradus, independenter ab omni conditione antecedente determinat.
units.tr: XV. Liberty is that perfection of the divine will by which it determines itself, independently of any antecedent condition, to actions concerning creatures and to the modes and degrees of those actions.

units.la: Hinc prima omnis convenientiæ & diffe-rentiæ radix in creatis est liberrima volitio di-vina : Nisi ejusmodi omni modo graduq; li-bertas Deo competat, tunc ipse non est ens summe ordinativum, sed etiam ordinabile, a-deoque non est simpliciter primum & indepen-dens, sed suo modo secundum & dependens.
units.tr: Hence the first root of all agreement and difference among created things is the most free divine volition. Unless such liberty in every mode and degree belonged to God, he would not be a being that orders supremely, but would himself be ordered, and so he would not be simply first and independent, but in his own way secondary and dependent.

units.la: XVI. Immutabilitas est divinæ voluntatis constantia perfectissima, quâ ipsa id quod semel voluvoluit vel noluit, non potest nolle vel velle, idque eo modo & gradu quo voluit vel noluit.
units.tr: XVI. Immutability is the most perfect constancy of the divine will, by which what it has once willed or not willed, it cannot not will or will, and it wills or does not will in the same mode and degree in which it willed or did not will.

units.la: Hanc immutabilitatem voluntatis divinæ evincit Dei perfectio, imprimis Omniscientia & Omnipotentia Dei.
units.tr: The perfection of God, above all the omniscience and omnipotence of God, proves this immutability of the divine will.

units.la: Quomodo autem absoluta Dei Libertas cum summâ ejus immutabilitate consistere queat, est unum ex profundissimis mysteriis divinis: Quare observandum est, actus divinæ volun-tatis considerari vel in se vel respectu objecto-rum suorum, id est, absolute vel terminative: Absolute & in se spectati actus divinæ voluntatis sunt simpliciter necessarii, cum sint ipsa essentia divina; Terminative vero sunt liberri-mi: Ratio hujus rei hæc est, quia scilicet, tanta est actuum divinæ voluntatis eminentia ut ipsi plane idem manentes possint, citra sui mutatio-nem, additionem vel subductionem, facere diversa, ita ut terminatio illa ad objecta creata ipsis non addat extrinsecam quandam perfectionem, sed tantum extrinsecam quandam relationem. Hoc ratiocinium excludit omnes in Deo actus contrarios.
units.tr: How absolute liberty can subsist together with the supreme immutability of God is one of the most profound divine mysteries. We must therefore observe that the acts of the divine will may be considered either in themselves or with respect to their objects, that is, absolutely or terminatively. Acts of the divine will considered absolutely and in themselves are simply necessary, since they are the divine essence itself. Terminatively, however, they are most free. The reason is that the acts of the divine will are of such eminence that they can remain altogether the same, without any change, addition or subtraction, and yet make different things, so that this termination in created objects adds to them not some extrinsic perfection but only some extrinsic relation. This reasoning excludes all contrary acts in God.

units.la: XVII. Sinceritas est divinæ voluntatis per-sectio, quâ omnes ipsius actus, executio, puta & Significatio accuratissimè inter se congruunt, sibiq; correspondent.
units.tr: XVII. Sincerity is the perfection of the divine will, by which all its acts, that is, its execution and its signification, agree most accurately with one another and correspond to each other.

units.la: Hinc voluntas Dei distinguitur in occultam & manifestam, seu in voluntatem beneplaciti & signi; Illa est Sapientissimum & efficacissi-mum de rebus omnibus decretum; Hæc est Significatio aliqua decretorum facta creaturis ratio-nalibus, quæ decretis divinis nunquam repugnat, licet ea perfectè non exprimat; neque enim modi docendi sunt norma vel perfectum divinorum decretorum speculum, sed sunt norma officii creaturarum intelligentium.
units.tr: Hence the will of God is distinguished into hidden and manifest, or into the will of good pleasure and the will of sign. The former is the wisest and most efficacious decree concerning all things. The latter is some signification of the decrees made known to rational creatures, which never contradicts the divine decrees, although it does not express them perfectly. For the modes of teaching are not the rule or the perfect mirror of the divine decrees, but the rule of the duty of intelligent creatures.

units.la: Unde inter facultatem occultam & manifestam nulla prorsus est vera contrarietas, licet ab hominibus signa cum suis signatis male conferentibus videatur quædam ἐναντιοφά-νεια. Deus voluntatem suam totaliter non manifestat, interim significat per sua præcepta quid velit ab hominibus fieri; sic officiosè fa-cit filius si oret pro patre ægroto, tamen etsi Deus decreverit ut moriatur: Quæ Theolo-gis, melius quam vulgò fit, observanda es-sent.
units.tr: Hence between the hidden and the manifest will there is no true contrariety at all, although to men, who compare signs badly with what they signify, a certain enantiophany [ἐναντιοφάνεια] seems to appear. God does not manifest his will wholly, yet he signifies through his precepts what he wills to be done by men. Thus a son acts dutifully if he prays for a sick father, even though God has decreed that the father should die. These matters ought to be observed by theologians better than they commonly are.

units.la: XVIII. Efficacitas est divinæ voluntatis per-sectio quâ ipsa intentionem suam, eo modo & gradu quo vult semper assequitur.
units.tr: XVIII. Efficacy is the perfection of the divine will, by which it always attains its intention in the mode and degree in which it wills.

units.la: Hinc voluntas Dei recte dicitur irrefistibi-lis, nam resistentiam creaturarum tollit, & ex resistentibus facit non resistentes, vel eam su-perat: Nam impossibile est ut in sensu composi-to creatura resistat Deo, in sensu diviso potest quodammodo, si scilicet divina efficacitate se non applicet Deus Creaturae. Praeterea resistere Deo dupliciter sumitur, vel voluntati Dei simpliciter & sic nemo resistit, vel praeceptis, & sic plurimi resistunt.
units.tr: Hence the will of God is rightly called irresistible: it removes the resistance of creatures and turns resisters into non-resisters, or overcomes their resistance. For in the composite sense it is impossible for a creature to resist God; in the divided sense it can, in a way, if God does not apply his divine efficacy to the creature. Moreover, to resist God is taken in two ways: either against the will of God simply, and in this sense no one resists; or against his precepts, and in this sense very many resist.

units.la: XIX. Sanctitas est divinae voluntatis perfectio, qua omnia ipsius decreta & actiones, sin-gulari modo & gradu aequitati congruunt.
units.tr: XIX. Holiness is the perfection of the divine will, by which all its decrees and actions agree with equity in a singular mode and degree.

units.la: Sanctissimus Deus dicitur quia est separa-tus ab omni incongruentia. Sanctitas est ex-cellentia quaedam puritatis, seu virtutis mo-ralis; Haec igitur in se eminenter complecti-tur virtutes Deo dignas, ita ut ne minima spe-cies imperfectionis in eius actionibus appare-at; quare haec sanctitas per omnes speciales vir-tutes est deducenda.
units.tr: God is called most holy because he is separated from all incongruity. Holiness is a certain excellence of purity, or of moral virtue. It therefore embraces eminently in itself the virtues worthy of God, so that not even the smallest kind of imperfection appears in his actions. For this reason holiness is to be deduced through all the special virtues.

units.la: XX. Prudentia est divinae voluntatis perfectio, qua media & rerum naturae & finibus suis accommodatissima ordinat.
units.tr: XX. Prudence is the perfection of the divine will, by which it orders means most suited both to the nature of things and to their ends.

units.la: Hinc irrefistibilis Dei ordinatio non tollit creaturarum intelligentium libertatem, sed eam ponit & confervat, neque enim Deus re-pugnat rerum à se creatarum naturæ, sed ei maxime congruit.
units.tr: Hence the irresistible ordering of God does not take away the liberty of intelligent creatures, but posits and preserves it. For God does not oppose the nature of the things he has created, but agrees with it most of all.

units.la: Itaque non est oppositio inter Dei determinationem, & determinationem creaturarum subordinatio, determinat etenim creaturas ut seipsas determinent: vide infra cap. 21. & 22.
units.tr: Thus there is no opposition between God's determination and the subordination of creatures' determination, for he determines creatures so that they themselves determine. See below, chapters 21 and 22.

units.la: XXI. Virtutes Speciales quæ divinæ voluntati tribuuntur, vel nullam includunt imperfectionem, vel aliquam includunt.
units.tr: XXI. The special virtues attributed to the divine will either include no imperfection or include some.

units.la: Virtutes speciales primi generis formaliter sunt in Deo, adeoque primario in se ipso, & secundario in Creaturis, tales virtutes sunt, justitia generaliter considerata, Charitas, Benevolentia, Fidelitas, justitia distributiva & vindicativa.
units.tr: The special virtues of the first kind are formally in God, and so primarily in himself and secondarily in creatures. Such virtues are justice considered generally, charity, benevolence, faithfulness, and distributive and vindicative justice.

units.la: Virtutes speciales quæ aliquam imperfectionem includunt, nimirum vel respectum quendam inferioris ad superiorem, vel respectum ad passiones, non sunt formaliter in Deo, sed tantum eminenter, ipsisque attribuendæ sunt ratione perfectionis, non imperfectionis, sic justitia accurate loquendo non potest intercedere inter Deum & creaturas, similiter nec modestia, nec patientia, nec fortitudo, formaliter possunt esse in Deo.
units.tr: The special virtues that include some imperfection, namely either a certain respect of the inferior to the superior, or a respect to the passions, are not formally in God but only eminently, and they are to be attributed to him by reason of perfection, not imperfection. Thus justice, speaking strictly, cannot hold between God and creatures; likewise neither modesty, nor patience, nor fortitude can be formally in God.

units.la: XXII.Idem judicium ferendum est de Affectibus qui Deo tribuendi secundum effectus.
units.tr: XXII. The same judgement is to be passed on the affections which are attributed to God according to their effects.

units.la: Affectus vel sumuntur physice, quatenus sunt ex alteratione humorum effluvia, sic nullatenus conveniunt Deo nec spiritibus intelligentibus: vel sumuntur Metaphysice pro inclinatione entis ad ens, dicamus & Symbiotice pro inclinatione personæ, sicq; sunt duplices, nam vel dicunt perfectionem sine imperfectione, ut Amor, Voluptas, Gaudium, Odium, Ira; vel dicunt perfectionem cum imperfectione, & hi sunt purgandi & Θεοπρεπῶς de Deo intelligendi, ut Tristitia, poenitentia, spes, admiratio, nimirum Deo tribuenda est perfectio, removenda vero imperfectio.
units.tr: Affections are taken either physically, insofar as they are effluvia arising from alteration of the humours; in this sense they do not belong to God or to intelligent spirits at all. Or they are taken metaphysically, for the inclination of a being toward a being, or let us also say symbiotically, for the inclination of a person. In this sense they are of two kinds: some express perfection without imperfection, such as love, delight, joy, hatred, anger; others express perfection with imperfection, and these must be purged and understood in a manner worthy of God [Θεοπρεπῶς], such as sorrow, repentance, hope, admiration. That is, perfection is to be attributed to God, but imperfection removed.

units.la: Cap. X. De potentia Dei executiva.
units.tr: Cap. X. On the executive power of God.

units.la: HActenus de voluntate Dei, sequitur ut de ipsius potentia executiva paucis agamus.
units.tr: Having treated the will of God, we must now briefly discuss his executive power.

units.la: I. Potentia Dei Executiva est Dei proprie-tas per quam essentia divina a nobis concipitur ut perfectissima facultas activa, qua, ad extra po-test facere quidquid est factibile.
units.tr: I. God's executive power is that property of God by which the divine essence is conceived by us as the most perfect active faculty, by which it can, outwardly, do whatever is capable of being done.
