units.la: Latius patet potentia Dei actiua quam executiua; potentia Dei actiua generaliter considerata est potentia, qua Deus potest producere omne producibile, siue illa productio sit adintra, siue ad extra: potentia Dei executiua est qua Deus potest facere extra se; quamvis in re ipsa sit una & eadem potentia, attamen quia nondum demonstravimus productionem adintra esse possibilem, ideo hoc in loco agemus tantum de potentia ad extra, praefer-tim cum potentia ad intra non sit productiva Entitatis seu Entis, sed personalitatis tan-tum.
units.tr: God's active power extends more widely than his executive power. Active power, considered in general, is the power by which God can produce whatever can be produced, whether that production is inward or outward. Executive power is the power by which God can act outside himself. In reality it is one and the same power. Yet since we have not yet shown that production inwardly is possible, we will here speak only of power outwardly, especially since the inward power does not produce being or an entity, but only personality.

units.la: Talem autem ac tantam Executivam potentiam Deo competere manifestum est ex eo quod sit Ens non factum, primum & independens; Etenim necesse est ut omnia entia facta, omnesque ipsorum operationes sint ab ente non facto, ideoque omnia entia possibilia fieri queunt ab ipso.
units.tr: That God possesses such a great executive power is clear from the fact that he is an uncreated, first and independent being. For all created beings, and all their operations, must come from an uncreated being; so all beings that are possible can be made by him.

units.la: II. Potentiam Dei Executivam considerabimus ratione ipsiusmet Dei potentis[?], ratione rerum possibilium, & ratione modi operandi.
units.tr: II. We will consider God's executive power in three respects: in respect of God himself, in respect of possible things, and in respect of the manner of operating.

units.la: III. Ratione Dei ipsius, potentia non est res in ipso distincta, sed ipsissima essentia, scientia & voluntas divina, & tantum ratione, ob inadæquatum nostrum conceptum, ab aliis diversa, estque purissimus actus, ac potentia dicitur non tam ratione Dei, quam rerum possibilium, estque simpliciter infinita.
units.tr: III. In respect of God himself, power is not a thing distinct within him, but his very essence, knowledge and will. It differs from these only in concept, because of our inadequate understanding. It is pure act. It is called power not so much in respect of God as in respect of possible things, and it is absolutely infinite.

units.la: IV. Ratione rerum possibilium est simpliciter universalis adeoque omnipotentia, qua nimirum potest facere omne factibile, id est, omne id quod vult & velle potest.
units.tr: IV. In respect of possible things, it is absolutely universal, and therefore omnipotence: that is, God can do everything that can be done, that is, everything that he wills and can will.

units.la: Factibile seu possibile est quod non includit repugnantiam entis, seu contradictionem, nimirum quod nulli perfectioni divinæ repugnat, neque sibi ipsi. Radices itaque omnis possibilitatis sunt divinæ perfectiones; neque enim divina potentia fundatur in rerum possibilitate, sed rerum possibilitas in divina fundatur potentia, cum omnis potentia passiva fundetur in activa.
units.tr: What can be done, or is possible, is what does not involve a contradiction of being, or a contradiction in terms; namely what does not conflict with any divine perfection, nor with itself. The roots of all possibility are therefore the divine perfections. For divine power is not grounded in the possibility of things; rather, the possibility of things is grounded in divine power, since every passive power is grounded in an active one.

units.la: Repugnantia autem illa tum intrinseca, tum respectu divinarum perfectionum, vel est ex-plicita vel implicita; absoluta vel secundum quid, seu respectu certi rerum status, quasi mediata vel immediata. Hinc Deus non potest facere impossibilia, non ob impotentiam, sed ob infinitam potentiam, qua non potest reliquis attributis suis repugnare, sic Deus non potest mentiri nec immediate, in suis Sermonibus, nec mediatè, in suis operibus, adeoque non potest facere facta, non facta, corpus reve-ra infinitum, ubique præsens, nonquantum, &c.
units.tr: That contradiction, whether intrinsic or in respect of the divine perfections, is either explicit or implicit; absolute or relative, that is, relative to a certain state of things; and it may be mediate or immediate. Hence God cannot do impossible things, not from lack of power, but because of his infinite power, by which he cannot act against his other attributes. So God cannot lie, neither immediately in his words, nor mediately in his works. Thus he cannot make what is made into what is not made, or make an infinite body that is actually present everywhere and not quantitative, and so on.

units.la: V. Præterea cùm potentia Dei sit infinita & nunquam exhauriri queat, duo hinc se-quuntur axiomata & corollaria, prima quidem fronte paradoxa sed verissima; primum est de intensiva rerum productarum perfecti-one alterum de extensiva rerum productione. dicimus itaque
units.tr: V. Moreover, since the power of God is infinite and can never be exhausted, two axioms and corollaries follow from this. At first sight they seem paradoxical, but they are most true. The first concerns the intensive perfection of created things, the second the extensive production of created things. So we say:

units.la: Primo, Deum nunquam posse facere res tam bonas, quin semper, si velit, facere possit melio-res: Sic posset Deus & meliora individua [ex-empli gratia Angelorum bonorum vel hominum] & meliores species facere: Omniaquidemquæ facit sunt optima, si conferantur cum Deo ipsiusque ideâ, sed non sunt optima si conferantur cum rebus possibilibus.
units.tr: First, God can never make things so good that he cannot, if he wishes, make better ones. Thus God could make both better individuals (for example, good angels or men) and better species. All the things he makes are indeed the best when compared with God and his idea, but they are not the best when compared with possible things.

units.la: Secundo, Deum posse facere omnia possibilia divisim, sed non posse facere omnia possibilia simul ac conjunctim, vel collectivè, secus illis factis nihil amplius posset facere, quæ res fundatur in divinæ potentiæ infinita perfectione.
units.tr: Second, God can make all possible things separately, but he cannot make all possible things at once and together, or collectively. Otherwise, once they were made, he could make nothing more. This is grounded in the infinite perfection of the divine power.

units.la: VI. Ex omnipotentia divina sequitur quod Deus omnium creaturarum efficientiam supplere possit, licet intrinsecam materiae vel formae causalitatem exercere nequeat, hoc etenim repugnat divinae independentiae, perfectioni ac simplicitati, nam causalitas materiae & formae necessario imperfectionem includit.
units.tr: VI. From divine omnipotence it follows that God can supply the efficiency of all creatures, although he cannot exercise the intrinsic causality of matter or form. For this would conflict with divine independence, perfection and simplicity, since the causality of matter and form necessarily involves imperfection.

units.la: VII. Ratione Modi, divina potentia distinguitur in Absolutam & Ordinatam.
units.tr: VII. In respect of mode, divine power is divided into absolute and ordinate.

units.la: Potentia Dei absoluta est qua Deus potest simpliciter facere omnia possibilia, sive sint futura, sive non.
units.tr: God's absolute power is that by which God can simply do all possible things, whether or not they are future.

units.la: Potentia Dei ordinata est qua Deus potest facere illa quae certo facere decrevit, dicitur autem ordinata, quia ordinem naturae, gratiae & gloriae a se constitutum servat. Utraque potentia Dei est infinita, non quidem ex parte termini, seu ex parte rei productae, nihil enim extra Deum potest esse infinitum, sed ex parte modi producendi nam Deus infinitam vim exerit.
units.tr: God's ordinate power is that by which God can do those things which he has decided with certainty to do. It is called ordinate because it keeps the order of nature, grace and glory which he has established. Both powers of God are infinite. Not indeed in respect of the term, or the thing produced, for nothing outside God can be infinite; but in respect of the manner of producing, since God exerts an infinite force.

units.la: VIII. Philosophus autem potest Omnipotentiam Dei considerare in genere satis facile, in specie vero non ita.
units.tr: VIII. The philosopher can consider God's omnipotence fairly easily in general, but not so easily in particular.

units.la: Quamvis etenim lumen naturae divinam omnipotentiam facile cognoscat in genere, non tamen eam eodem modo cognoscit in specie, ut sciat quid supernaturaliter fit possibile: Duplicia enim sunt ea quae supernaturaliter [?] sunt possibilia; Alia sunt talia quoad Substantiam, seu tam in fieri quam in esse, ut unio hypostatica duarum naturarum in Christo, alia vero quoad modum seu in fieri tantum: Et hæc iterum sunt duplicia; Nam alia tantum causis supernaturalibus possunt fieri, ut salvare per crucem, illuminatio caecitatis, resurrectio mortui; alia a canfis naturalibus possunt etiam fieri, ut generatio hominis, (sed productio hominis ex terra est supernaturalis ratione modi) miracula sunt res naturales, sed modus administrandi miracula est res supernaturalis, ut transmutatio aquæ in vinum: Gradus prior est cognitu difficilior secundo, secundus tertio: In plerisque mens Philosophi ita se habet ut si ea non affirmet tam aperte, tamen ea ne-gare nec debeat nec possit, sed de iis vel tra-ctet vel quadantenus disserat; loquimur interim de puris naturæ principiis in talibus ratio-ciniis congruè applicatis.
units.tr: For although the light of nature easily recognises divine omnipotence in general, it does not recognise it in the same way in particular, so as to know what becomes possible supernaturally. There are two kinds of things that are supernaturally possible. Some are such with respect to substance, that is, both in becoming and in being, as the hypostatic union of the two natures in Christ. Others are such with respect to manner only, that is, in becoming. These in turn are of two kinds. Some can be brought about only by supernatural causes, such as salvation through the cross, the healing of blindness, the resurrection of the dead. Others can also be brought about by natural causes, such as the generation of a man (though the production of man from earth is supernatural in its manner). Miracles are natural things, but the manner of performing miracles is supernatural, as in the turning of water into wine. The first degree is harder to know than the second, and the second harder than the third. In most cases the philosopher's mind is such that, if he does not affirm these things so openly, yet he neither ought nor can deny them, but either treats of them or discusses them to some extent. Meanwhile I am speaking of the pure principles of nature, applied fittingly in such reasonings.

units.la: CAP XI. De Divina Beatitudine.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI. Of the Divine Blessedness.

units.la: Hactenus egimus de divinis proprietatibus sigillatim, restat ut agamus de ipsarum statu conjunctim, qui spectatur in divina Beati-tudine.
units.tr: Hitherto we have treated of the divine properties one by one; it remains that we treat of their state taken together, which is seen in the divine Blessedness.

units.la: I. Beatitudo divina est perfectissimus Dei, omniumque ejus proprietatum & attributorum status, quo ita se habet ut nulla perfectio ipsi desit, sed sit independens & infinita beatitudo.
units.tr: I. The divine blessedness is the most perfect state of God and of all his properties and attributes, by which he is so disposed that no perfection is lacking to him, but it is an independent and infinite blessedness.

units.la: Hanc autem beatitudinem in se continet vel formaliter vel eminenter, adeoque omnis creatæ beatitudinis est fons & scopus; hinc oritur mirabilis omnium divinarum perfectionum immicatio[?], quæ in praxi diligenter est attendenda.
units.tr: He contains this blessedness in himself either formally or eminently, and so it is the source and goal of all created blessedness. Hence arises the wonderful interconnection of all the divine perfections, which is to be carefully attended to in practice.

units.la: II. Beatitudo Dei explicatur duobus attributis, Gloria scilicet & Gaudio.
units.tr: II. The blessedness of God is explained by two attributes, namely Glory and Joy.

units.la: III. Gloria Dei est infinita ejus dignitas, quâ scilicet ipse summum apud creaturas intelligen-tes meretur cultum.
units.tr: III. The glory of God is his infinite dignity, by which he alone deserves the highest worship from intelligent creatures.

units.la: Ex hac Dei gloria quæ est glorificabilitas oritur actualis ejus glorificatio, qua necessario omnia quæ in rerum natura occurrunt bona vel mala ipsius gloriæ & glorificationi pulcherrime inserviunt, secus non foret beatus sum-mus.
units.tr: From this divine glory, which is glorifiability, arises his actual glorification, by which all the good and evil things that occur in the nature of things necessarily serve his glory and glorification most beautifully; otherwise he would not be the supreme blessed one.

units.la: Dei autem cultus in eo consistit ut ipse omnis boni ac creatæ beatitudinis primum prin-cipium[?], prima causa exemplaris ac summus finis. finis, debito modo, agnoscatur ac celebre-tur.
units.tr: The worship of God consists in this: that he, as the first principle of all good and of all created blessedness, the first exemplary cause and the highest end, be acknowledged and celebrated in a due manner.

units.la: IV. Gaudium Dei est summa voluptas quâ ipse, in se, tanquam in summo bono omnique suo statu tanquam beatissimo perfectissimè acqui-escit.
units.tr: IV. The joy of God is the highest pleasure by which he himself, in himself, as in the highest good and in his whole state as most blessed, rests in perfect contentment.

units.la: Hoc gaudium divinum oritur ex divina αὐ-τάρκεια ἢ πανάρκεια, sibi sufficientia & omni-sufficientia.
units.tr: This divine joy arises from the divine self-sufficiency or all-sufficiency [αὐτάρκεια ἢ πανάρκεια], being sufficient to himself and all-sufficient.

units.la: Et sic de proprietatibus seu attributis divi-nis.
units.tr: And so on concerning the divine properties or attributes.

units.la: CAP. XII. De Consideratione essentiæ divinæ relata & in specie de ejus unitate.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII. On the consideration of the divine essence in relation, and in particular on its unity.

units.la: HActenus consideravimus Deum absolu-te, sequitur ut eum consideremus rela-te.
units.tr: Hitherto we have considered God absolutely; it follows that we consider him relatively.

units.la: Hîc notandum quòd ut relata fundantur in absolutis, sic etiam cognitio Dei relata funle-tur in cognitione ejus absoluta, ideoque quæ superius sunt demonstrata, repetenda sunt, ac inter se conferenda, nam ex illorum combina-tione oriuntur sequentia principia.
units.tr: Here it should be noted that, just as relations are founded on absolutes, so too the relative knowledge of God is founded on his absolute knowledge. Therefore what has been demonstrated above must be repeated and compared with itself, for the following principles arise from the combination of those truths.

units.la: Consideratio Dei relata considerat Deum vel in se seu natura sua, vel ad extra, seu respectu operum.
units.tr: The consideration of God relatively considers God either in himself, that is, in his own nature, or outwardly, that is, with respect to his works.

units.la: II. Quæ Deum considerat in natura sua vel respicit essentiæ divinæ unitatem, vel personarum pluralitatem.
units.tr: II. What considers God in his nature regards either the unity of the divine essence or the plurality of the persons.

units.la: Hic quæritur, an hæc duo lumine naturæ cognosci queant? Nam si nequeant cognosci lumine naturæ non pertinent ad Philosophiam nostram, sed ad Theologiam tantummodo. De primo, nimirum, Deum unum esse, non est quæstio adeo difficilis: de secundo, capite sequenti agetur.
units.tr: Here it is asked whether these two things can be known by the light of nature? For if they cannot be known by the light of nature, they do not belong to our philosophy but to theology alone. As to the first, namely that God is one, the question is not so very difficult; the second will be treated in the following chapter.

units.la: III. Fatemur quidem Gentiles multos finxisse Deos, aut lumine naturæ sunt abusi, nam sequentes demonstrationes à solo naturæ lumine petitæ sunt evidentissimæ: Accedit quod cordati inter ipsos illam Deorum pluralitatem haud quaquam credidêre: Nam Plato & Aristoteles per multos Deos intellexerunt Angelos, primas illas virtutes naturę, & politię magnos Heroes, ut Herculem, Neptunum &c.
units.tr: III. We grant that the Gentiles indeed invented many gods, or abused the light of nature. For the following demonstrations, drawn from the light of nature alone, are most evident. Moreover, the more sensible among them by no means believed in that plurality of gods. For Plato and Aristotle understood by the many gods the Angels, the first virtues of nature, and the great heroes of the state, such as Hercules, Neptune, and so on.

units.la: IV. Unitas essentiæ divinæ est perfectissima & summa, qua est Deus unus numero, ita scilicet ut summe impossibile sit essentiam divinam, adeoque Deum multiplicari.
units.tr: IV. The unity of the divine essence is most perfect and supreme, by which God is one in number, so that it is utterly impossible for the divine essence, and so for God, to be multiplied.

units.la: Hic itaque accurate notandum essentiam divinam non esse unam genere vel specie, sed numero, id est, singularissimam.
units.tr: Here, therefore, it must be carefully noted that the divine essence is not one in genus or in species, but in number, that is, most singularly one.

units.la: V. Unitas essentia divina demonstratur vel quasi a priori, vel quasi a posteriori: a priori, tum ab ejus existentia, tum ab attributis ac proprietatibus quæ respondent existentiæ modo & gradui.
units.tr: V. The unity of the divine essence is demonstrated either as it were a priori or as it were a posteriori. A priori, both from its existence and from the attributes and properties which correspond to the mode and degree of its existence.

units.la: VI. Ex Dei Existentia sic probatur ejus unitas;
units.tr: VI. From the existence of God his unity is proved thus:

units.la: Si Deus est, necessario est er s simpliciter necessarium, secus non esset ens non factum: Si est ens simpliciter necessarium, utique necessario existit: Si necessario existit, actu utique necessario, in quantum existit, est ens singulare, nam quidquid actu existit, singulare est, secus illa singularitas foret extra essentiam istius entis necessarii; Et sic ens non factum non esset necessarium, quia non necessario existeret actu.
units.tr: If God is, he is necessarily, and is simply necessary; otherwise he would not be an uncreated being. If he is a simply necessary being, he surely exists necessarily; if he exists necessarily, then surely he exists necessarily in act, insofar as he exists, he is a singular being. For whatever actually exists is singular; otherwise that singularity would lie outside the essence of that necessary being. And thus the uncreated being would not be necessary, because it would not exist necessarily in act.

units.la: VII. A Proprietatibus divinis, duo evidentissima sumuntur argumenta, primum ab infinita perfectione, alterum ab Omnipotentia.
units.tr: VII. From the divine properties two very evident arguments are drawn: the first from infinite perfection, the second from omnipotence.

units.la: VIII. Ab infinita Essentia divina perfectione, ejus unitas ac Singularitas, sic demonstratur.
units.tr: VIII. From the infinite perfection of the divine essence, its unity and singularity is demonstrated as follows.

units.la: Si Deus est necessario perfectionis infinitæ, Deus necessario est unicus ; Antecedens supra fuit probatum, consequentia vero sic probatur, quicunq; est infinitæ perfectionis, is necessario omnem perfectionem possibilem habet in se ; Secus posset concipi & esse aliquod ens ipso perfectius : At si plures essent Dii, nullus illorum infinitam perfectionem, nullus enim haberet essentialem perfectionem alterius, secus non essent plures Dii, & dein, singulorum perfectio aut ef-set summa, aut non esset summa ; Si non esset summa, non forent Dii ; Si esset summa, etiam quilibet ipsorum careret summa aliorum perfectione, adeoq; non haberet omnem possibilem perfectionem in se. Hæc demonstratio illustratur, si interrogetur, an plures illi Dij inter se differant numerice tantum, vel etiam specifice? Nam protinus deprehendetur absurdū.
units.tr: If God is necessarily of infinite perfection, God is necessarily unique. The antecedent was proved above; the consequence is proved thus: whoever is of infinite perfection necessarily has in himself every possible perfection. Otherwise some being more perfect than he could be conceived and could exist. But if there were several gods, none of them would have infinite perfection, for none would have the essential perfection of another; otherwise they would not be several gods. And then the perfection of each would either be supreme or not supreme. If it were not supreme, they would not be gods. If it were supreme, each of them would also lack the supreme perfection of the others, and so would not have in himself every possible perfection. This demonstration is made clearer if one asks whether those several gods differ from one another only numerically, or also specifically? For at once the absurdity will be discovered.

units.la: IX. Ab Omnipotentia Dei sic demonstratur ejus unitas.
units.tr: IX. From the omnipotence of God his unity is demonstrated thus.

units.la: Si Deus est omnipotens, Deus est numero unicus ; At Deus est omnipotens, ut supra probavimus, ergo est unicus : Patet consequentia, Si Deus est omnipotens, utq; potest facere quidquid vult. At si plures sunt Dij, nullus ipsorum potest facere quod vult ; Nam aut necessario idem volunt, aut possunt velle diversa vel prorsus opposita ; Si hoc, clarum est quód non possunt facere id quod volunt, sive enim unus alium impedire que-at, sive nequeat, necessario sequitur quód sal-tem unus non possit facere quod vult : Si autem necessario prorsus idem volunt, nec diversa aut opposita velle possunt, unde illa necessitas ? Vel est à libertate, & sic possent diversa aut opposita, vel est a natura necessitate, sic necessario habe-bunt prorsus eandem naturam seu essentiam, adeoque non erunt plures Dii.
units.tr: If God is omnipotent, God is one in number; but God is omnipotent, as we proved above; therefore he is one. The consequence is plain. If God is omnipotent, he can also do whatever he wills. But if there are several gods, none of them can do what he wills; for they either necessarily will the same things, or they can will different or entirely opposite things. If the latter, it is clear that they cannot do what they will, for whether one can hinder the other or cannot, it necessarily follows that at least one cannot do what he wills. But if they necessarily will entirely the same things and cannot will different or opposite things, whence that necessity? Either it comes from freedom, and then they could will different or opposite things; or it comes from the necessity of nature, and then they will necessarily have entirely the same nature or essence, and so there will not be several gods.

units.la: X. A posteriori unitas Dei demonstratur ex ejus effectibus, nimirum a panharmonia mundi.
units.tr: X. The unity of God a posteriori is demonstrated from his effects, namely from the harmony of the world.

units.la: Si Deus non est unus, non est universalis or-do in rerum natura, consequens est absurdum, ut supra docuimus, & breviter demonstravimus : Si sunt plures Dii, aut singula habent absolutum Dominium, adeoque absolutam potentiam ac potestatem in singulas rescreatas, aut non habent ; Si non habent, non sunt Dii ; Si singula habent, nullus ipsorum habet, nam si unus absoluto suo Dominio in res uti voluerit, alius nullatenus eo potest uti : Ergo nullus potest esse ordo universalis ; Consequentia sic patet, Si in rerum natura est ordo universalis, utique unus est rerum omnium summus finis, prima causa efficiens, prima causa exemplaris : At si plures sunt Dii, hæc omnia sunt impossibi-lia.
units.tr: If God is not one, there is no universal order in the nature of things; the consequent is absurd, as we taught above and briefly demonstrated. If there are several gods, either each has absolute dominion, and so absolute power and authority over the created things, or they do not. If they do not, they are not gods. If each has it, none of them has it, for if one should wish to use his absolute dominion over things, another can in no way use it. Therefore there can be no universal order. The consequence is plain: if there is a universal order in the nature of things, then surely there is one supreme end of all things, one first efficient cause, one first exemplary cause. But if there are several gods, all these things are impossible.

units.la: CAP. XIII. De Divinarum personarum pluralitate, quoad ejus cognoscibilitatem in genere.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII. On the plurality of the divine persons, as to their knowability in general.

units.la: ATque hæc de Unitate Dei, sequitur ut agamus de divinarum personarum plura-litate, de qua sequentia in genere præcognoscenda sunt.
units.tr: And so much for the unity of God. It follows that we should treat of the plurality of the divine persons, concerning which the following points must first be understood in general.

units.la: I. Hoc Mysterium est summum in universa rerum natura, agitq; de intima essentiæ divinæ perfectione quæ intellectui finito quoad distinctam & perfectam cognitionem est incomprehensibilis : Mens itaq; humana modestiæ quàm maximè studere, & omnem perfectionem ipsi attribuere, omnem verò imperfectionem ab ipso removere debet.
units.tr: I. This mystery is the highest in the whole of nature, and it deals with the innermost perfection of the divine essence, which is incomprehensible to a finite intellect as far as distinct and perfect knowledge goes. The human mind must therefore devote itself with the utmost modesty, ascribe to God every perfection, and remove from Him every imperfection.

units.la: II. Mysterium hoc non est tamen contra rationem humanam, secus nec credi nec intelligi possit, et quidquid est contra rationem illud est falsum & absurdum ; Credere est assentiri propositioni certæ.
units.tr: II. This mystery is nevertheless not contrary to human reason; otherwise it could be neither believed nor understood, and whatever is contrary to reason is false and absurd. To believe is to assent to a certain proposition.

units.la: III. Theologi ob sublimitatem & difficultatem hujus[?] mysterii existimant, quod Lumine naturæ nullatenus (pluralitas & trinitas personarum divinarum) cognosci queat, sic ferme sentiunt omnes etiam Scholastici.
units.tr: III. The theologians, on account of the sublimity and difficulty of this mystery, hold that the plurality and trinity of the divine persons cannot be known at all by the light of nature; almost all of them think so, including the Scholastics.

units.la: IV. Quamvis in contingentibus recta ratio possit aliquid nec affirmare nec negare, sed de eo vel tacere vel dubitare, attamen in simpliciter necessariis res secus se habet: Nam in simpliciter necessariis, eo ipso quo ostenditur aliquid non esse impossibile, eo quoq; ostenditur idem esse necessarium, præsertim in divinis. Ratio hæc est, quia id quod in divinis est possibile, id necessario summam dicit perfectionem, at summa perfectio necessario est in Deo: Itaque si recta ratio potest ostendere quod mysterium hoc non sit impossibile, quodque Adversariorum argumenta nullam imperfectionem evincant, indirecte quoque, satis aperte tamen, potest ostendere quod sit revera.
units.tr: IV. In contingent matters, right reason may neither affirm nor deny something, but may either keep silent about it or doubt it; in what is simply necessary, however, the case is otherwise. For in what is simply necessary, by the very fact that something is shown not to be impossible, by that same fact it is also shown to be necessary, especially in divine matters. The reason is this: what is possible in God necessarily implies the highest perfection, and the highest perfection necessarily belongs to God. Thus if right reason can show that this mystery is not impossible, and that the arguments of our opponents prove no imperfection, it can also, indirectly but still quite clearly, show that it is in fact true.

units.la: V. Actus rectæ rationis sunt incomplexi vel complexi: Actus rationis incomplexus est vel ad rem cogitandam, seu Thema, applicatio, vel Argumenti seu cogitationis inventio. Actus complexus est rationis de Thematis & Argumenti combinatione judicium; ad quod non nō requiritur distincta & omnimode perfecta terminorum cognitio, velut loquuntur, penetratio, sed sufficit cognitio confusa, quæ saltem aliquam, licet imperfectam, terminorum definitionem apprehendit, unde aliud est nullo plane momento aut indicante aliquod mysterium ratione inveniri, aliud mysterium indicatum demonstrare; illud est valde difficile in hoc statu generis humani, quia plerumque rebus sensibilibus est addictum; Hoc autem facile & frequenter fit & contingit, sic quamvis quidam Gentiles Philosophi de infinitate Dei, creatione rerum, similibusque mysteriis nunquam forsitan cogitarint, attamen de iis moniti, ea demonstrare & potuissent & debuissent.
units.tr: V. The acts of right reason are either incomplex or complex. An incomplex act of reason is either the application of the mind to a thing to be thought about, namely the theme, or the discovery of the argument, that is, of the thought. A complex act is the judgment of reason joining the theme and the argument. For this there is required not a distinct and altogether perfect knowledge of the terms, which is, as they say, penetration, but a confused knowledge is sufficient, one that grasps at least some definition of the terms, though an imperfect one. Hence it is one thing to discover by reason, with no indication at all, some mystery, and another to demonstrate a mystery that has been indicated. The former is very difficult in the present state of the human race, since it is for the most part given over to sensible things; the latter, however, is easy and happens frequently. Thus although some Gentile philosophers perhaps never thought about the infinity of God, the creation of things, and similar mysteries, nevertheless, when reminded of them, they both could and ought to have demonstrated them.

units.la: VI. Recta ratio consideranda est secundum tres status (confectionis, Defectionis & Re-sectionis. In statu confectionis, integra humana ratio non solum non poterat cognoscere Mysterium Trinitatis, verùm etiam maximè debebat, hoc enim erat primum & naturalissimum ejus objectum. In statu defectionis, ut circa universa intelligibilia est perturbata, ita maximè circa nobilissimum hoc objectum. Licet autem plurima & maxima se offerant obstacu-la, la, naturalis tamen intellectus capacitas non est sublata. In statu reflectionis, divina revelatio supplet defectum incogitantiae ac ignorantiae humanae, unde ratio per actum reflexum facile potest invenire argumenta mysterium hoc demonstrantia. Hic πρῶτ[?]ων Scho-lasticorum ψευδῶς[?] in hoc negotio est, quod praesupponunt hujus similiumque Mysterio-rum cognitionem in statu confectionis & in-tegritatis fuisse non naturalem sed supernatu-ralem, quod tam divinae sapientiae ac bonita-ti, quam humanae naturae perfectioni repu-gnat, nam Status naturae perfectus debet esse instructus omnibus mediis necessariis, quibus ad summam perfectionem homo deduci possit: At summa hominis perfectio natura-lis, est summa ejus cum Deo unio, adeoque cognitio & amor. In statu defectionis & cor-ruptionis Philosophi non possunt ita facile & perfecte concludere, tamen in magis affir-mantem quam negantem partem statuere de-bent, & ex recta ratione & experientia.
units.tr: VI. Right reason must be considered according to three states: of integrity (confectionis), of defection, and of restoration. In the state of integrity, human reason not only could not know the mystery of the Trinity, but indeed ought most of all to have known it, for this was its first and most natural object. In the state of defection, as it is disturbed with regard to all intelligible things, so most of all with regard to this most noble object. Although very many and very great obstacles present themselves, the natural capacity of the intellect is nevertheless not taken away. In the state of restoration, divine revelation supplies the lack of human thoughtlessness and ignorance, whence reason, by a reflexive act, can easily discover arguments demonstrating this mystery. Here the first error of the Scholastics in this matter is that they presuppose that the knowledge of this and similar mysteries in the state of integrity and wholeness was not natural but supernatural. This is contrary to the wisdom and goodness of God as much as to the perfection of human nature, for a perfect state of nature must be furnished with all the necessary means by which man can be led to the highest perfection. But the highest natural perfection of man is his supreme union with God, and therefore the knowledge and love of Him. In the state of defection and corruption, philosophers cannot conclude so easily and perfectly, yet they ought to take the side that affirms rather than denies, and this from right reason and experience.

units.la: VII. Demonstratio alia est a priori, alia a po-steriori; Et a priori duplex, alia quae a causis re-rum desumitur, alia quasi quae non a rebus ipsa sed menti nostrae prioribus deducitur, & haec scite scitè vocatur demonstratio ab æquiparantibus; Talis demonstratio ab æquiparantibus frequentissima est in metaphysica, & loco de Deo, cum attributum unum demonstratur ex altero, licet reipsa S.S. Trinitatis nulla sit causa, attamen ex essentialium attributorum summa perfectione necessario colligitur. Deinde à posteriori aliquid concluditur vel immediatè vel mediatè: Mediatè cum aliquid colligitur ex effectis de causa, ex quo, alio discur-su, aliud de causa colligitur. Itaq; hypothesis Scholasticorum falsa est, quòd ex creaturis non possint colligi tres personæ, sed singulæ etiam sufficiant ad ipsarum creaturarum productionem, non solum enim hoc posterius falsum est, cum ordo trium personarum divinarum in qualibet creatura etiam minima appareat: Verum etiam ejusmodi perfectiones creatoris & creaturæ colliguntur quæ sanè sine Trinitate locum habere nequeunt.
units.tr: VII. Demonstration is one kind a priori, another a posteriori. And the a priori is twofold: one kind is drawn from the causes of things, another, as it were, is not drawn from things themselves but deduced from what is prior to our mind; this is aptly called demonstration from equivalents. Such demonstration from equivalents is very frequent in metaphysics, and in the treatment of God, when one attribute is demonstrated from another; although in reality the Holy Trinity has no cause, nevertheless it is necessarily inferred from the supreme perfection of the essential attributes. Next, something is concluded a posteriori, either immediately or mediately. It is mediate when something is inferred from effects about the cause, and from this, by another line of reasoning, something else is inferred about the cause. Therefore the hypothesis of the Scholastics is false, that the three persons cannot be inferred from creatures, but that each one alone is sufficient for the production of the creatures themselves. For not only is this latter claim false, since the order of the three divine persons appears in every creature, even the smallest; but moreover such perfections of the Creator and of the creature are inferred as could by no means hold their place without the Trinity.

units.la: CAP. XIV. De Demonstratione S.S. Trinitatis à priori.
units.tr: CHAP. XIV. On the a priori demonstration of the Most Holy Trinity.

units.la: Personarum divinarum ternarius, sive Tri-
units.tr: The ternary of the divine persons, or the Tri-

units.la: A priori demonstratur vel ex terminorum generalium, vel specialium combinatione; Illa demonstratio suppeditat axiomata generaliora ac philosophis notiora; Haec specialiora ac Theologis fere propria; Itaq; his relictis, illa propo-nemus.
units.tr: A priori it is demonstrated either from the combination of general terms or of special terms. The former supplies more general axioms, better known to philosophers; the latter supplies more specialised ones that are almost proper to theologians. So, leaving these aside, we will set forth the former.

units.la: I. Ex Terminis Metaphysicis, divinisq; attributis interse combinatis sic procedemus.
units.tr: I. We shall proceed as follows, from the metaphysical terms and the divine attributes combined with one another.

units.la: Si in Deo, seu divina essentia est Substantia producens non producta, itemque producens & producta, utique in Deo sunt tres personae: At verum prius, Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: If in God, or the divine essence, there is a producing substance that is unproduced, and likewise a producing and produced substance, then certainly there are three persons in God. But the first is true; therefore so is the second.

units.la: Consequentia hinc patet, quia per personam intelligimus suppositum intelligens, & sub-stantia producens & producta necessario differunt saltem subsistentia, nihil enim produ-cit seipsum.
units.tr: The consequence is clear from this, because by person we understand an intelligent suppositum, and a producing and a produced substance necessarily differ at least in subsistence, for nothing produces itself.

units.la: Minor probatur & quidem per partes pri-mo, quod in Deo sit Substantia producens & pro-ducta.
units.tr: The minor is proved, and indeed part by part. First, that in God there is a producing and produced substance.

units.la: Secundo, quod in Deo sint personae tres, non plures nec pauciores.
units.tr: Second, that in God there are three persons, no more and no fewer.

units.la: II. Quod in Deo sit substantia producens & producta, sic demonstratur:
units.tr: II. That in God there is a producing and produced substance is demonstrated thus:

units.la: In quo ente est infinita vis producendi, produ-ctivitas, in eo quoq; est infinita productio, adeoq; infinitum productum, & per consequens, infinita substantia producens, itemque infinita substantia producta. Hic nota per infinitam productionem nos intelligere non infinitum numero, sed infinitum perfectione.
units.tr: In whatever being there is infinite power of producing, that is, productivity, in it there is also infinite production, and so an infinite product, and consequently an infinite producing substance and likewise an infinite produced substance. Here note that by infinite production we understand not infinite in number but infinite in perfection.

units.la: Consequentia ultima hinc patet, quia nihil est vere infinitum nisi Deus, & quidquid est in Deo, est ipse Deus, seu substantia divina; unde necessario sequitur quod illa productio non sit externa, sed interna, adeoque etiam sub-stantia producta talis.
units.tr: The last consequence is clear from this, because nothing is truly infinite except God, and whatever is in God is God himself, or the divine substance; whence it necessarily follows that this production is not external but internal, and so the produced substance is also of this kind.

units.la: Propositio Syllogismi sic demonstratur;
units.tr: The proposition of the syllogism is demonstrated thus:

units.la: 1. Omnis potentia est propter actum suum adæquatum, & qua[?] potentia non potest assequi actum suum adæquatum, illa est frustra, adeoque impossibilis, itaque ubi est infinita productio, ibi necessario est infinitum productum ; Adeoq; si in Deo non esset infinita productio, primo, actus non responderet potentiæ, nec operatio operanti, & secundo attributa divina, imprimis bonitas, minoris essent momenti & actualitatis, quàm essent attributa creaturarum, quod est inconveniens; Et deniq; nullum productum quod non est ipse Deus, qualecunque quantumcunq; sit, est & potest esse perfectio-ne infinitum.
units.tr: 1. Every power is for the sake of its adequate act, and a power that cannot attain its adequate act is in vain and so impossible; thus where there is infinite production, there is necessarily an infinite product. And so, if in God there were not infinite production, first, the act would not correspond to the power, nor the operation to the operator; and second, the divine attributes, especially goodness, would be of less weight and actuality than the attributes of creatures, which is inconsistent; and finally, no product that is not God himself, however great it may be, is or can be infinite in perfection.

units.la: Minor nimirum quod in Deo sit infinita vis producendi, supra fuit demonstrata, tum quod in Deo sit omnipotentia (potentia est ordinativitas ad actum). Itaque breviter,
units.tr: The minor, namely that in God there is infinite power of producing, was demonstrated above, and also because in God there is omnipotence (power is orderedness toward act). So, briefly:

units.la: Cum aeterna & infinita potentia necessario respondeat aeternus & infinitus actus, aeterno & infinito actui respondebit aeternum & infinitum productum.
units.tr: Since eternal and infinite power necessarily corresponds to eternal and infinite act, an eternal and infinite product will correspond to the eternal and infinite act.

units.la: Et denique perquam optimè notandum, in bono summo, aeterno & perfectione infinito, est communicatio summe bona, aeterna & perfectionis infinitæ. Ubicunq; autem est vera & realis communicatio, ibi quoq; necessario est vera & realis acceptio, ac proin vera & realis productio: Ubicunq; vera & realis est productio, ibi necessario est producentis & producti distinctio: Ergo necessario in Deo, summo, aeterno, & infinito bono est summa, aeterna & infinitè perfecta multitudo & Societas.
units.tr: And finally, it is very well worth noting that in the supreme good, eternal and infinite in perfection, there is communication of what is supremely good, eternal and of infinite perfection. Wherever there is true and real communication, there too there is necessarily true and real reception, and so true and real production. Wherever there is true and real production, there is necessarily a distinction between producer and produced. Therefore there is necessarily in God, the supreme, eternal and infinite good, a supreme, eternal and infinitely perfect multiplicity and society.

units.la: Absurdum autem est, bonum summum non posse esse sine bono non summo, id est, creato; Et bonum non summum esse adæquate capax communicationis summæ & infinitæ.
units.tr: Moreover, it is absurd that the supreme good cannot exist without a good that is not supreme, that is, a created one; and that a good that is not supreme is adequately capable of supreme and infinite communication.

units.la: III. Non esse autem plures vel pauciores per- sonas quam tres in Deo, sic evincitur, cum productum illud sit infinitum, ipsaque productio infinita, utique non erit extra Deum seu transi- ens, sed intra Deum, seu immanens adeoque productum erit ipse Deus, cum nihil sit infi- nitum praeter Deum, nihilque sit in Deo, quod non sit ipse Deus, ut supra in attributis proba- vimus.
units.tr: III. That there are not more or fewer than three persons in God is shown thus: since that product is infinite, and the production itself infinite, it will certainly not be outside God or transient, but within God, or immanent; and so the product will be God himself, since nothing is infinite except God, and nothing is in God that is not God himself, as we proved above in the attributes.

units.la: Si productio illa divina sit immanens necessa- rio erunt productiones duae, itemque necessario erunt tantum duae: At verum antecedens; Ergo & consequens.
units.tr: If that divine production is immanent, there will necessarily be two productions, and likewise necessarily only two. But the antecedent is true; therefore the consequent also.

units.la: Consequentia haec fit manifesta, quia in omni ordine ac multitudine necessario est aliquod pri- mum, adeoque in illis productionibus persona ali- qua prima, seu producens non producta; Reliquae vero personae sunt duae, & hinc patet.
units.tr: This consequence becomes manifest, because in every order and multitude there is necessarily something first, and so in those productions some person is first, that is, producing and unproduced. The remaining persons are two, and from this it is clear.

units.la: Si duae sunt facultates immanentes in Deo, utique duae erunt in eo productiones; At verum primus, Ergo & posterius. Ratio est, quia, omnis facultas immanens est productiva & actus & termini, secus non haberet naturalem perfectionem: posterius manifestum est, ex natura entis intelligentis quod necessario producit intellectu & voluntate; productio executiva autem respicit productiones ad extra, non ad intra.
units.tr: If there are two faculties immanent in God, certainly there will be two productions in him. But the first is true; therefore the second also. The reason is that every immanent faculty is productive both of act and of terms, otherwise it would not have natural perfection. The second is manifest from the nature of an intelligent being, which necessarily produces by intellect and will; executive production, however, regards productions ad extra, not ad intra.

units.la: IV. Sequitur ut probemus duas esse productiones in Deo, id ostendit sequens ratio, Tantæ perfectionis, efficacitatis ac actualitatis est divina voluntas, quantæ est divinus intellectus: At divinus intellectus est tantæ perfectionis, efficacitatis ac actualitatis ut producat personam infinitam, Ergo & voluntas.
units.tr: IV. It follows that we must prove there are two productions in God. The following reason shows this: The divine will is of as great perfection, efficacy and actuality as the divine intellect. But the divine intellect is of such perfection, efficacy and actuality that it produces an infinite person. Therefore so does the will.

units.la: Propositio patet ex æqualitate divinarum proprietatum.
units.tr: The proposition is evident from the equality of the divine properties.

units.la: V. Deinde restat ut ostendamus duas tantum productiones non plures esse.
units.tr: V. Next, it remains for us to show that there are only two productions and not more.

units.la: Si hæ duæ personæ productæ sint prorsus adæquati termini, utique non sunt plures productiones; At verum prius, ergo & posterius. Consequentia clara est, quia cum facultas, actus obtinuit terminum suum adæquatum perfecte quiescit, secus daretur processus in infinitum.
units.tr: If these two produced persons are wholly adequate terms, certainly there are not more productions. But the first is true; therefore the second also. The consequence is clear, because when a faculty's act has obtained its adequate term, it rests perfectly; otherwise there would be an infinite process.

units.la: Minor hinc patet, quia personæ productæ sunt perfectionis infinitæ, adeoque personæ productæ & producens perfecte adæquat productionem per intellectum, persona vero productæ & non producens perfecte adæquat productionem per voluntatem.
units.tr: The minor is evident from this, because the produced persons are of infinite perfection. Thus the producing and produced person perfectly matches the production through intellect, while the produced and non-producing person perfectly matches the production through will.

units.la: Cap. XV. De ratione refellendi obje-ctiones contra praecedentem demonstrationem.
units.tr: Chapter XV. On the method of refuting the objections against the preceding demonstration.

units.la: ADdere jam lubet quaedam fundamenta quibus Adversariorum objectiones sol-vuntur, quas contra praecedentem demonstrationem adferre possunt.
units.tr: Now it is worth adding some foundations by which the objections that our adversaries may bring against the preceding demonstration are answered.

units.la: I. Non sequitur, potentia Dei est infinita qua potest producere res creatas infinitas, nec tamen eas unquam producet; Ergo est frustra: Itaque nec sequitur, In Deo est infinita productivitas, Ergo necessario est in eo infinita productio, secus illa esset frustra.
units.tr: I. It does not follow that the power of God is infinite, by which he can produce infinitely many created things, and yet he will never produce them; therefore it is in vain. Nor does it follow that there is infinite productivity in God, and therefore necessarily there is in him infinite production, since otherwise that would be in vain.

units.la: Respondemus, per negationem consequentiae, quia est dispar ratio, nam impossibile est ut productio entium finitorum requiratur necessario ad perfectionem Dei; At consentaneum est ut infinita productivitas non possit esse sine infinito producto; & ideo frustra non est Dei omnipotentia, terminum su-um adaequatum assequitur in his personis productis, quae eminenter in se continent omnes
units.tr: We reply by denying the consequence, because the reasoning is different. For it is impossible that the production of finite beings should be required necessarily for the perfection of God; but it is consistent that infinite productivity cannot exist without an infinite product. And so the omnipotence of God is not in vain: it attains its adequate term in these produced persons, which eminently contain in themselves all

units.la: II. Nulla est inæqualitas inter personas producentes & productas, quia fluunt non ex imperfectione naturæ divinæ vel producentis, sed ex infinita perfectione & fœcunditate : Et quia personis productis non communicatur alia vel nova essentia per productionem, sed prorsus eadem quam habet producens, unde iis omnis perfectio est attribuenda, omnisq; imperfectio abiis removenda, nam tantæ perfectionis est una persona, quantæ est altera.
units.tr: II. There is no inequality between the producing and the produced persons, because they flow not from any imperfection of the divine nature or of the producer, but from infinite perfection and fecundity. And because no other or new essence is communicated to the produced persons by production, but altogether the same essence that the producer has, all perfection is to be attributed to them and every imperfection removed from them; for the one person is of as great perfection as the other.

units.la: III. Plures personæ simpliciter improductæ esse nequeunt, secus tolleretur ordo concordantiæ & Societas divina perfectione digna, & introduceretur confusio, discordantia & superfluitas, ut ex congrua applicatione videre est.
units.tr: III. Several persons cannot be simply unproduced, otherwise the order of harmony and the divine society worthy of perfection would be destroyed, and confusion, discord and superfluity would be introduced, as is seen from a suitable application.

units.la: IV. Licet intellectus & voluntas divina non differant re, sed ratione, sintque unum & idem, attamen sunt duo principia formalia productionum revera diversarum : Nam resta ratio omnino debet concedere duo principia admirabilia quidem, attamen verissima, scilicet
units.tr: IV. Although the divine intellect and will do not differ in reality but in concept, and are one and the same, nevertheless they are two formal principles of really diverse productions. For sound reason must necessarily concede two principles, admirable indeed yet most true, namely:

units.la: 1. Quòd unâ res absolutè prima necessario sit res plures respectivè,
units.tr: 1. That one thing which is absolutely first is necessarily many things relatively.

units.la: 2 Quòd unâ res simplicissima, & simpliciter prima in se possit producere actus revera diversos, eosq; in se eminenter continere. Nisi etenim haec principia concedantur, nulla multitudo poterit resolvi in ordinatam & congruam unitatem.
units.tr: 2. That one most simple thing, and simply first in itself, can produce acts really diverse, and eminently contain them in itself. For unless these principles are granted, no multitude can be resolved into an ordered and congruous unity.

units.la: Hic autem specialiter notandum, quod unica persona producta non possit adaequate productivitatem Intellectus & voluntatis divinae, sed requirantur omnino duae, secus nec duae illae, persona prima, nec producendi modus haberet infinitam perfectionem, quia modus producendi per intellectum non potest compensare modum producendi per voluntatem, quia productio per voluntatem formaliter dicit perfectionem infinitam.
units.tr: Here, however, it must be noted especially that a single produced person cannot adequately express the productive power of the divine intellect and will; rather, two are altogether required. Otherwise neither the first person nor the mode of producing would have infinite perfection, because the mode of producing through the intellect cannot compensate for the mode of producing through the will, since production through the will formally implies infinite perfection.

units.la: E [?] ftu [?] fteri [?] I. [?] utsi [?] tura [?] utili [?] veni [?] abe [?] nimi [?] reti [?] esti [?] II [?] ciali [?] nibu [?] proc [?] creat [?] senta [?]
