units.la: CAP. XVI. De Demonstratione S. S. Trinitatis à posteriori, eaq; communiori.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI. On the Demonstration of the Most Holy Trinity a Posteriori, and the More General Kind

units.la: Hactenus demonstratio à priori, jam sequi-tur demonstratio à posteriori, quâ ex constitu-tione ac proprietatibus creaturarum my-sterium hoc demonstratur.
units.tr: Hitherto the demonstration a priori; now follows the demonstration a posteriori, by which this mystery is demonstrated from the constitution and properties of creatures.

units.la: I. Demonstratio hæc non est tam evidens ut superior, quia nos veram Anatomen creaturarum non rectè intelligimus; Est tamen utilissima, præsertim in congruis similibus inveniendis & explicandis; procedit autem non ab æquali ad æquale, sed à minori ad majus, hoc nimirum principio innixa, quæ perfectio appa-ret in creaturis, ea longè nobiliori modo ac gradu est in creatore.
units.tr: I. This demonstration is not as evident as the former, because we do not rightly understand the true anatomy of creatures. It is nevertheless most useful, especially in finding and explaining fitting analogies. It proceeds not from like to like, but from the lesser to the greater, resting upon this principle: whatever perfection appears in creatures, is in the Creator in a far nobler manner and degree.

units.la: II. Demonstratio hæc est communior vel specialior: Illa est quæ observat proprietates omnibus creaturis communes, adeoque fermè procedit ex principiis metaphysicis: Prout creaturæ sunt nobiliores, ita illustriùs repræsentant hoc mysterium, hinc in ignobilioribus dicitur hujus mysterii vestigium, in nobi-lioribus vero imago & similitudo, ut in Angelo & homine.
units.tr: II. This demonstration is either more general or more specific. The former observes the properties common to all creatures, and so proceeds almost from metaphysical principles. The more noble the creatures, the more clearly they represent this mystery. Hence in the less noble things it is called a vestige of this mystery, but in the nobler ones an image and likeness, as in the angel and in man.

units.la: III. Ex communibus omnium Creaturarum proprietatibus, sic procedimus,
units.tr: III. From the properties common to all creatures we proceed thus:

units.la: 1. Si omne ens creatum est unum, verum, bo-num; Ergo in Deo est ordo ille personarum quem supra posuimus.
units.tr: 1. If every created being is one, true, and good, then in God there is that order of persons which we laid down above.

units.la: Ratio consequentia est, quia perfectio creaturarum est a perfectione creatoris, adeoque est ejus adumbratio: Deinde quia unitas entis transcendentalis est intima ac essentialis ejus cum seipso congruentia, id est, prima ac radicalis & possibilitas & operativitas; Veritas autem est intima illa entis assimilativitas, quâ sibi potest assimilare alia. Bonitas itaque est intima illa entis assimilativitas quâ potest se aliis communicare, seu radicalis illa assimila-tivitas cum aliis. Atque ex his tribus entium affectionibus, effluunt omnes ipsorum habi-tudines & operationes, & ad eas revocari que-unt, prima autem est radix secundæ, & secun-da tertiæ.
units.tr: The reason for the consequence is that the perfection of creatures comes from the perfection of the Creator and so is its shadow. Further, the unity of a being, as transcendental, is its intrinsic and essential agreement with itself, that is, its primal and radical both possibility and operativity. Truth, however, is that intrinsic assimilability of a being by which it can assimilate other things to itself. Goodness, then, is that intrinsic assimilability of a being by which it can communicate itself to others, or that radical assimilability towards others. And from these three affections of beings all their habitudes and operations flow, and they can be traced back to them; the first is the root of the second, and the second of the third.

units.la: Minor constat ex Metaphysicis.
units.tr: The minor premise is established from the metaphysicians.

units.la: 2. Si omne ens creatum necessario dicit respectum ad causam triplicem, Originalem, Exemplarem & finalem, sequitur quòd ordo personarum à nobis positus sit in Deo. Atqui verum prius, ergo & post. Ratio consequentiæ est quia tres illæ causæ evidentissimè ac distin-ctissimè debent reperiri in primo ente, secus transcendentalis hic creaturarum respectus esset absurdus & sine fundamento; At sine Trinitate personarum locum habere nequit, hinc Pater respondet primæ causæ originali, filius, Exemplari, & Spiritus sanctus, finali, quia in eo est ultima & perfectissima quies. Atq; hæc est basis altera catholicæ panharmoniæ rerum. Itaq;, nisi veritati manifestam vim facere velimus, fatendum est omnium rerum panharmoniâ fundari in sacro-sancta Trinitate, ipsamque esse omnis ordinis, fontem, norma, & finem. Ipsâ cognitâ & agnitâ, universa natura & Scriptura, mera lux est; Ipsâ verò ignorata vel negata, nil nisi tenebræ & horrendum chaos.
units.tr: 2. If every created being necessarily implies a respect to a threefold cause, original, exemplary, and final, it follows that the order of persons which we have posited is in God. But the first is true; therefore so is the second. The reason for the consequence is that these three causes must be found most evidently and most distinctly in the first being; otherwise this transcendental respect of creatures would be absurd and without foundation. But it cannot hold without the Trinity of persons. Hence the Father answers to the first cause, the original; the Son to the exemplary; and the Holy Spirit to the final, because in him is the ultimate and most perfect rest. And this is the second basis of the Catholic harmony of things. Therefore, unless we wish to do violence to manifest truth, we must confess that the harmony of all things is founded on the most holy Trinity, and that it is itself the source, norm, and end of all order. With it known and acknowledged, all nature and Scripture is pure light; without it, or with it ignored or denied, there is nothing but darkness and a horrible chaos.

units.la: Minor sive assumptio patet satis ex metaphysicis & logicis, hæ etenim causæ requiruntur ad quemlibet effectum; unde etiam in quolibet ente creato perpendenda est emanatio, manatio, & remanatio, sive egressus, progressus & regressus. Hæc duo argumenta metaphysica egregiè illustrant & confirmant.
units.tr: The minor premise, or assumption, is sufficiently plain from metaphysics and logic: these causes are required for every effect. Hence in every created being one must also weigh emanation, outflow, and return remanation, that is, egress, progress, and regress. These two metaphysical arguments illustrate and confirm this admirably.

units.la: CAP. XVII. De Demonstratione specia-liori à posteriori.
units.tr: CAP. XVII. On the more specific demonstration a posteriori.

units.la: Demonstratio à posteriori specialiter procedit vel ex entibus creatis intelligentibus, vel ex non intelligentibus.
units.tr: A demonstration a posteriori proceeds in a more specific way either from created intelligent beings or from non-intelligent ones.

units.la: 1. Entia intelligentia sunt Spiritus, Angeli scilicet & animæ rationales, quæ hîc conjungemus, & quidem hoc pacto,
units.tr: 1. Intelligent beings are spirits, namely angels and rational souls, which we will join together here, and indeed in this way:

units.la: Si in spiritus creatos prima ac radicalis potentia immediatè resultat ex eorum essentia, & ab illa producitur mens, & ab his Voluntas, (idque tum de facultatibus, tum de actibus intelligendo) sequitur quod in Deo sit talis ordo.
units.tr: If in created spirits the first and radical power results immediately from their essence, and from it the mind is produced, and from these the will (and this both as to their faculties and as to their acts of understanding), it follows that there is such an order in God.

units.la: Ratio consequentiæ est, quia inconveniens est ut hic perfectissimus ordo reperiatur in creaturis, quæ sunt imago Dei, & non reperiatur in Deo. An autem hæ tres facultates in spiritibus creatis reipsa differant? An verò sint unum? Controvertitur inter Philosophos, argumentum tamen manet firmum.
units.tr: The reason for the consequence is that it is unfitting for this most perfect order to be found in creatures, which are the image of God, and not to be found in God. Whether these three faculties in created spirits actually differ, or whether they are one, is disputed among the philosophers; the argument nevertheless stands firm.

units.la: II. Ex creaturis non intelligentibus sive corporibus sic demonstratur hoc mysterium,
units.tr: II. From non-intelligent creatures, or bodies, this mystery is demonstrated as follows:

units.la: Omne corpus constat tribus principiis hypostaticis quæ vocant, scilicet sale, mercurio & Sulphure, quorum secundum oritur ex primo, tertium ex secundo & primo: Hæc tria sunt accuratissimè maximeque proportionaliter interse unita, ita ut hæc constitutio naturaliter arguit aliquam perfectionem in creatore; Ergo summa ternaria perfectio est in Deo.
units.tr: Every body consists of three hypostatic principles, which they call salt, mercury and sulphur, of which the second arises from the first, and the third from the second and the first. These three are most closely and most proportionally united with one another, so that this constitution naturally points to some perfection in the Creator. Therefore a threefold perfection in sum is in God.

units.la: Huc quoque pertinet quod omne corpus animatum constat tribus hisce non solum Sale, Mercurio, & Sulphure, sed in specie corpore anima & spiritu, pulvere, aquâ & oleo (per salem intelligitur condivitas[?], & per mercurium, receptivitas[?]) unde oritur vehemens quasi pinguedo.
units.tr: To this also belongs the fact that every animated body consists of these three, not only salt, mercury and sulphur, but specifically of body, soul and spirit, dust, water and oil (by salt is understood condivitas[?], and by mercury receptivitas[?]), whence arises a kind of vehement fatness.

units.la: Hæc tria principia, nimirum Salem, Mercurium, Sulphur, non proprie sed propter maximam analogiam, & propter defectum vocabulorum vocamus ita.
units.tr: We call these three principles, namely salt, mercury and sulphur, thus not properly but on account of the great analogy and for lack of words.

units.la: In singulis autem corporibus tria illa principia occurrere demonstratur partim ratione, partim experientia.
units.tr: That these three principles are found in each body is demonstrated partly by reason, partly by experience.

units.la: Ratione, hoc pacto, Omne corpus est compositum, Ergo constat ex pluribus, non ex duobus, quia extrema malè junguntur sine medio; Ergo ex tribus, nam hic numerus suf-ficit, estque proportione convenientissimus.
units.tr: By reason, in this way: every body is composite; therefore it consists of more than two, since extremes are badly joined without a mean; therefore of three, for this number is sufficient and is most fitting in proportion.

units.la: Experientia, quia scientissima illa corporum naturalium anatome terminum illum admo-dum demonstrat aperte.
units.tr: By experience, because that most exact anatomy of natural bodies demonstrates this term quite openly.

units.la: Ternarium in omnibus fere, numerum videtur amâsse natura, annon ut S. S. Trinitatis mysterium quodammodo adumbraret.
units.tr: Nature seems to have loved the number three in almost all things, perhaps so that it might in some way foreshadow the mystery of the Holy Trinity.

units.la: In naturæ sexu, mas est, fœmina, & ex illis duobus Hermaphroditus: principia rerum naturalium vulgo constituuntur, materia forma & privatio: partes principes hominis sunt Cor, Cerebrum & Jecur; Spiritus tres, Animalis, Vitalis, & naturalis; Eorum vasa, seu canales tres, Nervi, Arteria, Vena &c.
units.tr: In the sex of nature there is male, female, and from these two the hermaphrodite. The principles of natural things are commonly given as matter, form and privation. The principal parts of man are the heart, the brain and the liver; the spirits are three, animal, vital and natural; their vessels or channels are also three, the nerves, the arteries, the veins, etc.

units.la: CAP. XVIII. De Demonstratione ex mathematicis, & in specie de Triangulo.
units.tr: CHAP. XVIII. On demonstration from the mathematical arts, and especially on the triangle.

units.la: HActenus fuere argumenta metaphysica, pneumatica & physica, sequitur ut etiam quædam ex mathematicis in medium producamus mus ad S.S. hoc mysterium Trinitatis perfo-narum, in Dei unitate essentiali, quodammodo demonstrandum.
units.tr: So far these have been the metaphysical, pneumatological and physical arguments. It follows that we should also bring forward some arguments from the mathematical sciences, to demonstrate in some measure this holy mystery of the Trinity of persons within the essential unity of God.

units.la: I. Ex Arithmetica; Ubi maxime notandum quod ex primo fit secundus, ex primo & secundo fit ternarius, modo perfectissimo: Ergo summa illa perfectio est in Deo.
units.tr: I. From arithmetic. Here it is especially to be noted that from the first comes the second, and from the first and second comes the third, in the most perfect way. Therefore that supreme perfection is in God.

units.la: II. Ex Geometria, ubi ex puncti longitudi-ne, latitudine, & altitudine nascitur omnis dimensio, etiam argumentum desumi potest.
units.tr: II. From geometry, where every dimension arises from the length, breadth and height of a point, an argument can also be drawn.

units.la: III. Sed Triangulum praecipue mysterium hoc egregie demonstrat; Ejus itaque & figuram & ἐξήγησιν[?] hic apponere fusius libet, prout id ipsum nobis indigitare solebat Eximius Vir Dei, ὁ νῦν ἐν ἁγίοις[?], Reverendus ac Praeclarissimus Vir, Dominus Samuel Grynaeus in Ecclesia Basileensi Pastor & Theologus Summus, olim praeceptor noster plurimum colendus.
units.tr: III. But the triangle especially illustrates this mystery admirably. I am pleased to set out its figure and explanation here at greater length, as that outstanding man of God, now among the saints [ὁ νῦν ἐν ἁγίοις], the Reverend and most distinguished Mr. Samuel Grynaeus, minister in the church of Basel and a most eminent theologian, my former teacher whom I greatly honour, was wont to point out to us.

units.la: IV. Primo itaque hoc pacto figuretur Triangulum cum peripheria,
units.tr: IV. First, then, the triangle is drawn in this way, with its circumference.

units.la: V. Adumbrantur autem & demonstrantur hoc Schemate, varia omnino in Deo mysteria summa, & quidem
units.tr: V. By this diagram are shadowed forth and demonstrated various great mysteries in God, namely:

units.la: 1. Vnitas & communitas Essentiæ divinæ communi centro peripheriæ & Arearum Trianguli; ita ut tres numero distincti anguli unam numero aream, radii unum centrum, anguli unam peripheriam continent, sic tres personæ unam numero essentiam habent in Deo.
units.tr: 1. The unity and communion of the divine essence: as the three angles, distinct in number, contain one area in number, and the radii one centre, and the angles one circumference, so the three persons have one essence in number in God.

units.la: 2. Trinitas[?] personarum etiam demonstratur tribus angulis A, B, C.
units.tr: 2. The Trinity of persons is also demonstrated by the three angles A, B, C.

units.la: a. Ut nec pauciores nec plures anguli sunt in Triangulo, ita tres personæ, non plures nec pauciores sunt in unitate Essentiæ Dei.
units.tr: a. As a triangle has neither fewer nor more than three angles, so there are neither fewer nor more than three persons in the unity of the essence of God.

units.la: b. Ut tres anguli figuram Trianguli concludunt[?], ita tres personae Essentiam divinam perficiunt.
units.tr: b. As the three angles complete the figure of the triangle, so the three persons complete the divine essence.

units.la: c. Ut angulus, A, respicit angulum, B, & uterque angulus A & B respiciunt simul angulum C, nec ullus praeterea respectus & re-latio requiritur; ita Deus Pater refertur ad Fi-lium, & uterque simul ad Spiritum Sanctum, sicque relatio divina asoluitur[?].
units.tr: c. As angle A looks to angle B, and each of the angles A and B looks at once to angle C, and no further looking or relation is required, so God the Father is referred to the Son, and both together to the Holy Spirit; and thus the divine relation is complete.

units.la: d. ut tres anguli numerica differentia & re-latione differunt, ita tres illae personae in Deo.
units.tr: d. As the three angles differ in numerical distinction and in relation, so do those three persons in God.

units.la: 3. Demonstratur personarum aequalitas,
units.tr: 3. The equality of the persons is demonstrated:

units.la: e. Omnes tres anguli sunt aequales, ita etiam tres personae: Quivis angulus constat ex lateribus aequalibus, & aequali basi, ita etiam quaelibet persona ex relati & correlati aequali respectu & eodem fundamento: Et deinde quilibet angulus totam aream Trianguli continet, ita quaelibet persona S. S. Trinitatis integram divinam essentiam habet.
units.tr: e. All three angles are equal, and so are the three persons. Each angle consists of equal sides and an equal base, and so each person consists of the relating and the related, with equal respect and the same foundation. Moreover, each angle contains the whole area of the triangle, and so each person of the Holy Trinity has the whole divine essence.

units.la: β. Omnes radii a centro ad angulos sunt aequales, utpote radii ejusdem peripheriae, ita & personae sunt aequales.
units.tr: β. All the radii from the centre to the angles are equal, as being radii of the same circumference; so the persons are equal.

units.la: γ. Iterum ut tres anguli & tres radii unam peripheriam continent, ita personae unicam essentiam[?].
units.tr: γ. Again, as three angles and three radii make up one circumference, so the persons make up one essence.

units.la: 4. Demonstratur personarum differentia ab Essentia, & ab invicem.
units.tr: 4. The difference of the persons from the essence, and from one another, is demonstrated.

units.la: Ab Essentia
units.tr: From the essence

units.la: 1. Ut angulus quivis non est area, ab area tamen reipsa non distinguitur, cum quivis angulus totam occupet aream; Ita quaelibet persona ut sic, id est, personalitas non est ipsa essen-tia divina, ab ea tamen re non distinguitur, quia quaevis persona in se considerata totam Essentiam habet.
units.tr: 1. As any angle is not the area, yet in reality is not distinguished from the area, since any angle occupies the whole area, so any person as such, that is, personality, is not the divine essence itself, yet is not really distinct from it, because each person considered in itself has the whole essence.

units.la: 2. Ut quilibet angulus aream Trianguli terminat, ita quaelibet persona terminat divinam Essentiam; Seu ut quilibet angulus areae ὅρον ὑπάρξεως[?], modum Subsistendi dat, ita quaelibet persona Essentiae divinae modus subsistentiae est.
units.tr: 2. As each angle terminates the area of the triangle, so each person terminates the divine essence; or, as each angle gives the area its boundary of existence [ὅρον ὑπάρξεως], that is, its mode of subsisting, so each person is a mode of subsistence of the divine essence.

units.la: Ab invicem differentia etiam ostenditur,
units.tr: The difference of the persons from one another is also shown:

units.la: Ut angulus A, non est angulus B, nec ille vel iste est angulus C, & vice versa, ita persona Patris non est persona Filii, nec illa, vel ista, est persona Spiritus Sancti: Ut singuli tres nonnisi numero distincti, ita singulae personae numero tantum distinctae.
units.tr: As angle A is not angle B, and neither this nor that is angle C, and vice versa, so the person of the Father is not the person of the Son, nor is that or this the person of the Holy Spirit. As the three angles are distinct only in number, so the persons are distinct only in number.

units.la: f.[?] Personarum Relationes, hoc etiam modo repraesentatae demonstrantur.
units.tr: f. The relations of the persons are demonstrated and represented in this way also.

units.la: 1. Ut angulus A, linea a, b, respicit angulum, B, & hic illum eadem lineâ; item ut angulus, A, lineâ a, c, & angulus lineâ, b, c, efficiunt & respiciunt angulum C; Ita Pater & Filius respiciunt Spiritum Sanctum, & hic respicit simul utrumque, Pater relatione reciprocâ respicit Filium & Filius Patrem.
units.tr: 1. As angle A, by the line a, b, looks to angle B, and this one back to it by the same line; and as angle A by line a, c, and angle B by line b, c, make up and look to angle C; so the Father and the Son look to the Holy Spirit, and he looks at once to both, the Father looking reciprocally to the Son and the Son to the Father by relation.

units.la: 2. Ut angulus A, ductu lineæ a, b, generat angulum B, & sic generatur; & ex A, lineâ a, c, & ex, B, lineâ b, c, producit angulum C. Ita Pater generat Filium, & hic generatur, & a Patre & Filio procedit Spiritus Sanctus.
units.tr: 2. As angle A, by the drawing of line a, b, generates angle B, and so is generated; and from A by line a, c, and from B by line b, c, it produces angle C. So the Father begets the Son, who is begotten, and from the Father and the Son proceeds the Holy Spirit.

units.la: 6. Addimus & Essentiæ S. S. Trinitatis pro-prietates.
units.tr: 6. We add also the properties of the essence of the Holy Trinity.

units.la: 1. Ut unum numero Triangulum, una peripheria, unum centrum, ita unus Deus.
units.tr: 1. As the triangle is one in number, one circumference, one centre, so God is one.

units.la: 2. Ut Triangulum figura prima, ita Deus est primum Ens.
units.tr: 2. As the triangle is the first figure, so God is the first being.

units.la: 3. Ut peripheria figura est simplicissima, ita Deus est simplicissimum Ens.
units.tr: 3. As the circumference is the simplest figure, so God is the simplest being.

units.la: 4. Ut peripheria principio & fine caret, ita Deus est æternus.
units.tr: 4. As the circumference has no beginning or end, so God is eternal.

units.la: 5. Ut peripheria est figura omnium perfectissima & capacissima, ita Deus est summè perfectissimus & immensus &c.
units.tr: 5. As the circumference is the most perfect and most capacious of all figures, so God is supremely perfect and immense, etc.

units.la: 7. Denique Cognitio Dei, Triangulo nostrostro optime adumbratur & demonstratur,
units.tr: 7. Lastly, the knowledge of God is very well shadowed forth and demonstrated by our triangle:

units.la: 1. Ut Triangulum non cognoscimus absque cognitione angulorum, ita nec Deum absque personarum S. S. Trinitatis consideratione.
units.tr: 1. As we cannot know a triangle without knowing its angles, so neither can we know God without considering the persons of the Holy Trinity.

units.la: 2. Ut qui unum angulum cognoscit, cognoscit & reliquos, ita qui unam S. S. Trinitatis personam congruè cognoscit, cognoscit & reliquas, aut saltem reliquas cognoscere debet & potest.
units.tr: 2. As one who knows one angle knows the others also, so one who rightly knows one person of the Holy Trinity knows the others also, or at least ought and is able to know the others.

units.la: 3. Ut qui unum angulum tollit, tollit Triangulum, ita qui negat unam S. S. Trinitatis personam, negat Deum.
units.tr: 3. As one who removes one angle removes the triangle, so one who denies one person of the Holy Trinity denies God.

units.la: 4. Ut quadratura circuli ineffabilis, ita Dei & S.S, Trinitatis cognitio est incomprehensibilis.
units.tr: 4. As the squaring of the circle is unspeakable, so the knowledge of God and of the Holy Trinity is incomprehensible.

units.la: 5. Ut omnes figuræ ex Triangulo oriuntur, & in Triangulum resolvuntur, ita omnes omnino creaturæ à Deo sunt, & ad Deum divinasque personas referuntur.
units.tr: 5. As all figures arise from the triangle and are resolved into the triangle, so all creatures altogether are from God and are referred to God and the divine persons.

units.la: Atque hæc sunt quæ de summis hisce mysteriis impræsentiarum ad eorum demonstrationem, ex lumine rectæ rationis afferre volui-mus, quæ certè sapientioribus ex Ethnicis non ita abstrusa fuere, ut clamitant nonnulli, videatur non solum Plato, Epistola secunda ad Dionem, & aliis locis, dum in Deo primum, secundum & tertium principium perfectissimum docet; Sed & Trismegistus, in pimandro, sectione prima, de Deo, mente, verbo & spiritu meditationem instituens, &c. Τὰ γὰρ ἀόρατα τῆς Θεοῦ ἀπὸ κτίσεως κόσμῳ τοῖς ποιήμασι νοούμενα καθοράται, ἥ τε ἀΐδιος αὐτοῦ δύναμις καὶ Θεότης, εἰς τὸ εἶναι αὐτὸς [?] ἀναπολογήτους, διότι γνόντες τὸν Θεὸν, οὐχ ὡς Θεὸν ἐδόξασαν, ut perquam optimè ait summus Christianorum Gentilium & judæorum Theologus & Philosophus.
units.tr: These are the things concerning these supreme mysteries which, for the present, I have wished to offer for their demonstration from the light of right reason. They were certainly not so obscure to the wiser among the Gentiles as some clamour; see not only Plato, in the second letter to Dion and elsewhere, where he teaches that in God there is a first, second and third most perfect principle; but also Trismegistus, in the Pimander, first section, where he sets out a meditation on God, mind, word and spirit, etc. "For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse: because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God" [Τὰ γὰρ ἀόρατα αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ κτίσεως κόσμου τοῖς ποιήμασι νοούμενα καθορᾶται, ἥ τε ἀΐδιος αὐτοῦ δύναμις καὶ θειότης, εἰς τὸ εἶναι αὐτοὺς ἀναπολογήτους· διότι γνόντες τὸν θεὸν οὐχ ὡς θεὸν ἐδόξασαν], as the most excellent theologian and philosopher of Christians, Gentiles and Jews puts it most admirably.

units.la: CAP. XIX. De operibus Dei.
units.tr: CAP. XIX. Concerning the works of God.

units.la: Sic fuit consideratio Dei respectiva, respectu sui ipsius, restat ut eum consideremus respectu creaturarum.
units.tr: Thus far we have considered God in relation to himself; it remains that we consider him in relation to creatures.

units.la: Hic itaque offert sese locus insignis de operibus Dei,
units.tr: Here, accordingly, presents itself a notable topic concerning the works of God.

units.la: I. Unde quàm diligentissimè principia generalia metaphysica, itemq; axiomata de Deo supra demonstrata hic sunt repetenda.
units.tr: I. Hence the general metaphysical principles and the axioms about God demonstrated above must be repeated here as carefully as possible.

units.la: II. Omnium Dei operum summopere notandus tandus finis summus & Architectonicus, qui est congruentissima divinæ gloriæ manife-statio.
units.tr: II. The highest and architectonic end of all God's works is to be especially noted: it is the most fitting manifestation of the divine glory.

units.la: Hinc primo, divina gloria est summa & universalissima omnium operum mensura; Et secundo Deus non hisce indiget, cum opera producantur non ex ejus imperfectione & necessitate, sed perfectione quam suis creaturis liberrime communicat; Et sicut Sol non indiget rerum inferiorum communione, sed tamen amplissimam suam lucem & communica-tivitatem, creaturis communicat & patefacit propter gloriam.
units.tr: From this, first, the divine glory is the chief and most universal measure of all works; and second, God does not need these things, since the works are produced not from any imperfection or necessity in him, but from the perfection which he communicates most freely to his creatures. And just as the Sun does not need the fellowship of lower things, yet communicates and displays its very ample light and its power of communicating to creatures, for the sake of glory.

units.la: II. Opera Dei sunt duplicia, Deliberatio & Executio decreti.
units.tr: II. The works of God are twofold: deliberation and execution of the decree.

units.la: Cum Deus sit Spiritus infinitus & perfectissimus, utique in ipsius voluntate dabitur [?] deliberatio & decretum ab æterno:
units.tr: Since God is an infinite and most perfect Spirit, there must surely be in his will deliberation and decree from eternity.

units.la: III. Decretum est divinæ voluntatis deliberatio & sententia, quâ omnia omnino in univer-sa rerum natura occurrentia, tam quoad essentiam, quàm quoad modum & gradum, perfectis-sime ab æterno præordinata sunt; Hæc satis appo-site prædestinatio vocabitur, quæ ob rerum crea-tarum varietatem variè considerari poterit.
units.tr: III. The decree is the deliberation and judgement of the divine will, by which all things whatsoever occurring in the whole nature of things, both as to their essence and as to their mode and degree, have been most perfectly foreordained from eternity. This may quite fittingly be called predestination, which, because of the variety of created things, can be considered in various ways.

units.la: IV. Executio est divinæ potentiæ efficien-tia tia quâ in tempore, reipsa, omnes creaturas actu-at & ordinat, prout ab æterno præordinaverat.
units.tr: IV. Execution is the efficacy of the divine power by which, in time, actually, he activates and orders all creatures, just as he had foreordained from eternity.

units.la: Ubi notanda sunt sequentia,
units.tr: Here the following points are to be noted:

units.la: 1. Quòd decretum & Executio accuratissimè inter se congruant, hæcque illius speculum, illud hujus exemplar.
units.tr: 1. That the decree and the execution agree most exactly with each other, the one being the mirror of the other, the latter the pattern of the former.

units.la: 2. Quod respondeant sibi ordine retrogrado, ita ut primum in intentione, ultimum sit in executione, & vicissim.
units.tr: 2. That they correspond to each other in reverse order, so that what is first in intention is last in execution, and vice versa.

units.la: 3. Quòd utrumq; nitatur divinâ omnisuf-ficientiâ, & omniefficientiâ.
units.tr: 3. That both rest upon the divine all-sufficiency and all-efficiency.

units.la: V. Executio est rerum productio vel conser-vatio, ac Gubernatio quò concursus.
units.tr: V. Execution is the production or conservation of things, and government, which is by concurrence.

units.la: VI. Productio est actio Dei quâ Deus facit ut omnes creaturæ, omnesq; ipsarum perfectiones primò sint.
units.tr: VI. Production is the action of God by which God causes all creatures, and all their perfections, first to be.

units.la: Hæc primò est universalissima creatio, & dein formatio quorundam individuorum. In hisce nō valdè opus, ut multum simus prolixi.
units.tr: This is first the most universal creation, and then the formation of certain individuals. On these matters there is no great need for us to be very lengthy.

units.la: CAP. XX. De Conservatione.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX. On Conservation.

units.la: COnservatio est actio Dei quâ Deus facit ut omnes creaturæ ipsarumque facultates congruè durent.
units.tr: Conservation is God's action by which he causes all creatures and their faculties to endure in a fitting way.

units.la: I. Confervat Deus res quoad vel individua, vel species. Quoad species confervat eas res quae sunt corruptibiles, hoc est, morti, vel destructioni, quoad individua, obnoxiae, qua-lia sunt mixta, tam animata quam inanimata.
units.tr: I. God conserves things either as to their species or as to their individuals. As to species, he conserves those things which are corruptible, that is, liable to death or destruction, such as mixed bodies, both animate and inanimate; as to individuals, he conserves things that are subject to destruction in the same way.

units.la: Quoad individua, confervat res quae sunt, & videmus eas incorruptibiles quoad individua, quales sunt spiritus & corpora simplicia: Interim & corruptibilium rerum individua, eorumque agendi vires confervat, quousque ipsi libet.
units.tr: As to individuals, he conserves things that exist, and we see that some are incorruptible as individuals, such as spirits and simple bodies. Meanwhile he also conserves the individuals of corruptible things, and their powers of acting, for as long as he pleases.

units.la: II. Necessaria rebus creatis haec est conservatio, quia res creatae omnibus modis a creatore, dependet, quoad fieri, quoad permanere & operari: Hinc cessante conservatione hac prorsus in nihilum abiret creatura.
units.tr: II. This conservation is necessary for created things, because created things depend on the Creator in every way: as to their coming into being, as to their remaining in being, and as to their operating. Hence, if this conservation ceased, the creature would pass utterly into nothing.

units.la: III. Confervat Deus res immediate vel mediate: Immediate conservari dicuntur quae foli Deo subjiciuntur, & a causarum fecundarum influxu non dependent, ita confervat Deus Angelos, coelum & stellas. Haec conservatio dicitur a nonnullis creatio continuata, & sola ratione creditur a creatione differre, quia licet creatio novitatem includit quam excludit conservatio, & praecedentem existentiam excludit, quam conservatio includit. Mediate confervantur quæ ita Deo subjiciuntur, ut ni-hilominus quoq; à causarum secundarum in-fluxu pendeant, eoque conservantur; Ita con-servat Deus mundum sublunarem per cœle-stem & per mutua sublunarium ministeria.
units.tr: III. God conserves things either immediately or mediately. Those are said to be conserved immediately which are subject to God alone and do not depend on the influence of secondary causes; thus God conserves the angels, the heavens and the stars. This conservation is called by some "continued creation", and it is believed to differ from creation only in our way of reasoning, since creation includes a newness which conservation excludes, and excludes a prior existence which conservation includes. Things are conserved mediately when they are so subject to God that they nevertheless also depend on the influence of secondary causes, and are conserved by means of it; thus God conserves the sublunary world through the heavenly bodies and through the mutual ministries of sublunary things.

units.la: IV. Gubernatio est actio Dei quâ omnes & singulas res creatas sapientissimè & efficatissimè ad suum finem ordinat.
units.tr: IV. Government is God's action by which he orders all and each created thing most wisely and most effectively to its end.

units.la: Vel Gubeanatio est quâ Deus pro summa sua authoritate, sapientia, & potentia de rebus omnibus disponit, easque pro arbitrio suo regit.
units.tr: Or, government is that by which God, by his supreme authority, wisdom and power, disposes of all things and rules them at his pleasure.

units.la: V. Gubernat Deus omnia Sapientissime, Liberrime, Potentissime & Optime.
units.tr: V. God governs all things wisely, freely, powerfully and best.

units.la: Sapientissime, quia oculis ejus omnia sunt apertissima, omnia aptissimè disposita, effectis convenientissimæ causæ destinatæ, & in bonos certosque fines omnia destinata: Li-berrime quia à nemine cogitur ad universi administrationem, neque ex naturæ necessita-te, extra se quicquam agit, sed ex arbitrii sui plenissima libertate. Potentissime quia solo nutu jussuque, quidquid vult assequitur, sine ulla molestia, sine defatigatione, neque actio ejus ullius viribus inhiberi potest. Optime, quia nunquam & nuspiam in agendo deficit. nullo intellectus errore seductus, nullaque voluntatis ἀταξίας à bonitatis tramite abreptus.
units.tr: Wisely, because all things lie most open to his eyes, all things are most aptly disposed, the most suitable causes are appointed for their effects, and all things are destined to good and certain ends. Freely, because he is compelled by no one to the administration of the universe, nor does he act outside himself from necessity of nature, but from the fullest liberty of his will. Powerfully, because by a mere nod and command he accomplishes whatever he wills, without any trouble and without weariness, and his action can be hindered by no one's strength. Best, because he never and nowhere fails in acting, is led astray by no error of the intellect, and is carried away from the path of goodness by no disorder [ἀταξία] of the will.

units.la: Atque sese offert immensus meditationis campus, dum consideramus in specie res singulas quae à Deo diversimode gubernantur.
units.tr: And an immense field of meditation opens before us when we consider in particular the individual things that are governed by God in various ways.

units.la: V. Irrationales creaturas praeter conservationem, gubernat Deus solo impulsu ad fines praestitutos, quos ipse non agnoscunt. Sicut ab initio Deus voluit res principiis internis diversas producere, ita etiam diversimode, & ad illa ipsa principia accommodatissime, singulas gubernat: Actiones enim Dei non pugnant inter se, & Dei gubernatio non tollit sed ordinat principia creationis.
units.tr: V. Besides conservation, God governs irrational creatures only by impulse toward the ends appointed for them, which they do not recognise. Just as from the beginning God willed to produce things diverse in their internal principles, so also he governs each of them in diverse ways, and most suitably to those very principles; for the actions of God do not conflict with one another, and God's government does not abolish but orders the principles of creation.

units.la: 2. Gubernatio Dei in inanimatis est quâ Deus illa ad actus & fines movet, secundum vires illis insitas, naturali quadam ῥοπή, citra ullam actus vel finis ad quem feruntur cognitionem, & in operando determinationem, sic levia sursum, gravia deorsum, interno naturae suo principio feruntur.
units.tr: 2. God's government of inanimate things is that by which he moves them to their acts and ends, according to the powers implanted in them, by a certain natural inclination [ῥοπή], without any knowledge of the act or end toward which they are borne and without any determination in acting. Thus light things are borne upward and heavy things downward, by their internal natural principle.

units.la: 3. Gubernatio Dei in creaturis animalibus irrationalibus spectata est illarum ad actus & ad fines suos motio, instinctu naturali, praevia cognitione & determinatione sensus, sed valde imperfecta, utpote mere sensuali, secundum quam quoque tantum ad τὸ ἡδύ, & ad τὸ χρήσιμον[?] feruntur; neque finem universalem, sed tantum particularem, nec qua talem apprehendunt, nec connexionem mediorum cum fine assequuntur.
units.tr: 3. God's government of irrational animals is regarded as their motion to their acts and ends by natural instinct, with prior perception and determination by the senses; but it is very imperfect, being merely sensory. By it they are borne only toward the pleasant [τὸ ἡδύ] and the useful [τὸ χρήσιμον]; they grasp not the universal end but only a particular one, nor do they grasp it as an end, nor do they follow the connection of means with the end.

units.la: VI. Gubernatio Dei in creaturis intelligen-tibus considerata est illarum & ad actus, & ad fines motio, conveniens naturæ principiis, tum directivis tum imperativis, intercedente quippe ac præcedente apprehensione directiva intellectus, & subsequente inclinatione & determinatione libera voluntatis, salvo itaq; mentis judicio, salvâ voluntatis libertate. Ut etenim duo ista agendi principia sibi a Deo insita habent, ita Deus per illa, & per illorum usum, illas gubernat, sine ulla vel natura vel co-actionis necessitate.
units.tr: VI. God's government of intelligent creatures is considered as the motion of these creatures both to acts and to ends, agreeing with the principles of their nature, both directive and imperative: a directive apprehension of the intellect intervenes and precedes, and a subsequent inclination and free determination of the will follows. Thus the judgment of the mind is preserved, and the liberty of the will is preserved. For just as God has implanted these two principles of acting in them, so he governs them through those principles and through their use, without any necessity either of nature or of compulsion.

units.la: CAP. XXI. De Concursu Dei.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXI. On the Concurrence of God.

units.la: UT opus Dei in rebus omnibus confer-vandis & gubernandis facilius cognosca-tur, tur, Doctrina de Dei concursu hic subjicien-da erit.
units.tr: So that the work of God in preserving and governing all things may be more easily recognised, the doctrine of God's concurrence must be set out here.

units.la: I. Concursus Dei est actio Dei qua concurrit ad quamlibet causarum secundarum operationem, sic ut immediate ac per se influat in omnem actionem creaturæ; Consequenter in omnem effectum; Sitque Deus immediata, principalis, totalis causa actionis & effectus æque atq; causa secunda.
units.tr: I. The concurrence of God is the action of God by which he concurs in the operation of any secondary cause, in such a way that he flows immediately and of himself into every action of a creature, and consequently into every effect; and God is the immediate, principal and total cause of the action and effect, just as the secondary cause is.

units.la: II. Deus in concurrendo causa est actionis causæ secundæ principalis, totalis ac immediata.
units.tr: II. God, in concurring, is the principal, total and immediate cause of the action of the secondary cause.

units.la: Est causa principalis, quia non est necesse ejus virtutem aliunde excitari; Totalis, quia in suo genere & ordine totam actionem producit; Immediata, quia ipsam actionem & effectum causæ secundæ attingit sine ullo medio.
units.tr: He is the principal cause, because his power need not be stirred up from elsewhere; total, because within his own kind and order he produces the whole action; immediate, because he touches the action and effect of the secondary cause itself without any intermediary.

units.la: III. Etsi causa prima operetur mediis secundis, tamen omnes earum actiones & effectus attingit immediate.
units.tr: III. Although the first cause works through secondary means, nevertheless he touches all their actions and effects immediately.

units.la: Deum agere mediis causis secundis, nihil est aliud, quam Deum admittere concausam, vel causam sociam & consortium alterius agentis, quod nihil impedit, quo minus omnes causarum secundarum actiones atq; esse-
units.tr: To act through secondary causes is nothing other than God admitting a concause, that is, a co-cause and partner of another agent, which prevents nothing from attaining immediately all the actions and effects of the secondary causes.

units.la: ctus[?]
units.tr: ctus[?]

units.la: Ita immediatè attingat: Quòd ut intelligatur, explicandum est, quomodo aliqua causa, & Deus, dicatur agere immediatè, alia mediatè.
units.tr: So that this may be understood, it must be explained how one cause, and God, is said to act immediately, and another mediately.

units.la: IV. Causa dicitur agere vel mediatè, vel immediatè, tum quoad suppositum, tum quoad virtutem.
units.tr: IV. A cause is said to act either mediately or immediately, both with respect to its subsistence and with respect to its power.

units.la: 1. Illa causa agit immediatè immediatione suppositi, inter quam & effectum, seu rem patientem, nullum aliud suppositum singulare per se subsistens interjectum est, quo pacto ignis urit lignum, aqua manum abluit, refrigeratque.
units.tr: 1. That cause acts immediately by immediacy of subsistence, between which and the effect, or the thing suffering, no other singular, self-subsisting subsistence is interposed; in this way fire burns wood, and water washes and cools the hand.

units.la: 2. Contra mediatè agit causa mediatione suppositi, inter quam & effectum, seu rem quæ patitur, aliud cadit suppositum, ut inter fabrum & statuam securis.
units.tr: 2. On the other hand, a cause acts mediately by mediacy of subsistence, between which and the effect, or the thing that suffers, another subsistence intervenes, as the axe does between the carpenter and the statue.

units.la: 3. Illa causa agit immediatè immediatione virtutis, quæ agit per virtutem sibi propriam, & non, ut ageret, mutuò acceptam, quo pacto ignis calore suo, sibi proprio, & ad calefaciendum non aliunde commodato, aquam calefacit.
units.tr: 3. That cause acts immediately by immediacy of power, which acts through a power proper to itself and not borrowed in order to act, as fire heats water by its own heat, which is its own and not lent from elsewhere for the purpose of heating.

units.la: 4. Contrà, illa causa agit mediatè mediatione virtutis, quæ per virtutem, non suam & sibi propriam, sed aliunde acceptam ac commodatam, operatur, ut cùm luna, lumine à sole mutuatitio, terram illuminat, aut aqua calida manum calefacit: Virtus illuminandi, non lunæ sed solis, media est inter lunam illuminan-tem & illuminationem, quæ virtus quia alteri-us est corporis, dicitur luna illuminare mediate mediatione virtutis, ist est, mediante virtute solis; Sic aqua calefacit mediante virtute ignis, unde etiam dicitur calefacere mediate me-diatione virtutis.
units.tr: 4. Conversely, that cause acts mediately by mediacy of power, which operates through a power not its own and proper, but received and lent from elsewhere; as when the moon, with light borrowed from the sun, illuminates the earth, or warm water warms the hand. The power of illuminating belongs not to the moon but to the sun, and is the intermediary between the illuminating moon and the illumination; and because that power belongs to another body, the moon is said to illuminate mediately by mediacy of power, that is, through the power of the sun. So water warms through the power of fire, whence it is also said to warm mediately by mediacy of power.

units.la: V. Deus cum quovis agente creato concurrit immediate, immediatione virtutis & suppositi. immediatione virtutis, quia agit propria virtute non aliunde commodata, cum sit ens non factum simpliciter primum & independens: Immediatione suppositi, quia per suam substantiam rem attingit, ipsa enim Dei substantia & essen-tia ejus est virtus.
units.tr: V. God concurs with every created agent immediately, both by immediacy of power and by immediacy of subsistence. By immediacy of power, because he acts by his own power and not borrowed from elsewhere, since he is simply the first and independent non-made being; by immediacy of subsistence, because he touches a thing through his own substance, for the very substance and essence of God is his power.

units.la: At inquiat quis, nulla causa secunda, hoc pacto, ageret immediate immediatione virtutis, quandoquidem omnis causa secunda virtus, a prima est quasi mutuo accepta, commodata & communicata; Respond. certe nullum agens creatum agit immediate immediatione virtutis, si per virtutem immediatam intelligas omni modo independente & nullo modo aliunde accep-tam: Sed si intelligas virtutem, licet a Deo acceptam & dependentem, causæ tamen fe- cundæ ingenitam & nativam, non aliunde, cùm jam est & operabitur ; Sicut frigus est aquæ nativum, calor verò adventitius ; Jam multa ex agentibus creatis agunt immediatè immediatione virtutis, alia non item: Breviter, distingui potest, inter agens immediatè, immediatione virtutis; in genere entis & absolutè, & agens immediatè immediatione virtutis, in certo entium genere & secundum quid.
units.tr: But someone may object: no secondary cause would then act immediately by immediacy of power, since every secondary cause's power is, as it were, received, lent and communicated from the first. I answer: certainly no created agent acts immediately by immediacy of power if by immediate power you understand power that is in every way independent and in no way received from elsewhere. But if you understand a power which, though received from God and dependent, is nevertheless innate and native to the secondary cause, and not borrowed, since it already is and will operate: just as cold is native to water while heat is adventitious. Thus many created agents act immediately by immediacy of power, others not. In short, one may distinguish between an agent acting immediately by immediacy of power in the genus of being and absolutely, and an agent acting immediately by immediacy of power in a certain genus of beings and in a qualified sense.

units.la: VI. Deum immediatè ac verè influere cooperando in omnem actionem & effectum causæ secundæ probat catholicum & verissimum axioma, modus operandi sequitur modum essendi.
units.tr: VI. That God truly and immediately flows into every action and effect of a secondary cause by cooperating is proved by the catholic and most true axiom: the mode of operating follows the mode of being.

units.la: Sic etenim concludimus, Si omnes causæ secundæ dependent à Deo in esse dependent quoque in suo operari, ita ut non minus Deus verè & immediatè concurrat ad earum operationes quam ad earum essentiam & consistentiam. Atqui omnes omnino causæ secundæ dependent à Deo quoad suum esse; Ergo.
units.tr: For thus we conclude: if all secondary causes depend on God in their being, they depend also in their operating, so that God truly and immediately concurs in their operations no less than in their essence and continuance. But all secondary causes altogether depend on God as to their being; therefore...

units.la: Tota consequentiæ ratio innititur axiomate allato, quo modo & gradu res se habet in suo esse, ita se habet in suis attributis & operationibus.
units.tr: The whole force of the consequence rests on the axiom cited: in whatever manner and degree a thing stands in its being, it stands in its attributes and operations.

units.la: Hic solent Adversarii distinguere, sed ineptè valdè, Creaturam à Deo dependere, ut permittente concedunt, ut eo efficiente negant. Profecto nulla plane est eorum distinctio; Nam si modus essendi proprius creaturae est esse dependenter à Deo non solum permittente, sed revera, physicè, & immediatè influente, sequitur ejus modum operandi pendere similiter à Deo non permittente solum, sed revera, physicè & immediatè influente; Sed est verum prius, Ergo & posterius.
units.tr: Here the adversaries are accustomed to distinguish, but very foolishly, that the creature depends on God as they concede by permission, but deny as by his efficiency. Truly there is no distinction of theirs at all. For if the proper mode of being of a creature is to be dependent on God not merely by permission, but in reality, physically and by immediate influence, it follows that its mode of operating likewise depends on God not merely by permission, but in reality, physically and by immediate influence. But the former is true; therefore the latter too.

units.la: VII. Aliquid amplius in Dei concursu dandum esse quàm virium suppeditationem, earum conservationem, aut nudam agendi permissionem, hoc modo bene demonstratur. Si Deus concessa & conservata agendi vel non agendi facultate, solum permittit creaturam agere vel non agere, tum nihil amplius praestat, cum creatura agit, quàm cum non agit, cum hoc modo agit quàm cum alio modo, cum bene agit, quàm cum male: At ista sunt absurda;
units.tr: VII. That something more must be given in God's concurrence than the supply of powers, their preservation, or a bare permission to act, is well demonstrated thus: if God, having granted and preserved the faculty of acting or not acting, merely permits the creature to act or not to act, then he does nothing more when the creature acts than when it does not act, nothing more when it acts in this way than in another, nothing more when it acts well than when it acts badly. But these things are absurd.

units.la: Ergo & absurdum est, Deum in operationibus creaturarum nihilo plus agere quàm vires dare, conservare, & permittere ut agant; Imò verò praeter ista, occasiones & incitamenta causis secundis ad agendum objicit, im-pedimenta suspendit, ipse actu cum iis influit, conconcurrit, coefficit, cooperatur, & earum actiones, concurrendo, dirigit, determinat &c.quæ plus significant quàm nudam permissionem, aut facultatis in agendo largitionem aut conservationem.
units.tr: Therefore it is also absurd that God in the operations of creatures does no more than give powers, preserve them, and permit them to act; indeed, beyond these, he sets before secondary causes occasions and incitements to act, suspends impediments, himself actually flows together with them, concurs, co-efficiently cooperates, and by concurring directs, determines and so on his creatures' actions; which signify more than a bare permission, or a grant or preservation of the faculty of acting.

units.la: VIII. Hæc efficacitas ac realitas concursus divini poni & asseri debet circa omnes omnium causarum secundarum actiones.
units.tr: VIII. This efficacy and reality of divine concurrence ought to be affirmed and asserted with respect to all the actions of all secondary causes.

units.la: Imò etiam circa illas ipsas actiones debet asseri, quæ sunt peccaminosæ, id est, afficiuntur malitiâ; dicimus expresse circa actiones malas, non circa malitiam actionum, sic enim bonæ sunt in genere entis & natura, ac suo modo entia, consequenter & dependent à Deo, cùm exercentur. Itaque licet actiones quædam respectu meræ[?] actiones non exercentur nisi dependenter à concursu divino, alioquin aliquid quod revera est, & existit, eximeretur Dei providentiæ & Efficientiæ: Quare nuda Dei permissio à nonnullis invecta circa actiones creaturarum, vel in genere vel in specie malas, figmentum est, & a Durando primum excogitatum.
units.tr: Indeed it must be asserted even with respect to those very actions which are sinful, that is, which are affected by malice; we say expressly with respect to evil actions, not with respect to the malice of the actions, for thus they are good in the genus of being and nature, and in their own way beings, and consequently they too depend on God when they are exercised. And so, although certain actions are not exercised except dependently on divine concurrence, otherwise something which really is and exists would be exempted from the providence and efficiency of God. Wherefore the bare permission of God, introduced by some with respect to the actions of creatures, whether evil in genus or in specie, is a fiction, first devised by Durandus.

units.la: CAP. XXII. De Concursu Dei praevio in specie.
units.tr: CAP. XXII. On God's Prior Concurrence in Particular.

units.la: Distingui plerumque solet concursus Dei in praevium sive praedeterminantem, & simultaneum sive concomitantem.
units.tr: God's concurrence is usually distinguished into prior, or predetermining, and simultaneous, or concomitant.

units.la: Duplex enim intelligi potest Dei motio circa voluntatem & facultatem creatam, una quasi antecedens, non tempore, sed in ignorationis, actualem concursum ad facultatis creatae actum; altera in ipso actuali concursu consistens; Illam vulgo dicunt esse ex praere-quisitis ad agendum: Per illam causae secundae moventur ad suas actiones; Per hanc vere agunt;
units.tr: God's motion upon the will and the created faculty may be understood in two ways: one, as it were antecedent, not in time but in the order of nature, which is the actual concurrence to the act of the created faculty; the other consists in the actual concurrence itself. The former, they commonly say, belongs to the prerequisites for acting: through it secondary causes are moved to their actions; through the latter they truly act.

units.la: Praeter concursum Dei simultaneum, dari concursum praevium, qui nihil est aliud quam motio quaedam, virtutem activam creaturae complens, eam excitans, applicans, & ad agendum determinans, firmissime probari potest.
units.tr: Besides God's simultaneous concurrence, there is a prior concurrence, which is nothing other than a certain motion, completing the active power of the creature, arousing it, applying it, and determining it to act. This can be most firmly proved.

units.la: I. Quod est in potentia, non potest reduci in actum, nisi per aliquid, quod sit in actu; Sed omnis causa secunda est in potentia ad agendum, antequam agat, ergo non potest reduci ad agendum nisi per aliquid quod sit actu; Major patet, exempli gratia, quod est in potentia calidum, non fit actu calidum, nisi per aliquid quod sit actu calidum vel formaliter vel eminenter.
units.tr: I. What is in potency cannot be reduced into act except through something which is in act. But every secondary cause is in potency to act, before it acts; therefore it cannot be brought to act except through something which is actual. The major is plain: for example, what is potentially hot does not become actually hot unless through something which is actually hot, either formally or eminently.

units.la: Minor probatur ; Quodcunq; modo facit, modo non facit, modo facit unum, modo alterum, illud est in potentia ad actionem : Sed omnis causa secunda modo agit, modo non, modo agit hoc, modo illud, quod ex inductione patet, ignis enim modo agit, modo non, modo cespitem comburit, modo lignum, & sic in caeteris : Jam sic pergo.
units.tr: The minor is proved thus: whatever sometimes produces one thing and sometimes not, sometimes produces one thing, sometimes another, is in potency to action. But every secondary cause sometimes acts, sometimes does not, sometimes acts on this, sometimes on that, as is clear from induction: for fire sometimes acts and sometimes does not, sometimes burns a sod, sometimes wood, and so on in other cases. Now I proceed thus.

units.la: Omnis causa secunda debet fieri actu causa, & actu agere, per aliquid quod sit actu causa : Sed haec causa quae est actu causa, per quam creatura debet fieri actu causa, non est ulla secunda & creata, sed prima & increata, nempe solus Deus.
units.tr: Every secondary cause must be made actually a cause, and actually act, through something which is actually a cause. But this cause which is actually a cause, through which the creature must be made actually a cause, is not any secondary and created cause, but primary and uncreated, namely God alone.

units.la: Ergo solus Deus reducit omnem causam secundam de potentia agente ad actu agentem : Atqui in eo consistit concursus Dei prævius & prædeterminans, ut Deus faciat actu agere causas secundas, quæ non agunt, sed agere possunt, ut eas ad agendum moveat, excitet, applicet & determinet.
units.tr: Therefore God alone reduces every secondary cause from acting in potency to acting in act. But this is what God's prior and predetermining concurrence consists in: that God causes secondary causes, which do not act but are able to act, actually to act, so as to move, arouse, apply and determine them to act.

units.la: Quòd autem non fit alia causa actu quàm Deus, patet, quia, omnis causa secunda est causa in potentia; Ergo sola causa prima est causa actu, est enim purus imò purissimus actus.
units.tr: That no cause is actually other than God is plain, because every secondary cause is a cause in potency. Therefore only the primary cause is a cause in act; for it is pure, indeed most pure, act.

units.la: II. Inter argumenta pro concursu praevio, efficax valde est quod desumitur ab ipso concursu simultaneo. Nam Deus non potest concurrere concursu simultaneo, si non praemoveat creaturam ad agendum, nisi quis statuat aut ipsam creaturam determinare Deum, aut causam primam & secundam determinari ab alia tertia, ut eas concurrere fortuito & casu, quae omnia cum sint absurda, necessario admittenda est praedeterminatio & praemotio illa, in qua concursus hic praevius consistit.
units.tr: II. Among the arguments for prior concurrence, a very strong one is drawn from the simultaneous concurrence itself. For God cannot concur in simultaneous concurrence unless he first moves the creature to act, unless someone holds either that the creature itself determines God, or that the primary and secondary causes are determined by some third thing, so that they concur by chance and accident. Since all these are absurd, that predetermination and premotion in which this prior concurrence consists must necessarily be admitted.

units.la: III. Qui concursum Dei dicunt indifferentem & universalem, eumque faciunt determinabilem, & determinari asserunt a concursu causae secundae, illi indigentiam, potentialitatem & imperfectionem Deo attribuunt, quod Deo est indignum & injurium. Aqui Ad-versarii, &c. Ergo.
units.tr: III. Those who call God's concurrence indifferent and universal, and make it determinable, and assert that it is determined by the concurrence of the secondary cause, attribute to God indigence, potentiality and imperfection, which is unworthy of God and injurious to him. But the Adversaries, etc. Therefore.

units.la: Injuriam Deo fieri ex hac sententia manifestissimum : Deus concurrit cum voluntate nostra ut purus actus, ergo non expectat aliquem concursum voluntatis nostræ quo ejus in-differentia universalis in agendo determinetur, ut quidem volunt & loquuntur Jesuitæ.
units.tr: That this opinion does injury to God is most manifest. God concurs with our will as pure act; therefore he does not wait for some concurrence of our will by which his universal indifference in acting is determined, as indeed the Jesuits want and say.

units.la: Ratio consequentiæ est, quia, repugnat pu-rissimo actui esse determinabilem & determinari per aliud; Quod enim determinat, perfectius est determinabili & eo quod determinatur: At Deo, qui est purissimus actus nihil est perfectius, imò quia purissimus est actus, ipse omnia determinat, & a nullo determinatur, ipse omnia actuat, & a nullo actuatur.
units.tr: The reason for the consequence is that it is repugnant to purest act to be determinable and determined by another. For what determines is more perfect than what is determinable and what is determined. But nothing is more perfect than God, who is the purest act. Indeed, because he is purest act, he determines all things and is determined by none; he actuates all things and is actuated by none.

units.la: Certè, sicut summa perfectio est, a nullo determinari vel actuari, ita imperfectio quæ-dam, potentialitas, & indigentia est ab alio determinari & actuari.
units.tr: Certainly, as it is the highest perfection to be determined or actuated by none, so it is a certain imperfection, potentiality and indigence to be determined and actuated by another.

units.la: IV. Si concursus Dei indifferens esset & de-terminaretur a causa secunda, in genere causæ ef-ficientis, non solum determinaretur Dei con-cursus, sed Deus ipse, id est, non solum determi-naretur ejus actio, sed ipsemet qui est causa & principium actionis : Hoc est absurdum, ergo est illud.
units.tr: IV. If God's concurrence were indifferent and were determined by the secondary cause, in the genus of efficient cause, not only would God's concurrence be determined, but God himself, that is, not only his action would be determined, but he himself, who is the cause and principle of the action. This is absurd; therefore that hypothesis is absurd too.

units.la: Probatur major hoc modo ; prioritas inter actiones, respiciendo genus causæ efficientis, respicit ipsas actiones, quatenus formaliter egrediuntur a suis agentibus : Actio enim quâ actio, est formaliter ab agente, & per illam in materiam subjectam agens dicitur agere. Ergo prioritas inter actiones formaliter ut actiones, est prioritas quoad modum illum procedendi ab agentibus: Si igitur actio unius causæ, puta, secundæ, ex sententia Adversariorum, est prior actione alterius causæ, puta, primæ, in genere causæ efficientis, non tantum operabitur in ipsam actione, sed & in causam aqua procedit, quia non potest operari in acti-onem, nisi in quantum ea procedit ab agente, ac proin operabitur, determinando, in ipsum agens.
units.tr: The major is proved thus. Priority among actions, regarding the genus of efficient cause, concerns the actions themselves, insofar as they formally proceed from their agents. For action as action is formally from the agent, and through it the agent is said to act upon its subject matter. Therefore priority among actions formally, as actions, is priority as regards the mode of proceeding from the agents. If, then, the action of one cause, say the secondary, according to the opinion of the Adversaries, is prior to the action of another cause, say the primary, in the genus of efficient cause, it will operate not only upon the action but also upon the cause from which the action proceeds. For it cannot operate upon the action except insofar as the action proceeds from the agent, and so it will operate, by determining, upon the agent itself.

units.la: Philosophi sane omnes ordinant eodem plane modo & actiones & agentia, a quibus proveniunt actiones; & in ordine ac genere causæ efficientis, esse unam actionem priorem altera, est unum agens esse prius altero, & consequenter, unam actionem habere influxum efficienter in aliam, si sic loqui liceat, est unum agens habere influxum in aliud; Ergo si voluntas nostra suo concursu, in genere causæ effici-entis in genere causæ efficientis ita determinet concursum divinum, ut ejus concursus expe-ctet nostrum, voluntas nostra determinabit concursum divinum efficienter, per consequens, determinabit ipsam causam Deum< quod ἀπροσδιόνυσον[?].
units.tr: Indeed all philosophers order actions and the agents from which actions come in exactly the same way. In the order and genus of efficient cause, for one action to be prior to another is for one agent to be prior to another; and consequently for one action to have efficient influence on another, if I may so speak, is for one agent to have influence on another. Therefore, if our will by its concurrence so determines the divine concurrence, in the genus of efficient cause, that the divine concurrence waits for ours, our will will efficiently determine the divine concurrence, and consequently will determine the cause itself, God; which is absurd [ἀπροσδιόνυσον].

units.la: V. Præterea concursum Dei indifferentem & à causa secunda determinabilem, quo per modum causæ universalis concurrit, ita explicant ejus patroni, ut Deus concurrat tantum ad esse genericum actionis, causa secunda verò det esse specificum actioni ad quam ambæ con-currunt: Exempli gratiâ, quod homo se moveat, Deo debetur, sed quod ambulet, homini, quia De-us sit causa universalis, homo particularis; Ergo hoc pacto Deus tantum concurrit ad esse genericum ipsius actionis in quantum est motus, non ad esse specificum, in quantum est ambulatio, multò minus ad esse individuale, in quantum est ambulatio talis.
units.tr: V. Moreover, the defenders of God's indifferent concurrence, determinable by the secondary cause, by which he concurs as a universal cause, explain it thus: God concurs only to the generic being of the action, but the secondary cause gives the specific being to the action to which both concur. For example, that a man moves himself is owed to God, but that he walks is owed to the man, because God is the universal cause and man the particular. Therefore in this way God concurs only to the generic being of the action, insofar as it is motion, not to its specific being, insofar as it is walking, much less to its individual being, insofar as it is this particular walking.

units.la: At verò hoc est contra rationem; Nam sic τὸ εἶναι[?] esse specificum & individuale eximerentur, in hoc motu & quovis alio, efficientiæ & concursui divino: Unde tale potest exstrui argumentum,
units.tr: But this is against reason. For in this way being [τὸ εἶναι], specific and individual being, would be exempted, in this motion and in any other, from efficiency and divine concurrence. Whence the following argument can be constructed:

units.la: Si efficientia & concursus divinus requiritur ad id omne producendum quod habet aliquam entitatem physicam & veram; Ergo etiam efficientia & concursus divinus requiritur ad specifica-tionem & individuificationem actionum; quia
units.tr: If efficiency and divine concurrence is required for producing everything which has some physical and real entity; therefore efficiency and divine concurrence is also required for the specification and individuation of actions, because

units.la: Specificatio uti & individuificatio actionum est entitas vera & Physica:
units.tr: The specification, and likewise the individuation, of actions is a true and physical entity.

units.la: Imo à specifica ista entitate actiones omnesque res in suas classes entium dispescuntur: quare, qui dicit, Deum tantum concurrere ad actionis esse genericum, is potissimam rerum entitatem & physicam realitatem, efficientiæ, influxi, & concursui divino admit:
units.tr: Indeed, it is by this specific entity that all actions and all things are sorted into their classes of beings. Whoever says that God concurs only to the generic being of an action thereby admits that the chief entity and physical reality of things, along with efficacy, influence and divine concurrence, belongs to the creature.

units.la: Adhæc plus conferret creatura quæ speciem largiretur suæ actioni quàm Deus qui generice & indifferenter concurreret.
units.tr: Moreover, the creature that bestowed the species on its action would contribute more than God, who would concur only generically and indifferently.

units.la: Sed porro, quomodo Deus ut causa universalis poterit concurrere ad actionem in genere, quatenus est motus, & non concurrat idem ad actionem in specie, quatenus est ambulatio, cùm nemo possit ignorare quod τὸ esse genericum contineatur in τῷ esse specifico, & utrumque includatur in τῷ esse individuali. Quemadmodum itaque homo producens hominem, & hunc hominem producit in individuo, & hominem in specie, & animal in genere, & vivens & corpus, & sic porro, eundo per omnes entitatis gradus, ita & Deus concurrendo ad quamlibet actionem causæ secundæ producit actionem, & quà est ens, & quà est motus, & quà est ambulatio in specie, & quà est hæc ambulatio in individuo; Et sic utraq; causa prima & secunda ratione modi agendi est particularis, quia utraque hoc modo agit, ut ambæ omnem gradum entitatis in actione & effecto, concurrendo, attingant: Ratione vero obiecti potest causa prima dici universalis, quia ad omnia obiecta, effecta, actiones; Secunda particularis, quia ad certa obiecta, effecta, actiones, operando concurrit, & ex hac proin discriminatio & denominatio desumenda.
units.tr: But further, how can God, as universal cause, concur to an action in its genus, insofar as it is a motion, and not concur to the same action in its species, insofar as it is a walking? For no one can fail to know that the generic being is contained in the specific being, and both are included in the individual being. Just as a man who produces a man produces this particular man, both as an individual, as a man in his species, and as an animal in its genus, and as living and a body, and so on, passing through all the grades of being, so also God, by concurring to any action of a second cause, produces the action as being, as motion, as walking in its species, and as this walking in the individual. Thus both the first and the second cause are particular in their mode of acting, because each acts in such a way that by concurring they both reach every grade of being in the action and its effect. But by reason of the object the first cause may be called universal, because it concurs to all objects, effects and actions; the second is called particular, because it concurs by operating on certain objects, effects and actions, and from this the distinction and the naming are therefore to be drawn.

units.la: Atque hæc de concursu divino, materia valde utili, ardua præsertim ac sublimi, paulo fusius adduxisse visum fuit.
units.tr: I have thought it right to set out these matters concerning divine concurrence somewhat more fully, since it is a very useful subject, and especially difficult and lofty.

units.la: CAP. XXIII. De Deo colendo.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII. On the Worship of God.

units.la: HActenus de Deo cognoscendo satis fusè egimus, sequitur ut de eodem colendo paucis agamus.
units.tr: Hitherto we have treated at sufficient length of the knowing of God; it follows that we should briefly discuss the worshipping of the same God.

units.la: I. Deum esse summè & perfectissimè colendum, ex præcedentibus liquido liquidiùs liquet. Ex eo quòd Deus sit Ens non [illegible, ~5 letters] omnes essentiæ divinæ proprietates ut optimè demonstrantur, ità exinde omnes omnino cultus divini partes, modos & gradus ob ocu-los Ios[?] ponere haud quaquam difficile erit.
units.tr: I. That God is to be worshipped most highly and most perfectly is made clearer than clear from what has gone before. Since God is a Being [illegible], and all the properties of the divine essence are most excellently demonstrated, it will be by no means difficult to set before our eyes from these all the parts, modes and degrees of the divine worship.

units.la: II. Hinc itaque tum Pietatem, tum Honesta-tem, tum Charitatem ac Iustitiam, elicies quam optime.
units.tr: II. Hence you will be able to derive, most excellently, piety, honesty, charity and justice.

units.la: III. Pietas est qua Deus omni omnino affectu & effectu, ut summum ens independens, simplicissimum, perfectissimum, infinitum & immutabile, colitur.
units.tr: III. Piety is that by which God is worshipped with every affection and every effect, as the supreme, independent, most simple, most perfect, infinite and unchangeable Being.

units.la: Hic haud obscure docebis
units.tr: Here you will teach, not obscurely:

units.la: 1. Fidem, spem, fiduciam in Deum & eius infinitas proprietates.
units.tr: 1. Faith, hope and trust in God and his infinite properties.

units.la: 2. Charitatem, sive summum Dei amorem & gratiarum actionem.
units.tr: 2. Charity, that is, the highest love of God, and thanksgiving.

units.la: 3. Summae illius Majestatis timorem & re-verentiam & coram ipsa humilitatem.
units.tr: 3. Fear and reverence of that supreme Majesty, and humility before him.

units.la: 4. Ejus per totam vitam humanam in omnibus cogitatis, dictis & factis glorificati-onem & laudem.
units.tr: 4. Glorifying and praising him throughout the whole of human life, in all thoughts, words and deeds.

units.la: IV. Honestas est qua mores nostros con-gruere[?] recteq; componimus.
units.tr: IV. Honesty is that by which we fashion and rightly order our manners so that they agree.

units.la: V. Charitas est qua amicabili affectu erga proximos, debito modo, ferimur[?].
units.tr: V. Charity is that by which, with a friendly affection, we are carried toward our neighbours in the due manner.

units.la: VI. Iustitia est qua unicuique tribuimus quod suum est.
units.tr: VI. Justice is that by which we render to each person what is his own.

units.la: CAP XXIV. De Beatitudine Hominis.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIV. On the Blessedness of Man.

units.la: Hactenus de Deo cognoscendo & colendo, sequitur de hominis beatitudine.
units.tr: Thus far concerning God, to be known and to be worshipped; there follows concerning the blessedness of man.

units.la: I. Hominis beatitudo est summum ipsius bonum, quo liberatas ab omni miseria omnia omnino bona, naturæ suæ congrua plenissime possidet.
units.tr: I. The blessedness of man is his highest good, by which he fully possesses, freed from all misery, all goods wholly fitting to his nature.

units.la: Hominis beatitudinem, & ad illam aliquod perfectissimum dari medium, lumen naturale rectæ rationis, ex præcedentibus haud difficulter demonstrat ac commonstrat: Et certe universum genus humanum frustra non est conditum, nullumq; hominem attingere perfectionem naturæ debitam divinæ perfectioni omnino repugnat.
units.tr: From the foregoing, the natural light of right reason readily demonstrates and makes clear that there is a most perfect means given to man's blessedness and to that end. And surely the whole human race has not been created in vain, and it is entirely contrary to the divine perfection that any man should fail to attain the perfection due to his nature.

units.la: Atque hæc de Theosophia nostra impræsentiarum sufficiant, Deum Ter Optimum Maximum supplicibus votis veneramur, ut lumen nostrum, virtute suâ, magis magisq; accendat & perficiat, quo ipsum perfecte cognoscentes congrue colere valeamus, ad ipsius gloriam & summum nostrum bonum, Amen,
units.tr: And let these things concerning our Theosophy suffice for the present. We venerate God, Best and Greatest, with suppliant prayers, that he may kindle and perfect our light more and more by his own power, so that knowing him perfectly we may be able to worship him fittingly, to his glory and our highest good. Amen.
